We ask a different, dynamic question: while an LLM reasons through an ambiguous problem, does it keep the competing interpretations alive in parallel, or does it silently collapse to one branch too early, then reason confidently down it? We hypothesize premature disambiguation: the model commits to a single reading before it has the evidence to select one, and this collapse is a proximal cause of confidently-wrong answers on ambiguity-sensitive tasks. We define a per-step interpretation-branch signal read from hidden states and test three claims. First, branch collapse is real and premature: the number of live interpretation branches drops sharply early in reasoning, often before any disambiguating cue appears. Second, the branch signal is diagnostic: how early and how completely the model collapses predicts final-answer errors on genuinely ambiguous items, beyond confidence and entropy. Third, it is causally fixable: inducing the model to keep multiple branches alive (via a branch-maintenance intervention and by steering a located branch-diversity direction) improves correctness and reduces confidently-wrong answers relative to no-intervention, abstention prompting, and 'consider alternatives' prompting. We evaluate on lexical, syntactic, and scope-ambiguity reasoning across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where an ambiguous symptom description silently collapses to one diagnosis. Our work reframes ambiguity handling as parallel-hypothesis maintenance and offers an interpretable failure signal and a training-free intervention. We name a single primary application (general reasoning reliability) and treat the clinical vignette as a bounded high-stakes instance rather than a parallel aim. We pre-register the operational definition of collapse and run sensitivity analyses over the number of sampled continuations, the clustering method, the entropy threshold, and the decoding strategy. A distinct, reusable contribution is a controlled late-disambiguation benchmark (cue placed at a known late position, with a labeled premature-commit lure and a matched unambiguous control) plus a naturally-occurring-ambiguity subset, so the setting itself is reusable. If confirmed, downstream practice shifts from ambiguity DETECTION/abstention toward monitoring branch-collapse and applying branch-maintenance prompting or decoding; a strong null (models collapse only after cues) is itself informative, showing LLM ambiguity handling is well-calibrated.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). A "live interpretation branch" is a distinct reading the model is still pursuing; "premature disambiguation" means collapse to one branch before any disambiguating cue appears.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Branch collapse is real and occurs before disambiguating evidence): Tests whether the number of live interpretation branches drops early, before the resolving cue. Data: an ambiguity-reasoning battery of 250 items per type where the ambiguity is decision-relevant -- (a) lexical ambiguity (a key word has two answer-changing senses), (b) syntactic/attachment ambiguity (PP-attachment, coordination scope), (c) quantifier/scope ambiguity -- 750 ambiguous items plus 250 matched unambiguous controls (one reading only) for selectivity, adapted where possible from AmbiEnt/AmbAdv-style ambiguity datasets and templated construction; each ambiguous item places its disambiguating cue at a known late position and carries a labeled correct behavior (hedge when unresolvable, single reading when a later cue resolves it) and a premature-commit lure (the answer if the model locks onto the more frequent reading early). 250/type is the smallest sample giving stable collapse-position estimates under sampling-based branch counting within budget. Branch signal: at each step we sample N=10 continuations (temperature 0.7), cluster them by which interpretation they pursue (embedding + manual-validated rubric), giving a per-step live-branch count / interpretation entropy. Decisive metric first: the gap between collapse position (first step where a single branch dominates, entropy below threshold) and the resolving-cue position, on ambiguous items; secondary: whether collapse is toward the higher-frequency reading, versus unambiguous controls that should start single-branch. Convincing result: mean collapse position precedes the cue position by a reliable margin on ambiguous items (CI on the difference excludes 0 and is directional), collapse is biased toward the frequent reading, and unambiguous controls show no premature multi-branch collapse. Indecision band: a collapse-minus-cue position difference whose CI overlaps 0 (within about +/-0.5 steps) means we cannot show prematurity. Negative result: collapse at or after the cue means the model resolves only on evidence -- well-calibrated, not premature -- refuting H1.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- A locatable branch signal, cross-validated behaviorally and representationally): Tests that branch diversity is readable from hidden states. Data: the same battery, split 70/30 by item. A linear probe (only probe trainable) on per-step hidden states decodes which interpretation(s) are active and estimates a branch-diversity score (per-layer held-out AUROC), validated against the sampling-based branch proxy from Experiment 1. Decisive metric first: held-out probe AUROC for the active-interpretation set; secondary: rank correlation between probe branch-diversity and the sampling branch count. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.70 and Spearman rho >= 0.4 agreement with the behavioral proxy (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: AUROC 0.55-0.65 or agreement rho 0.2-0.35 means the cheap probe cannot stand in for the behavioral measure. Negative result: chance AUROC means no locatable branch signal, and later steering (Experiment 5) is uninterpretable.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Earliness/completeness of collapse is diagnostic of error beyond confidence and entropy): Tests whether collapse predicts final error. Data: the same items. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC for final-answer error predicted from collapse earliness and completeness; secondary: delta-AUROC over verbalized confidence, token entropy, and a semantic-uncertainty baseline. Convincing result: collapse-based AUROC >= 0.65 exceeding the best baseline by >= 0.05 (CI excludes 0), specifically predicting confidently-wrong answers. Indecision band: delta-AUROC over baselines within +/-0.03 means collapse adds no diagnostic value. Negative result: AUROC ~ 0.5 refutes H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Branch-maintenance improves correctness and reduces confidently-wrong answers): Tests the behavioral intervention. Data: the 750 ambiguous items plus 250 unambiguous controls. Systems: no-intervention; abstention/clarify prompting (prior framing); generic "consider alternative interpretations" prompting; and structured Branch-Maintenance (enumerate both readings and carry them in parallel until a resolving cue, then commit); a length-matched control equalizes tokens with the generic-alternatives arm. Decisive metric first: task correctness on ambiguous items, primary contrast Branch-Maintenance minus generic-alternatives; secondary: confidently-wrong rate, appropriate-hedge rate on truly-unresolvable items, and cost on unambiguous controls. Convincing result: Branch-Maintenance beats generic-alternatives and abstention prompting by >= 3 points correctness on ambiguous items (CI excludes 0), especially on premature-lure-prone items, lowers confidently-wrong rate, and costs <= 2 points on unambiguous controls. Indecision band: within +/-2 points of the generic-alternatives arm means parallel maintenance adds nothing beyond extra deliberation. Negative result: no gain over "consider alternatives" refutes H3's intervention claim.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- Steering a branch-diversity direction causally delays collapse): Tests the mechanism. Data: matched multi-branch-minus-collapsed-branch step contrasts yield a difference-in-means "branch-diversity" direction at the best probe layer. Systems: plus-direction steering (delay collapse), minus-direction (force early collapse), random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: change in premature-lure error rate under plus-direction versus random-direction steering; secondary: minus-direction induced error, dose-response, whether per-item branch-diversity increase mediates the correctness gain (Spearman), and specificity (unambiguous-item accuracy within 1 point, fluency preserved). Convincing result: plus-direction steering reduces premature-lure errors by >= 3 points over random-direction (CI excludes 0) with monotonic dose-response and preserved unambiguous accuracy, minus-direction increases them, and branch-diversity change mediates correctness. Indecision band: effects within +/-2 points of random-direction leave the direction unproven; the behavioral Experiment 4 then stands alone. Negative result: no steerable effect means branch diversity is not a causal lever.

Experiment 6 (H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests premature collapse to the common diagnosis. Data: 300 clinical vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) and constructed cases where an ambiguous symptom description supports two plausible diagnoses until a later detail resolves it; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Systems: no-intervention, Branch-Maintenance, and branch-diversity plus-direction steering. Decisive metric first: confident-misdiagnosis rate on resolve-late cases under no-intervention versus the two mitigations; secondary: overall diagnostic accuracy. Convincing result: the model prematurely collapses to the common diagnosis at baseline and both mitigations cut confident misdiagnosis by >= 5 points (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: mitigation effects within +/-2 points are inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no baseline premature collapse or no mitigation effect bounds the claim to benign tasks.

Experiment 7 (Construct validity, matched-uncertainty controls, and natural ambiguity): We validate the sampling-based branch proxy with human annotation of a stratified subset of sampled continuations and, additionally, on synthetic items whose true branch set is formally known by construction. To separate branch maintenance from generic uncertainty/verbosity/token expansion, the Branch-Maintenance intervention is compared not only to length-matched 'consider alternatives' but to a matched-UNCERTAINTY control (equal entropy raised by a neutral means). We test whether the hidden-state branch-diversity probe predicts error BEFORE any observable output divergence (probe at the pre-collapse step, evaluate against the eventual divergence point). For steering (Experiment 5) we state the layer-selection rationale (best held-out probe layer), intervention locality, and add a generic entropy-raising / random-residual-perturbation control. Finally we add a naturally-occurring ambiguous-query subset (non-templated user questions with genuine multiple readings) to show robustness beyond constructed late-cue items.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The behavioral branch proxy via sampling is expensive and noisy; we mitigate with moderate N, clustering validation, and cross-checking against the cheaper representational probe. (2) 'Premature' requires distinguishing collapse-before-cue from legitimate early resolution; we control this by placing the disambiguating cue at a known late position and comparing collapse position to cue position, and by using truly-unresolvable items where no early commitment is warranted. (3) Instruction-tuned models may already hedge or abstain heavily, muting collapse; we include base variants, calibrate item difficulty, and measure the confidently-wrong rate specifically. (4) Branch-Maintenance prompting could help simply by adding tokens/deliberation; the 'consider alternatives' and length-matched controls isolate genuine parallel-maintenance from mere extra thinking. (5) The branch-diversity direction may entangle with generic uncertainty rather than interpretation multiplicity; mitigated by matched multi- vs single-branch contrasts, random-direction steering, unambiguous-control specificity, and comparison to the existing ambiguity/verbal-uncertainty linear features. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (models keep branches alive or collapse only after cues) is itself informative, showing LLM ambiguity handling is well-calibrated rather than prematurely committing. (8) The parallel-hypothesis framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not a claim of human-like processing.

Name: information_burst_reasoning
Title: Bits Per Step: Do Information-Density Bursts Cause LLM Reasoning Failures, and Can Pacing Them Fix It?
Short Hypothesis: LLM reasoning failures are causally linked to information-density bursts — individual reasoning steps that try to transmit too many bits at once (violating local Uniform Information Density) — rather than merely being correlated with them; a locatable internal 'information-pacing' signal governs how many bits a step emits, and causally reducing bursts at high-risk steps (by inducing the model to decompose them into more, lower-density steps) improves reasoning more than length-matched extra computation. We hold a strict claim hierarchy: the PRIMARY claim is causality (bursts cause failure), the internal information-pacing locus is SECONDARY, and steering the pacing signal is TERTIARY; the proposal stands on the causal claim even if the locus or steering claims are weak.
Related Work: The Uniform Information Density (UID) hypothesis (Jaeger 2008; Genzel & Charniak 2001) posits humans pace information evenly. Recent LLM work (Gwak, Son & Kim, ACL 2025; 'Revisiting UID in LLM Reasoning Traces', 2025) computes entropy-based stepwise information-density metrics and finds a robust pattern: correct reasoning is locally uniform (smooth step-to-step transitions) but globally non-uniform, and that information-density spikes/bursts predict incorrect traces — they use this as a trace-SELECTION signal (reranking many samples). Entropy-rate work (Revisiting Entropy Rate Constancy, 2023; Constant Conditional Entropy, 2013) studies text-level uniformity but not reasoning. Crucially, ALL existing LLM-UID work is (1) purely correlational — it selects among traces the model already produced but never intervenes to change pacing, (2) treats information density as a passive readout with no internal locus, and (3) offers no causal test that bursts CAUSE failure rather than co-occur with hard steps. My prior proposals covered linguistic relativity, cognitive-analogy transfers, tokenization granularity, and difficulty-gated language-agnostic steering — none address information-density pacing, bursts, or a bits-per-step controller. We uniquely (a) causally test whether an induced information burst at a step degrades reasoning and whether burst-reduction repairs it, (b) locate an internal information-pacing signal, and (c) turn UID from a reranking heuristic into a training-free, single-pass pacing intervention, with a high-stakes clinical instance. Closest baseline family, delta in one sentence: Gwak, Son & Kim (ACL 2025) and 'Revisiting UID in LLM Reasoning Traces' (2025) use stepwise information density as a PASSIVE trace-SELECTION signal that reranks many sampled traces, whereas we convert that same signal into a single-pass CAUSAL intervention with an internal locus and a steerable controller. What would be genuinely new if true: that bursts CAUSE rather than merely flag failure and that single-pass pacing beats cost-matched reranking; if instead the causal (Experiment 1) and placement (Experiment 3) contrasts fall in the indecision band, we would have shown only a stronger version of UID reranking, and we say so explicitly.
Abstract: A striking recent finding is that an LLM's step-by-step reasoning is locally smooth but globally uneven in information density, and that sharp information-density bursts — steps that pack many bits into few tokens — reliably flag incorrect reasoning. Existing work exploits this only correlationally, as a signal for reranking many sampled traces. We ask the causal question: do information bursts CAUSE reasoning failures, and can pacing them fix reasoning in a single pass? We propose that each reasoning step has a controllable information budget, that overloading a step (a burst) is a proximal cause of downstream errors, and that an LLM carries a locatable internal 'information-pacing' signal governing how many bits it commits per step. We test three claims. First, bursts are causal, not incidental: experimentally inducing a burst (forcing the model to compress a multi-inference step into one dense token span) raises error rates beyond matched-difficulty controls, and correct traces avoid bursts at genuinely hard steps. Second, pacing is a locatable internal quantity: a probe reads a step's committed information load from hidden states before the step completes, predicting impending bursts and errors. Third, pacing is a steerable, useful lever: at high-risk (predicted-burst) steps only, we causally reduce density by inducing decomposition into more, lower-density steps, and show this Burst-Aware Pacing improves accuracy more than length-matched extra reasoning, blanket 'think more' prompting, or random-step decomposition. We evaluate on math, logic, and multi-hop QA across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical-reasoning instance where a single overloaded inference step silently produces a wrong diagnosis. Our work reframes information density from a passive reranking signal into a causal, controllable resource for machine reasoning. We report the contributions as a strict hierarchy (primary: causality, Experiment 1; secondary: internal locus, Experiment 2; tertiary: steering, Experiment 5) and do not overclaim them equally. Beyond accuracy we add application-facing metrics: calibration (expected calibration error) and, in the clinical instance, confident-error severity, because the concrete payoff is a training-free, single-pass inference-time knob. If bursts are causal, inference-time prompting, best-of-N reranking, and safety monitoring should pace or flag high-density steps rather than blanket 'think more'; if bursts are non-causal, the field should abandon burst-based control and treat UID strictly as a passive reranking correlate.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights (logistic or ridge regression on frozen hidden states). Decoding is greedy for the primary condition and temperature 0.7 for any sampled condition, each sampled/steered run repeated over seeds 0, 1, 2. All effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) over 1000 item-level resamples, and behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts for model and item, written (1|model)+(1|item). Reasoning traces are segmented into steps at sentence/newline boundaries; per-step information density is mean token surprisal under the generating model plus a bits-per-inference measure normalized by content tokens, following the stepwise Uniform-Information-Density metrics of Gwak et al. 2025; a burst is a step whose density exceeds that item's within-trace running-median density by more than 1.5 standard deviations.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Bursts causally degrade reasoning rather than merely co-occurring with hard steps): Tests whether a forced information-density burst at a step raises error beyond what step difficulty alone predicts. Data: 500 items sampled from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), 500 from the MATH test split (5,000 available) stratified across difficulty levels 1-5, 400 synthetic deductive-logic chains we construct (modus-ponens chaining templates, branching depth 2-6, answers auto-checkable), and 400 questions sampled from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), 1,800 items total; these sizes give a few hundred items per task for stable step-level mixed-effects estimates across five models while staying within a single-GPU-week budget. On items each model first solves correctly under free reasoning, four systems are compared: (i) free baseline; (ii) burst-injection -- re-prompt with a structural constraint forcing one target multi-inference step to be compressed into a single dense token span, total reasoning content held constant; (iii) length-matched control -- add equal token count elsewhere without compressing the target step; (iv) decomposition control -- expand the same step into more, lower-density steps. Decisive metric first: final-answer accuracy of burst-injection minus the length-matched control at genuinely hard steps (top difficulty tercile), from mixed-effects logistic regression accuracy ~ condition * step_difficulty + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary metric: error-localization rate (fraction of induced errors whose first wrong step is the injected step or its direct consequence). Convincing result: burst-injection is at least 5 percentage points below the length-matched control with a CI excluding 0, at least 60% of induced errors localize to the injected step, and the decomposition control sits at or above free baseline. Indecision band: a burst-minus-length-matched gap within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) is uninformative -- compression is not separable from added content at our power, and we report that rather than a causal claim. Negative result: if burst-injection does not fall below the length-matched control (gap <= 0), bursts are not a distinct causal factor beyond difficulty and length, and H1's causal claim collapses to the prior correlational finding; only injection-compliant trials (verified content preservation) are analyzed.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- A locatable pre-emission information-pacing signal): Tests whether hidden states at a step boundary, before the step's content is emitted, encode the impending step's information load. Data: reuse the traces from Experiment 1, split 70/30 by item into probe-train and held-out sets. At each step-boundary position we extract residual-stream activations at every layer and train (only the probe is trainable) a ridge regressor to predict the impending step's density and a logistic probe to predict whether it will be a burst, reporting per-layer held-out AUROC and R-squared; baselines are boundary token-entropy, post-hoc per-step surprisal, and verbalized confidence elicited from the model. Decisive metric first: held-out burst-prediction AUROC from pre-step hidden states; secondary: Spearman correlation between an item's mean pre-step burst probability and final-answer error. Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.70 on held-out items, exceeding the best baseline by >= 0.05, with pre-step burst probability predicting item error at Spearman rho >= 0.2 (CI excludes 0). Indecision band: AUROC in 0.55-0.65 is a weak signal we cannot separate from generic entropy, and we would decline to claim a dedicated pacing readout. Negative result: AUROC ~ 0.5 or no gain over the entropy baseline means no locatable pre-emission pacing signal exists, refuting H2 and leaving pacing a post-hoc description.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Burst-Aware Pacing beats length-matched extra computation): Tests whether reducing density only at predicted-burst steps improves accuracy more than simply computing more. Data: the same 1,800 items. Five single-pass systems at matched token budgets: no-intervention; blanket "think step by step / think more" prompting; random-step decomposition (matched number of interventions and tokens); a Uniform-Information-Density reranking baseline (Gwak et al. 2025, cost-matched to the same token budget); and Burst-Aware Pacing -- flag high-risk steps online with the Experiment-2 pre-step probe (or a surprisal-threshold proxy) and inject a decomposition instruction only at flagged steps. Decisive metric first: accuracy at matched token budget, reported as an accuracy-versus-token-cost curve, with the primary contrast Burst-Aware Pacing minus random-step decomposition; secondary: accuracy versus blanket prompting and versus reranking at equal cost. Convincing result: Burst-Aware Pacing matches or exceeds blanket prompting and reranking at equal or lower token cost and beats random-step decomposition by >= 3 points (CI excludes 0), showing that where you pace matters, not merely that you pace. Indecision band: Burst-Aware Pacing within +/-2 points of random-step decomposition means placement is not demonstrably load-bearing though pacing may still help. Negative result: no gain over no-intervention, or a deficit versus blanket prompting at equal cost, refutes H3's usefulness claim.

Experiment 4 (H1 and H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests whether a single overloaded clinical inference step silently causes misdiagnosis and whether Burst-Aware Pacing mitigates it. Data: 300 differential-diagnosis vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) fine-distinction items plus constructed vignettes in which multiple clinical inferences can be compressed into one dense assertion; we use 300 because expert spot-checking of ground truth is costly and 300 supports the paired burst/pace contrasts. Systems: free baseline, burst-injection at the pivotal clinical step, and Burst-Aware Pacing. Decisive metric first: confident-misdiagnosis rate (wrong diagnosis emitted with high stated confidence); secondary: overall diagnostic accuracy. Convincing result: burst-injection raises confident misdiagnosis and Burst-Aware Pacing lowers it by >= 5 points on fine-distinction cases (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: a pacing effect within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no movement means the pacing lever does not transfer to high-stakes reasoning, bounding the claim to benign benchmarks.

Experiment 5 (H2 and H3 -- Causal pacing-direction steering, mechanistic depth): Tests whether directly lowering the internal pacing signal reproduces the Burst-Aware Pacing benefit without any decomposition prompt. Data: the 1,800 items from Experiment 1. We derive a difference-in-means "pacing" direction from high-density-minus-low-density step-boundary activation contrasts (matched content) at the best probe layer, then steer minus-direction at flagged steps; controls are random-direction steering of matched norm and no-steer. Decisive metric first: accuracy gain of minus-direction steering over random-direction steering, with a dose-response sweep over steering magnitude; secondary: specificity (accuracy change on easy items, which must stay within 1 point, and fluency by perplexity). Convincing result: a monotonic dose-response and a >= 3-point accuracy gain over random-direction steering with preserved easy-item accuracy. Indecision band: a gain within +/-2 points of random-direction steering leaves the direction unproven, in which case the prompt-based Burst-Aware Pacing and the burst-injection causal result stand independently. Negative result: no benefit from a clean direction, or benefit indistinguishable from random steering, means the internal pacing quantity is not a usable causal lever even if it is readable.

Experiment 6 (Pre-registered identification and robustness ablations): We pre-register the causal identification strategy before running: the decisive contrast is burst-injection minus the length-matched control at genuinely hard steps, with a semantic-preservation check (content-preservation verified by entailment both ways plus exact preservation of required operations) as an inclusion gate. We report the exact fraction of burst-injection trials excluded for non-compliance and run a sensitivity analysis that re-includes excluded trials under worst-case labels to bound selection bias. Ablations: (a) burst threshold swept over 1.0/1.5/2.0 within-trace SD and a median-absolute-deviation variant; (b) segmentation over sentence, newline, and clause boundaries; (c) alternative density definitions (mean token surprisal, bits-per-inference normalized by content tokens, and a local entropy-rate estimate). For the Experiment-2 probe we add explicit controls regressing out step difficulty, verbalized confidence, and step length, report probe calibration (ECE), and test cross-task and held-out-model (out-of-distribution) generalization of the burst probe. Convincing result: the sign and rough magnitude of the causal and diagnostic effects are stable across thresholds, segmentations, and density definitions, and the probe retains its edge after difficulty/confidence/length controls and under OOD transfer.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Surprisal-based information density is model-internal and confounded with step difficulty — hard steps are naturally denser; mitigated by matched-difficulty controls, by testing the burst-injection vs length-matched vs decomposition CONTROLS (isolating compression from content/length), and by error-localization checks that show the injected step specifically drives failure. (2) Burst injection via prompting may be non-compliant or change content, not just density; we verify compliance, hold reasoning content constant, and analyze only compliant trials. (3) The pacing probe may capture generic difficulty/confidence rather than a genuine bits-per-step controller; mitigated by held-out validation, comparison to confidence/entropy baselines, the pre-step (before-emission) prediction requirement, and random-direction steering controls. (4) BAP's decomposition prompt could help simply by adding tokens/'thinking time'; the random-step-decomposition and cost-matched reranking baselines isolate the value of WHERE pacing is applied. (5) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (6) Global-non-uniformity findings (Gwak et al.) suggest LLM reasoning legitimately needs some bursts; our claim is specifically about bursts at HARD/pivotal steps, and a null result (bursts are benign or even helpful) would itself be informative, refining when UID applies to machine reasoning. (7) The optional steering variant depends on a clean pacing direction; if unavailable, the prompt-based BAP and the causal burst-injection results stand independently. (8) The UID framing is operationalized information-theoretically and behaviorally, not as a claim of human-like production planning. (9) Negative-result value: a clean null (bursts non-causal, or pacing no better than length-matched compute) is decision-relevant, not a failed study -- it would tell the community to stop pursuing burst/UID-based test-time control knobs and to treat information density strictly as a passive reranking correlate.

Name: acquisition_prerequisite_gating
Title: Skill Tree, Not Timeline: Does an Earlier-Acquired Linguistic Capability Causally Gate the Emergence of a Later One?
Short Hypothesis: The developmental order in which LLMs acquire linguistic capabilities (e.g., part-of-speech/morphology -> syntax -> semantic composition -> discourse) is not a mere timeline but a causal prerequisite chain: selectively delaying or degrading a model's acquisition of an earlier capability during training causally prevents or slows the emergence of the later capability that normally builds on it, even when abundant data for the later capability is present, whereas degrading a non-prerequisite (parallel) capability leaves it unaffected. We prioritize two to three well-separated, theoretically-motivated edges (morphology->syntax, syntax->semantic composition) as primary claims and treat discourse as exploratory.
Related Work: A large literature establishes that LLMs acquire linguistic structure in a consistent DEVELOPMENTAL ORDER that qualitatively mirrors children: phonemic->lexical->syntactic emergence (Emergence of Phonemic/Syntactic/Semantic Representations, 2026), POS-first (LMs Learn POS First, 2018), consistent one-dimensional grammar-learning trajectories across seeds/architectures (Grammar-Learning Trajectories, 2021), chronological probing showing discourse last (Is neural language acquisition similar to natural?, 2022), n-gram-then-refinement dynamics (N-Gram Learning, 2025), a window of maximal cognitive-developmental alignment (Development of Cognitive Intelligence in PLMs, 2024), and age-ordered curriculum effects on semantic learning (Order matters, 2018/2019). CRUCIALLY, all of this is DESCRIPTIVE and CORRELATIONAL: it characterizes WHEN capabilities emerge and in what order, but never tests whether the order reflects a CAUSAL DEPENDENCY. No prior work asks whether an earlier capability is a functional PREREQUISITE whose disruption causally blocks a later one, nor uses targeted training-data ablation to sever a specific rung of the ladder and observe downstream failure with prerequisite-vs-parallel specificity controls. We uniquely convert the observed acquisition timeline into a testable causal skill-tree via a Formation-Tracing + Causal-Intervention strategy (data-ablation re-training + checkpoint probing), distinguishing genuine prerequisite gating from co-occurrence. Novelty locus: the contribution is threefold and methodological — cross-capability causal-graph discovery (not intervention on a single construction), edge-specific rescue/reversibility, and a demonstration that the causal skill tree is strictly SPARSER than the temporal order — which is what distinguishes genuine prerequisite gating from co-occurrence. It differs from prior single-construction causal-intervention work (which perturbs one phenomenon inside an already-trained model) by manipulating acquisition itself during from-scratch training, with matched non-prerequisite and generic-slowdown baselines. Communities that would cite it include developmental and mechanistic interpretability, curriculum learning, and data curation.
Abstract: Language models acquire linguistic capabilities in a strikingly consistent developmental order that echoes child development: coarse lexical/part-of-speech knowledge first, then syntax, then semantic composition, then discourse. Existing work treats this order as a descriptive timeline. We ask a causal question: is the order a prerequisite chain? That is, does mastering an earlier capability causally enable the emergence of the later capability that builds on it, such that disrupting the earlier rung blocks the later one even when its own training signal is abundant? We test this by training small language models from scratch under controlled interventions that selectively delay or degrade the acquisition of one target capability (e.g., syntactic hierarchy) via surgical training-data ablation or curriculum manipulation, while holding total data and the later capability's signal fixed. We then probe, across training checkpoints, whether a downstream capability (e.g., semantic composition, discourse coherence) still emerges on schedule. Our central prediction is a prerequisite-specificity dissociation: disrupting a genuine prerequisite delays or prevents the downstream capability, whereas disrupting a matched non-prerequisite (parallel) capability of equal difficulty leaves the downstream capability intact. We further predict the intervention shifts the downstream capability's emergence checkpoint and lowers its ceiling in proportion to prerequisite degradation (dose-response). We characterize the resulting empirical skill tree, quantify per-edge gating strength, and test whether a late 'remedial' injection of the prerequisite can rescue the stalled downstream capability. Across several from-scratch model configurations and seeds, we convert the well-documented acquisition timeline into a causal dependency graph, revealing whether language capabilities in LLMs are a skill tree rather than a mere schedule. A simpler rival account — that any targeted degradation slows training generally or lowers data quality — is controlled by matched non-prerequisite ablations, random-token-corruption matched for signal loss, and matched perplexity/loss trajectories. If gating is confirmed, practitioners could reorder curricula, filter or augment data toward prerequisite skills, and target remediation at a blocked rung; a translational check tests whether such skill-tree-informed ordering improves sample efficiency versus standard training. If null — order is a data-statistics schedule, not a causal tree — that equally revises the developmental analogy and indicates prerequisite-targeted intervention is not worthwhile.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup for H1 - Baseline acquisition order and emergence checkpoints): Establishes the reference developmental ladder and per-capability emergence checkpoints that all interventions are measured against. Data (training): a ~100M-word corpus mixing child-directed speech (the CHILDES/BabyLM strict-small 100M-word set, used as is) with Simple Wikipedia; this size is affordable for an academic lab and prior child-directed-speech work shows it suffices for the target capabilities. Data (evaluation probes, existing sets used as is): (a) lexical/POS + morphology - POS/agreement probing plus BLiMP morphology subsets (BLiMP has 67 paradigms x 1,000 pairs); (b) syntactic hierarchy - BLiMP/Zorro structural minimal pairs plus a hierarchical-generalization test on question-formation/passivization; (c) semantic composition - compositional-entailment / predicate-argument probes (adapted from existing NLI minimal pairs); (d) discourse - coreference and discourse-connective cloze. Models (trained from scratch, all weights trainable): small GPT-2-style transformers at ~10M, ~30M, ~100M parameters, depth-varied, 3-5 seeds each (seeds 0-4); dense checkpointing every ~2M tokens. Decisive metric: the ordered sequence of per-capability emergence checkpoints (first checkpoint where a probe reliably exceeds its chance/threshold band) and its cross-seed consistency (Kendall's tau across seeds). Convincing result: baselines reproduce the standard order (POS/morphology -> syntax -> composition -> discourse) with cross-seed rank consistency tau >=0.8, giving well-separated emergence checkpoints to serve as the causal baseline. Indecision band: tau 0.5-0.8 or overlapping (poorly separated) emergence windows for adjacent rungs - order is noisy and later causal edges on those rungs will be underpowered; we add seeds and denser checkpoints. Negative result (for setup): tau <0.5 or no stable order - the developmental ladder is not reliably present at this scale, so the causal test is deferred to the well-separated rungs only (POS/morphology -> syntax -> basic composition).

Experiment 2 (H1 - Severing a prerequisite blocks the downstream capability): Tests the core causal claim that degrading an earlier capability's learnable signal delays or lowers a later capability that builds on it, even with the later capability's own signal preserved. Data (training, constructed by ablation): matched corpora that selectively DEGRADE one target capability while preserving others and total token count - e.g., to degrade syntactic hierarchy, apply clause-local word-order scrambling that destroys hierarchical cues but preserves lexical co-occurrence and morphology; to degrade morphology, lemmatize/strip inflection; to degrade discourse, shuffle sentence order across documents. Each ablation passes a manipulation check (its target probe drops) while the downstream capability's own input cues are verified intact via probes. Models/protocol: retrain the same from-scratch transformers (all weights trainable, 3-5 seeds) on each single-capability-degraded corpus; probe every ~2M tokens. Decisive metric: the downstream capability's emergence-checkpoint shift and asymptotic ceiling versus baseline, modeled as downstream_probe ~ intervention*checkpoint + (1|seed). Convincing result: degrading a genuine prerequisite (e.g., syntax) delays the downstream capability's (e.g., composition) emergence checkpoint by >=25% of its baseline emergence step (CI across seeds excluding 0) AND lowers its asymptotic ceiling by >=5 pp probe accuracy, beyond what its preserved own-signal predicts. Indecision band: a 10-25% checkpoint delay or a 2-5 pp ceiling drop - a directional block that is not decisive. Negative result: <10% delay and <2 pp ceiling drop - degrading the prerequisite does not gate the downstream capability, evidence that the acquisition order is a data-statistics schedule, not a causal skill tree.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Prerequisite-vs-parallel specificity dissociation): The key control ruling out generic training disruption or lost tokens. Data (training, constructed): degrade a matched NON-PREREQUISITE / parallel capability of comparable probe difficulty and token footprint, plus a random-token-corruption corpus matched for total signal loss. Models/protocol: as Experiment 2, same seeds. Decisive metric: the downstream capability's checkpoint/ceiling change under the parallel-capability (and random-corruption) ablation, contrasted with the prerequisite ablation. Convincing result: the downstream capability is spared under the parallel-capability and random-corruption ablations (checkpoint shift <10% and ceiling drop <2 pp), while the prerequisite ablation from Experiment 2 shows the full effect - a clean prerequisite-specific dissociation. Indecision band: the parallel/random ablations cause a partial downstream effect (10-25% of the prerequisite effect) - the block is only partly prerequisite-specific. Negative result: parallel-capability and random-corruption ablations harm the downstream capability as much as the prerequisite ablation - the effect is generic disruption / lost signal, not prerequisite gating.

Experiment 4 (H1 - Dose-response): Tests that downstream disruption scales with how much the prerequisite is degraded. Data (training, constructed): graded degradation of the prerequisite (25/50/75/100% of its cues scrambled), total tokens fixed. Models/protocol: as above, same seeds. Decisive metric: the monotonic relation between prerequisite-degradation level and downstream emergence-delay / ceiling-drop (slope across the four levels). Convincing result: emergence-delay and ceiling-drop increase monotonically with degradation level (slope CI excluding 0), strengthening the causal reading. Indecision band: a non-monotonic or shallow trend (slope CI grazing 0) - dosage relation unclear. Negative result: no dose-response (flat across levels) - the block, if any, is threshold-like or artifactual rather than a graded prerequisite dependency.

Experiment 5 (H1 - Remedial rescue / reversibility): Tests whether restoring the prerequisite signal later lets the stalled downstream capability emerge, quantifying reversibility. Data/protocol: train under prerequisite degradation up to a fixed checkpoint, then switch to clean data restoring the prerequisite; continue probing; same models/seeds. Decisive metric: whether the downstream capability emerges after the switch, and its delay relative to baseline emergence. Convincing result: the downstream capability emerges after the prerequisite is restored (probe crosses threshold) but delayed by a measurable margin versus baseline (CI excluding 0) - the block is real but reversible once the prerequisite is supplied. Indecision band: partial recovery (downstream reaches an intermediate ceiling that neither matches baseline nor stays blocked) - reversibility is incomplete/ambiguous. Negative result: no post-switch emergence within the remaining budget - either the block is irreversible (a strong prerequisite claim) or the earlier delay was not prerequisite-driven; interpreted jointly with Experiments 2-3.

Experiment 6 (H1 - Skill-tree construction and per-edge gating strength): Aggregates the interventions into an empirical causal dependency graph and compares it to the correlational timeline. Data/protocol: across all (degraded-capability, downstream-capability) pairs from Experiments 2-5, compute a per-edge Gating Strength = downstream delay/ceiling-drop attributable to that prerequisite, normalized by the parallel-control effect; assemble the causal graph; same models/seeds; robustness across model depth/width, corpus, and probe choice. Decisive metric: for each temporally-ordered capability pair, whether a significant causal edge exists (Gating Strength CI excluding 0) and whether the causal graph matches the temporal order. Convincing result: a subset of temporally-ordered pairs show significant causal edges while others do not, yielding a skill tree that is strictly sparser than the full temporal order - demonstrating that acquisition order is partly, not wholly, causal. Indecision band: edges whose Gating Strength CIs graze 0 - their causal status is undetermined and reported as such. Negative result: no significant edges anywhere - the acquisition timeline is a pure schedule with no causal prerequisite structure; all-edges-significant-and-equal would instead suggest generic coupling rather than a differentiated tree, and is flagged against the Experiment 3 specificity control.


Experiment 7 (H1 translational - Does skill-tree knowledge improve training efficiency?): Tests whether ordering or up-weighting data by the discovered prerequisite edges improves sample efficiency versus a standard shuffled-data control. Data/protocol: using the significant edges from Experiment 6, build a prerequisite-first curriculum (up-weight the prerequisite capability's cues early, then release the downstream capability's signal) and compare against (a) standard i.i.d. training and (b) a reversed/anti-prerequisite curriculum, total tokens fixed, same from-scratch models and seeds. Decisive metric: tokens-to-emergence and asymptotic ceiling of the downstream capability under prerequisite-first vs standard vs reversed. Convincing result: prerequisite-first reaches the downstream capability's emergence threshold in >=15% fewer tokens than standard training (CI across seeds excluding 0) without lowering its ceiling, while the reversed curriculum is no better than standard - showing the skill tree is actionable for curriculum design. Indecision band: a 5-15% token saving - directional but modest. Negative result: <5% saving or no advantage over standard training - the causal skill tree, even if real, does not translate into a training-efficiency gain, bounding its practical value.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Data-ablation may reduce a downstream capability simply by removing tokens or lowering overall data quality rather than by severing a specific prerequisite; mitigated by holding token count fixed, the matched non-prerequisite and random-corruption specificity controls, and manipulation checks confirming the ablation hits only the target probe. (2) Capabilities are entangled -- scrambling syntax may inadvertently degrade semantics in the input; we design ablations that preserve the downstream capability's own cues (verified via probes) and interpret results relative to the parallel-capability control rather than to the clean baseline alone. (3) Small from-scratch models may not cleanly exhibit higher capabilities like discourse (prior work shows they underperform an 8-year-old); we focus on well-measurable rungs (POS/morphology->syntax->basic composition) and treat discourse as exploratory. (4) Emergence-checkpoint estimates are noisy; we use dense checkpointing, multiple seeds, and smoothed learning curves with CIs. (5) Probes are correlational readouts of capability; we use established minimal-pair behavioral benchmarks alongside probes to avoid probe-artifact confounds. (6) Compute: from-scratch retraining across conditions x seeds is the main cost; we keep models small (10-100M) and corpora modest (<=100M words), which prior child-directed-speech work shows suffices for these capabilities and is affordable for an academic lab. (7) A null result (degrading a prerequisite does NOT block the downstream capability, or all disruptions harm everything uniformly) is itself highly informative: it would show the acquisition order is a mere schedule driven by data statistics rather than a causal skill tree, refining a widely-assumed developmental analogy. (8) The 'skill tree / prerequisite' framing is operationalized as a training-time causal dependency, not a claim about human-like developmental necessity.

Name: canonicalization_convergence
Title: Mental Paraphrase: Do LLMs Normalize a Problem Toward a Canonical Form Before Reasoning, and Do Failures Come From Not Getting There?
Short Hypothesis: Before reasoning, an LLM internally normalizes a problem's varied surface phrasings toward a shared canonical representation ('mental paraphrase'); reasoning errors on awkward or unfamiliar surface forms are caused by incomplete convergence to that canonical form rather than by the reasoning steps themselves, and the degree of convergence is a readable, causal signal that predicts correctness and can be causally restored by injecting the canonical representation. Primary novelty separator: convergence is measured at the PRE-reasoning problem representation (before any reasoning token), distinguishing a canonicalization bottleneck from convergence that only appears during answer production; the canonical form is defined by multiple operationalizations (centroid, medoid, consensus latent, pairwise convergence) rather than by frequent/terse phrasing alone.
Related Work: Prior work documents that LLMs are brittle to surface form: subtle rephrasings change math solve rates (Paraphrase and Solve / SCoP, 2024), reasoning traces are robust to some CoT interventions but not style-invariant and paraphrasing shortens traces and harms accuracy (Are Reasoning LLMs Robust to Interventions on Their CoT?, 2026), and CoT is often unfaithful (Measuring Faithfulness in CoT, 2023). Representation studies show reasoning representations converge across languages when reasoning succeeds (Under the Shadow of Babel, 2025), that NMT paraphrase-invariance is largely shallow (Neurons Invariant to Sentence Structural Changes, 2022), and that abstract concept vectors exist but are not always output-invariant (Concept Vectors, 2025; Abstract Activation Spaces, 2026). Content-effect work steers a 'validity vs plausibility' direction to debias reasoning (How LMs Conflate Validity with Plausibility, 2025; K-CAST, 2025). ALL of these are either (a) behavioral surface-form robustness studies with no internal mechanism, or (b) steering of a content/validity concept. NONE propose that the model performs an internal canonicalization step that maps diverse phrasings toward a shared normal form before reasoning, that reasoning failure is caused by INCOMPLETE convergence to that canonical form, that per-item convergence is a diagnostic signal of correctness, or that injecting the canonical representation causally rescues hard-phrasing errors. My prior proposals covered word-order, morphology, tokenization granularity, lexical gaps, and grammatical-mood effects, but none address surface-form-invariant canonicalization as a locatable, causal computation. We uniquely reframe paraphrase brittleness from a behavioral quirk into a mechanistic canonicalization-convergence account with a Location + Causal Intervention strategy and a high-stakes clinical instance. Delta and alternative mechanisms: prior representation-convergence work (Under the Shadow of Babel 2025) observes convergence during SUCCESSFUL reasoning, whereas we test whether INCOMPLETE pre-reasoning convergence CAUSES failure. We explicitly pre-register and discriminate competing explanations for the convergence-accuracy link -- confidence, pretraining familiarity, shallow lexical normalization, and retrieval-to-nearest-pretraining-neighbor -- rather than assuming a canonicalization mechanism, and 'canonical form' is defined rigorously (multiple operationalizations, held-out layer selection) so it does not collapse into an embedding-centroid or terse-style artifact.
Abstract: Large language models solve the same problem at different rates depending only on how it is worded, yet why remains unclear. We propose a mechanistic account: before reasoning, the model performs a 'mental paraphrase', normalizing a problem's diverse surface forms toward a shared canonical representation, and reasoning failures on awkward or unfamiliar phrasings arise because the model never fully reaches that canonical form. We make three claims. First, canonicalization is real and graded: across paraphrase clusters (many wordings of one problem), the internal representations converge toward a common form in intermediate layers, and convergence is stronger for the phrasings the model solves correctly. Second, convergence is diagnostic: per-item distance from the paraphrase cluster's canonical representation predicts whether that phrasing will be solved, beyond confidence and entropy, and pinpoints which surface forms are 'lost in translation' before any reasoning error appears. Third, convergence is causal, not incidental: patching the canonical representation (derived from easy, frequent phrasings) into the model's processing of a hard phrasing rescues correctness, and steering along a located 'canonicalization' direction moves reasoning accuracy up or down. We test these on math, logic, and multi-hop QA with controlled paraphrase clusters spanning register, syntax, and verbosity across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where a benign rephrasing of a case description silently degrades diagnostic accuracy through failed canonicalization. Our work reframes paraphrase brittleness as incomplete internal normalization and offers an interpretable pre-reasoning failure signal and a training-free rescue. Deployment implications if confirmed: new robustness metrics (pre-reasoning convergence as a wording-fragility score), targeted data augmentation toward hard phrasings, and inference-time repair by canonical-representation patching; the communities most likely to reuse the artifacts are mechanistic interpretability, robustness/evaluation, safety, and medical NLP. Either outcome is useful -- a positive result gives intervention targets, a null rules out a prominent mechanism and redirects robustness research toward reasoning-stage sensitivity. We temper the clinical claim from 'misdiagnosis' to model error under a defined error taxonomy (colloquial-vs-formal phrasing of identical findings), framed as user-facing reliability for multilingual, colloquial, and accessibility-sensitive interfaces.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts. "Canonicalization convergence" means the degree to which the internal representations of many wordings of one problem approach a shared form before reasoning; the "Convergence Score" is negative distance from a phrasing's pre-reasoning representation to its cluster's canonical (frequent/terse-formal) centroid at the layer of maximal within-cluster convergence.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Canonicalization is real, graded, and stronger for correctly solved phrasings): Tests within-cluster convergence and its link to correctness. Data: for each base problem we build a cluster of 8-12 meaning-preserving paraphrases spanning controlled axes (register formal/colloquial, syntax simple/embedded, verbosity terse/padded, voice active/passive), over 200 base problems from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), 200 from the MATH test split (5,000 available), 150 synthetic deductive-logic chains (depth 2-6, auto-checkable), and 150 from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), 700 clusters / roughly 5,600-8,400 phrasings; paraphrases are generated by templated transforms plus an LLM paraphraser and meaning-preservation is verified by back-translation and human spot-check on a 10% sample. 700 clusters gives enough within-cluster behavioral variance for stable convergence estimates within budget. We extract pre-reasoning hidden states at the end-of-problem position per phrasing per layer, compute within-cluster dispersion by layer and each phrasing's distance to the canonical centroid, controlling for length and word-overlap by regression. Decisive metric first: within-cluster representational dispersion as a function of layer (does it fall to a minimum in intermediate layers?) and the Convergence Score difference between correctly and incorrectly solved phrasings; secondary: the layer of maximal convergence per model. Convincing result: dispersion shows a clear intermediate-layer minimum and correctly solved phrasings have reliably higher Convergence Score than incorrect ones (CI excludes 0) after controlling for length/word-overlap. Indecision band: a correct-minus-incorrect Convergence difference whose CI lies within +/-0.05 standardized units means convergence is not graded by correctness. Negative result: flat dispersion across layers or no correctness link means there is no canonicalization computation, refuting H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Convergence is diagnostic of solve probability before reasoning): Tests pre-reasoning error prediction. Data: the same clusters, split 70/30 by cluster. Decisive metric first: from mixed-effects logistic regression correct ~ Convergence + length + word_overlap + (1|cluster)+(1|model), the Convergence coefficient's significance beyond shallow features; secondary: held-out AUROC of a probe on Convergence features for predicting correctness versus verbalized confidence, token entropy, and per-token surprisal baselines. Convincing result: Convergence retains a reliable positive coefficient beyond length/word-overlap (CI excludes 0) and its AUROC exceeds the best baseline by >= 0.05, measured before any reasoning tokens. Indecision band: a Convergence coefficient CI overlapping 0, or delta-AUROC within +/-0.03, means convergence carries no diagnostic value beyond shallow similarity. Negative result: no predictive power refutes H2.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- Patching the canonical representation causally rescues hard-phrasing errors): Tests the causal rescue. Data: hard phrasings the model fails, paired with an easy/canonical phrasing of the SAME problem. We cache the pre-reasoning representation from the canonical phrasing and patch it into the hard-phrasing forward pass at the convergence layer. Controls: patch from a DIFFERENT problem's canonical representation (specificity), patch a random-matched representation, and no-patch baseline; we verify no answer tokens are present in the patched pre-reasoning representation (rules out answer-leakage). Decisive metric first: accuracy recovery on failed hard phrasings under same-problem canonical patching versus no-patch; secondary: same-problem versus cross-problem/random patching. Convincing result: same-problem canonical patching recovers accuracy by >= 8 points (CI excludes 0) while cross-problem and random patching do not (within 2 points of no-patch). Indecision band: a same-problem recovery within +/-3 points, or a same-versus-cross gap within +/-3 points, means patching does not selectively restore canonicalization. Negative result: no selective recovery, or equal recovery from cross-problem patches, refutes the causal canonicalization-bottleneck claim (and would indicate answer-leakage if cross-problem also rescues).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Steering a canonicalization direction moves accuracy): Tests the mechanism's generality. Data: matched converged-minus-non-converged phrasing contrasts (content matched) yield a difference-in-means "canonicalization" direction at the convergence layer. Systems: plus-direction steering on hard phrasings, minus-direction on easy phrasings, random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: accuracy gain from plus-direction steering on hard phrasings versus random-direction; secondary: minus-direction induced failure on easy phrasings, dose-response, whether per-item convergence increase from patching/steering predicts per-item accuracy gain (Spearman), and specificity (easy-item accuracy within 1 point, fluency preserved). Convincing result: plus-direction steering raises hard-phrasing accuracy by >= 3 points over random-direction (CI excludes 0) with monotonic dose-response and preserved easy-item accuracy, minus-direction lowers easy-phrasing accuracy, and convergence change mediates the gain. Indecision band: steering effects within +/-2 points of random-direction leave the direction unproven; the patching result (Experiment 3) then stands alone. Negative result: no steerable effect means the canonicalization direction is not causal.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests whether colloquial phrasing degrades diagnosis through failed canonicalization and patching rescues it. Data: 300 clinical case clusters adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions), each pairing colloquial patient-reported phrasing with formal chart phrasing of identical findings for a differential-diagnosis task; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Decisive metric first: confident-misdiagnosis rate on colloquial versus formal phrasings, and its relation to a lower Convergence Score on colloquial phrasings; secondary: misdiagnosis reduction under canonical-representation patching on fine-distinction cases. Convincing result: colloquial phrasings show lower convergence and higher confident misdiagnosis, and canonical patching reduces misdiagnosis by >= 5 points (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: a colloquial-versus-formal gap or patching effect within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no phrasing effect on diagnosis, or no patching rescue, bounds the claim to benign benchmarks.

Experiment 6 (Rigorous operationalization, shallow-similarity controls, and competing-hypothesis discrimination): The convergence layer is selected on held-out clusters (nested evaluation) to avoid post-hoc picking. We report robustness across multiple canonicalization operationalizations (centroid, medoid phrasing, consensus latent, pairwise convergence, and a latent-factor model). Against shallow similarity we add matched lexical-overlap subsets, adversarial paraphrases with matched length and word-overlap, and analyses on representations residualized against lexical features. Causal patching (Experiment 3) is validated with timing sweeps, token-position sweeps, and partial-patch ablations, and we verify rescue is not generic confidence inflation and is answer-identity specific -- same-item canonical patching rescues the correct answer but does NOT transfer to semantically related distractor items. We add discriminating tests for the competing mechanisms (pretraining familiarity, retrieval-to-neighbor, parser load, difficulty/confidence) and report expected detectable effect sizes/power for the rescue and steering thresholds across 7B-14B models. Paraphrase quality assurance is strengthened with expert review and explicit exclusion criteria for MedQA and math clusters.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Convergence may be a shallow artifact of lexical/length similarity rather than genuine semantic canonicalization; mitigated by controlling for length/word-overlap in all analyses, by the NMT-paraphrase-style confound checks, and by the causal patching test (which holds content fixed and manipulates only the representation). (2) Paraphrases may not be perfectly meaning-preserving, confounding 'hard phrasing' with subtle meaning shifts; mitigated by back-translation and human verification and by using controlled templated transforms. (3) Instruction-tuned models may be robustly paraphrase-invariant, flattening convergence differences (ceiling); we include harder/awkward phrasings, multiple models, and base variants, and focus on clusters with genuine behavioral variance. (4) The convergence layer may vary across models/tasks; we scan all layers and report the layer of maximal within-cluster convergence per model. (5) Same-problem patching could rescue accuracy simply by leaking the answer rather than restoring canonicalization; we patch only the PRE-reasoning problem representation (before any solution content), verify no answer tokens are present, and use cross-problem/random patching specificity controls. (6) The canonicalization direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by matched converged/non-converged contrasts, random-direction steering, and easy-item specificity checks. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (convergence does not predict or cause correctness) is itself informative: it would indicate paraphrase brittleness is not driven by a canonicalization bottleneck but by reasoning-stage sensitivity, distinguishing surface-form failures from representation-normalization failures. (9) The 'mental paraphrase' framing is operationalized representationally and causally, not as a claim of human-like paraphrasing. (10) We report the clinical outcome as model error under a defined error taxonomy rather than clinical 'misdiagnosis', and we justify the pre-reasoning boundary operationally (end-of-problem position, before any solution token) with token-position sweeps confirming the chosen state precedes latent solution steps.

Name: curse_of_knowledge_teaching
Title: The Curse of Knowledge in LLMs: Is Explanation Quality Causally Gated by an Internal Model of the Learner?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs exhibit a curse of knowledge: by default they produce audience-agnostic explanations pitched near their own knowledge level rather than the learner's, so their teaching underperforms; explanation quality is causally gated by whether the model first forms and uses an internal representation of the learner's knowledge state (a 'learner model'), and this learner model is locatable and steerable, so amplifying it improves how much a downstream learner actually learns while suppressing it reproduces expert-blind explanations.
Related Work: Cognitive science and neuroscience establish the Prediction-Transmission hypothesis: effective human teachers first predict a learner's knowledge state via mentalizing (Theory of Mind) and then select what to say, with teaching quality tracked by mentalizing regions (Teachers recruit mentalizing regions, 2023; Enhancement of teaching outcome through neural prediction of students' knowledge state, 2018; utility-based Bayesian-ToM teachers, 2023; mentalizing-vs-heuristics in teaching, 2024/2025). The 'curse of knowledge' / expert blind spot is a robust human bias where knowing something impairs adapting to a novice. In LLMs, interpretability work shows belief/ToM representations exist and are steerable (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others, 2024; Decomposing Theory of Mind, 2025; Emergent Social World Models, 2026), and audience-design theory formalizes tailoring speech to listeners (Toward a Comprehensive Theory of Audience Design, 2012). However, ALL LLM-teaching work is applied (personalized tutoring systems) or ToM-in-comprehension; NONE (a) test whether an LLM's own explanations suffer a curse of knowledge that measurably reduces downstream learner gains, (b) test whether teaching quality is CAUSALLY gated by an internal learner-knowledge-state representation the model forms before explaining, or (c) locate and steer that learner model to causally improve or degrade teaching effectiveness measured by actual learner learning. We uniquely transfer the Prediction-Transmission hypothesis and the curse of knowledge into LLMs with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes patient-education instance. Novelty locus: prior LLM-teaching benchmarks (e.g., EducationQ, PEARL) and mentalizing-in-teaching studies (e.g., 'Do LLMs Mentalize When They Teach?') measure tutoring quality or ToM in comprehension but never (a) score explanations by an independent learner's downstream gain, (b) test that this quality is CAUSALLY gated by an internal learner-knowledge representation the model forms before explaining, or (c) locate and steer that representation to raise or degrade actual learning — the exact behavioral gap their metrics cannot reach. The problem-definition delta is 'default audience-agnostic explanations pitched near the model's own knowledge' versus 'teaching that first infers and conditions on the learner's knowledge state.' That teaching can worsen as teacher competence rises is reported as a new result in this setting, not a new theory of expert blind spots.
Abstract: Good teaching is an act of audience design: effective human teachers first predict what a learner already knows, then tailor their explanation, and teaching outcomes track this predictive, mentalizing step. Humans who know a subject also suffer a 'curse of knowledge' that makes them explain past novices. We ask whether large language models, whose intelligence is expressed through language, teach well or fall prey to the same curse, and whether their teaching is causally driven by an internal model of the learner. We measure teaching effectiveness the way cognitive scientists do: an explanation is good to the extent that an independent, simulated learner who reads it then answers downstream questions correctly. We make three claims. First, the curse of knowledge is real: by default LLMs produce explanations pitched near their own knowledge level, and forcing them to first infer and state the learner's knowledge state (a prediction step) improves downstream learner gains, especially for low-knowledge learners, while offering little benefit for expert learners. Second, teaching quality is diagnostic of an internal learner model: a probe can decode the learner's inferred knowledge level from the teacher model's hidden states before it explains, and how accurately it does so predicts explanation effectiveness. Third, the learner model is causal and steerable: steering along a located 'learner-knowledge-level' direction shifts explanations up or down the expertise gradient and changes how much the learner actually learns, while suppressing it reproduces expert-blind explanations. We evaluate across several open-weight models and knowledge domains, plus a high-stakes patient-education instance where a curse-of-knowledge explanation leaves a lay patient misinformed. Our work reframes language as audience design and teaching quality as gated by an internal model of the mind being taught. Beyond patient education, the same audience-design failure bears on classroom tutoring, customer support, and workplace training; we treat a >=5 pp change in downstream learning gain as the threshold that would justify revising how LLM tutors are prompted and evaluated. We separate the phenomenon (a behavioral warning that stronger models can teach worse) from the fix (causal learner-model steering), since different audiences would adopt each. If null — LLMs already audience-design adequately and teaching is not gated by an internal learner model — that too informs how tutoring systems and their benchmarks should be built.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - The curse of knowledge is real and predict-then-teach relieves it): Tests that default LLM explanations are pitched too high and that forcing the model to first infer the learner's knowledge state improves how much an independent learner actually learns, selectively for low-knowledge learners. Data: a constructed teaching set over four domains, ~150 topics each (~600 topics), every topic paired with 5-8 held-out downstream comprehension questions. Seed sources: elementary science (topics/questions adapted from the ARC and OpenBookQA science-question pools), statistics/probability (authored), one technical CS concept family (authored from standard curricula), and medicine (adapted from MedQA/MedMCQA stems). We author/adapt because teaching-effectiveness measurement needs topic-linked downstream question sets that off-the-shelf QA lacks; 150/domain balances two-annotator question-validity checking against power. Learner personas span a knowledge gradient (novice/intermediate/expert) via short profiles. Models: TEACHER in {Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B}, all frozen; LEARNER is a separate, different-family/smaller panel {Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B}, also frozen, to avoid teacher=learner shared-bias; decoding temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Conditions (content held constant): (i) DEFAULT (topic only, no learner info); (ii) LEARNER-AWARE (persona provided); (iii) PREDICT-THEN-TEACH (model first states the learner's likely prior knowledge, then explains); (iv) length-matched NON-AUDIENCE reflection control (reflect on the topic's structure). Decisive metric: learner downstream accuracy gain over a no-explanation baseline (learner answers the same questions with no explanation), modeled as learner_gain ~ teaching_condition*learner_level + (1|teacher) + (1|topic). Secondary: objective explanation level (readability grade, count of presupposed/undefined concepts). Convincing result: PREDICT-THEN-TEACH raises novice-learner gain by >=5 pp over DEFAULT with the condition x learner_level interaction 95% CI excluding 0 (novices benefit, expert-learner gain unchanged within +/-2 pp), beats the NON-AUDIENCE control by >=3 pp, and DEFAULT explanations sit objectively near expert level (readability/presupposed-concept counts above the novice-appropriate threshold) - the curse signature. Indecision band: a 2-5 pp novice gain, or an interaction CI grazing 0 - audience design helps directionally but is not established over mere extra deliberation. Negative result: <2 pp gain, or no advantage over the NON-AUDIENCE control - LLMs already audience-design adequately and teaching quality is not gated by an explicit prediction step.

Experiment 2 (H1 - The curse scales with teacher expertise): Tests the counterintuitive prediction that a teacher model explains worse to novices on topics it knows better. Data/protocol: the same ~600 topics; per topic estimate teacher topic-competence (its own solve rate / logit margin) and compute the novice-learner effectiveness gap (DEFAULT novice gain minus expert gain); same five frozen teachers and learner panel. Decisive metric: Spearman correlation between teacher topic-competence and the novice effectiveness gap. Convincing result: rho >=0.30 with 95% CI excluding 0 - higher teacher competence predicts a larger novice penalty, the expert-blind-spot signature. Indecision band: rho 0.15-0.30 - a weak trend. Negative result: rho <0.15 or CI including 0 - the curse magnitude is independent of teacher expertise, weakening the human-analogy framing while leaving Experiment 1's core intact.

Experiment 3 (H2 - A locatable learner model predicts teaching quality): Tests that the learner's inferred knowledge level is linearly decodable from teacher hidden states before it explains and that decodability predicts effectiveness. Data: teacher hidden states at the pre-explanation position on LEARNER-AWARE and PREDICT-THEN-TEACH trials across all topics; 70/30 topic-disjoint split. Protocol: per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds) decoding the learner's specified/inferred level (novice/expert); same five frozen teachers. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC for novice-vs-expert learner level (chance 0.5). Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.80, probe-decoded learner-level predicts per-topic teaching effectiveness (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0), and on DEFAULT trials the probe reads a near-expert default audience - direct evidence the model assumes an expert reader. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.80, or effectiveness correlation rho 0.15-0.30 - a learner representation exists but its link to teaching quality is tentative. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 - no decodable learner model, so teaching quality cannot be attributed to one.

Experiment 4 (H3 - The learner model is causal and steerable): Tests that steering a learner-knowledge-level direction shifts explanation level and actual learner gains, with mediation. Data/protocol: derive a difference-in-means learner-knowledge-level direction (novice-minus-expert learner-model contrasts); steer -direction (toward novice) on DEFAULT explanations and +direction (toward expert) across 4 coefficients; controls random-direction and no-steer; same five frozen teachers and learner panel; specificity tracked on expert-learner gains and fluency. Decisive metric: change in novice-learner gain under steering versus no-steer. Convincing result: novice-ward steering lowers presupposed-concept counts and raises novice-learner gain by >=4 pp with monotonic dose-response, expert-ward steering reproduces expert-blind explanations that reduce novice gain, random-direction moves gain <1.5 pp, expert-learner gain and fluency preserved, and steering-induced change in the Exp-3 learner-level probe predicts the change in learner gain (mediation, CI excluding 0). Indecision band: a 1.5-4 pp steering effect or absent mediation - a causal contribution that is present but not clearly routed through the learner representation. Negative result: <1.5 pp effect or no better than random-direction - the learner-level direction is not causally load-bearing for teaching quality.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - High-stakes patient-education instance): Tests whether default explanations leave a lay patient unable to answer safety-critical questions and whether predict-then-teach and novice steering fix it. Data: ~150 diagnosis/medication-regimen topics (medicine domain subset/extension), each with safety-critical comprehension/action questions (e.g., when to take a drug, warning signs), targeted at a lay-patient learner persona. Protocol: same five frozen teachers, lay-patient learner persona from the panel; compare DEFAULT, PREDICT-THEN-TEACH, and novice-ward steering on the fine-distinction subset; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: safety-critical comprehension/action failure rate of the lay-patient learner. Convincing result: PREDICT-THEN-TEACH and/or novice steering cut the safety-critical failure rate by >=6 pp versus DEFAULT (CI excluding 0) without reducing accuracy for an expert-clinician learner on the same material. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp reduction - safety-relevant but modest. Negative result: <2 pp reduction - the audience-design benefit does not transfer to high-stakes patient education, bounding its practical value.
