Robustness across the whole battery: multiple independent learner models guard against shared-bias artifacts, and a small human-learner validation on a random subset checks that model-learner gains track human-learner gains.

Baselines and leakage safety: the primary suite compares PREDICT-THEN-TEACH against prompt-only audience design, length-matched non-audience reflection, generic simplification, and self-consistency, so gains cannot be attributed to verbosity or extra tokens alone; downstream comprehension questions are authored/held out separately from the explanations and checked to be leakage-safe (not answerable from the topic prompt alone); and every effect is reported as a mixed-effects estimate with 95% CIs and the pre-registered null for the novice/expert interaction, probe AUROC, and steering effect stated per experiment.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Using an LLM as the simulated learner risks shared-bias artifacts (teacher and learner fail on the same items); mitigated by using multiple, weaker/different-family learner models, by measuring gain over a no-explanation baseline (isolating the explanation's contribution), and by a small human-learner validation on a subset. (2) PREDICT-THEN-TEACH may help simply by adding pre-explanation reasoning tokens rather than genuine audience modeling; the length-matched NON-AUDIENCE reflection control and the learner-level x condition selectivity (helps novices, not experts) isolate audience design from mere extra deliberation. (3) The curse may be small if instruction-tuned models already adapt to explicit personas; we include the DEFAULT (no persona) condition where the curse should be strongest, harder technical topics, and measure objective explanation level, and a null there is still informative. (4) The learner-knowledge-level direction may entangle with generic simplicity/verbosity rather than a genuine learner model; mitigated by matched novice/expert learner-model contrasts (same topic), held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and the mediation test linking probe change to learner-gain change. (5) Teaching-effectiveness measurement is noisy and depends on downstream-question design; we use multiple questions per topic, report CIs, and validate against human learners. (6) Effects may be small or model/domain-specific; we test multiple models and domains and report effect sizes. (7) A null result (LLMs already audience-design optimally, no curse, teaching quality independent of an internal learner model) is itself informative, indicating LLM explanation is not gated by mentalizing the learner. (8) The curse-of-knowledge / Prediction-Transmission framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like pedagogical intent; patient-education experiments are run in controlled research settings with only aggregate reporting.

Name: articulated_rule_repair
Title: Say-Do Gap: Can an LLM's Own Correctly-Articulated Rule Repair Its Rule-Violating Behavior?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs frequently state a linguistic or symbolic rule correctly (articulation) while violating that same rule during free generation (execution). Our headline contribution is NOT documenting this say-do gap (already established) but a training-free causal SELF-REPAIR: we read out the model's OWN correctly-articulated rule representation and inject it into the execution stream (via activation patching / difference-in-means steering) to increase compliance without any external label or fine-tuning. We hypothesize the gap reflects a representational dissociation between articulation and execution (consistent with, but not proof of, separate 'pathways'), so the correct rule is decodable even on violating trials and is exploitable - including for LATENT rules the model can apply but cannot conveniently restate in the generation prompt, where explicit-rule prompting is unavailable.
Related Work: Prior work establishes the say-do / comprehension-competence gap behaviorally and treats it as a limitation. Hu & Levy (2023) and Language Models Fail to Introspect (2025) show metalinguistic responses diverge from and underperform direct probability measurements; Comprehension Without Competence (2025) frames a 'computational split-brain' with geometrically dissociated instruction and execution pathways; Large Language Models as Neurolinguistic Subjects (2024) distinguishes performance from competence. On the reasoning side, When Less Language is More (2025) and On Representational Dissociation of Language and Arithmetic (2025) show reasoning/arithmetic occupy separable regions. Methodologically, activation steering, task vectors, and activation patching are established tools. What is new here is their composition into a self-supervised repair: rather than documenting the gap or steering with an externally supplied direction, we extract the model's OWN articulated-rule representation and inject it rule-specifically into execution, and we test it where explicit-rule prompting cannot help (latent/implicit rules). We tone down causal 'pathway' language: our evidence supports a representational dissociation consistent with, not proof of, separate pathways. The delta over ask-then-generate prompting is that ARR transfers an internally recovered rule that is never restated in the execution prompt, and over generic steering/task-vector baselines that the injected direction is the model's own correct articulation rather than an externally constructed one.
Abstract: Large language models routinely state a rule correctly yet break the very same rule when they generate freely: they will explain that a sentence should use the subjunctive, avoid a repeated word, respect an order-of-operations convention, or obey a stated constraint, and then produce output that violates it. Prior work documents this say-do gap and concludes that metalinguistic self-report should not be trusted as evidence of a model's generalizations. We take the opposite stance: if the model can articulate the correct rule, the knowledge exists somewhere in the network, and the failure is a representational dissociation between an articulation process (used when asked to state a rule) and an execution process (used when generating) rather than an absence of knowledge. We test three claims. First, the gap is real and graded: across linguistic (grammar, style, morphology) and symbolic (arithmetic conventions, format constraints) rule families, models articulate rules they systematically violate in generation. Second, articulation and execution are representationally dissociated: a probe can decode the correct rule from hidden states even on trials where the generated output violates it, and the components carrying articulation differ from those driving execution (evidence consistent with, not proof of, separate pathways). Third, and the headline contribution, the dissociation is exploitable: we read out the model's own articulated-rule representation and inject it (via activation patching / steering) into the execution stream, causally increasing rule compliance without any external label or fine-tuning (Articulated-Rule Repair, ARR). Crucially we include a LATENT-rule setting where the rule is inducible from examples but not conveniently restatable in the generation prompt, so ARR is tested where explicit-rule prompting is unavailable; the headline novelty is the mechanism (training-free self-repair), not the say-do phenomenon. We compare ARR against no-intervention, random-direction, incorrect-articulation, explicit-rule prompting, and a parameter-matched non-articulation steering baseline across several open-weight models, reporting compliance gains, dose-response, specificity, and fluency cost, and set a practitioner-relevant bar: an ARR gain that meaningfully exceeds cheap explicit-rule prompting on latent/hard-to-state rules. If ARR fails or only matches random/prompting, that supports the alternative that the gap is an architectural execution limit rather than a retrievable, injectable dissociation. Confirming these claims reframes a diagnosed weakness of LLMs as a controllable bridge between what a model knows and what it does.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Is the say-do gap real and graded across rule families?): Tests whether models articulate rules they systematically violate in generation. Data: a battery of ~15 rules across five families - (a) grammatical (subjunctive, agreement, negative-polarity) using minimal pairs sampled from BLiMP (Warstadt et al. 2020, 67 paradigms x 1000 = 67k pairs; we draw ~500 pairs per selected paradigm), (b) stylistic/discourse (avoid repeating a specified word, maintain a required register), (c) morphological (produce a required inflection), (d) symbolic conventions (order-of-operations formatting, specified numeral base or separator), (e) explicit instruction constraints (do not use the letter e; answer in exactly N words). For each rule we build an ARTICULATION test (forced-choice grammaticality judgment or explicit rule statement scored against ground truth) and an EXECUTION test (free generation where the rule applies, automatically compliance-checked), ~200 items each. We use ~15 rules to span families while keeping five-model coverage affordable. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus one greedy pass. Decisive metric: per-rule Say-Do Gap = articulation accuracy minus execution compliance. Convincing result: at least 5 rules show a Say-Do Gap whose 95% bootstrap CI excludes zero while articulation accuracy is near ceiling (knowledge present, execution fails), and the gap tends to grow with rule complexity/output length. Indecision band: rules whose gap 95% CI lies within +/-5 percentage points are counted as no-gap; if fewer than 3 rules clear the band, the premise (a real, exploitable gap) is undecided. Negative result (no reliable gap anywhere) would remove the phenomenon the rest of the hypothesis depends on: articulation and execution would be equally (in)competent, not dissociated.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Are articulation and execution representationally dissociated?): Tests whether the correct rule is decodable from hidden states on trials whose output violates it, and whether articulation-driving and execution-driving components differ. Data: execution trials from Experiment 1 for the rules with a confirmed gap, split 70/15/15 over items, including a labeled subset whose final output violates the rule. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer logistic-regression linear probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}); component localization uses activation patching, no weights trained. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for whether the correct rule is satisfied, computed specifically on rule-VIOLATING trials (best layer). Secondary: the Jaccard overlap between components that causally drive the articulation response and those that drive execution compliance, from activation patching. Convincing result: probe AUROC on violated trials clears 0.70 (the rule is internally represented yet not enacted) and the articulation/execution component overlap is low (Jaccard below 0.5), evidencing two pathways. Indecision band: probe AUROC in [0.55, 0.65] on violated trials, or Jaccard in [0.5, 0.7], leaves dissociation undecided. Negative result (rule not decodable on violated trials) would indicate the gap reflects genuinely absent/inaccessible knowledge in the execution context rather than a representational dissociation, predicting the repair in Experiment 3 should fail.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Can the model's own articulated rule be injected to close the gap without supervision?): Tests Articulated-Rule Repair (ARR). Data: a held-out 150-item execution set per gap-rule, disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained. ARR runs the ARTICULATION prompt, caches the correctly-articulated-rule representation (and, as a more transferable alternative, a difference-in-means rule-active direction from articulation-correct vs articulation-absent contexts), then injects it at mid layers during EXECUTION over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: no intervention; explicit-rule prompting (restate the rule in the generation prompt); random-direction steering; patching from an INCORRECT articulation; and single-prompt self-consistency (ask-then-generate). Decisive metric: execution compliance gain (percentage points) under ARR versus no intervention. Convincing result: ARR closes at least 30% of the say-do gap, exceeds both the random-direction and incorrect-articulation controls (95% CIs excluding them) - showing it transfers the model's own correct rule, not generic follow-the-rule pressure - shows a monotone dose-response, preserves off-target rules and fluency (external-LM perplexity and unrelated-task accuracy within +/-3 pp of baseline), and rules with a larger probe-decodable-but-violated signal from Experiment 2 benefit more (Spearman rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: an ARR compliance gain whose 95% CI lies within +/-3 pp of zero, or overlaps the random-direction control, means the repair is undecided. Negative result (ARR fails, or only matches random) would support the alternative that the say-do gap reflects a deeper execution-pathway limitation (an architectural split-brain) rather than a retrievable, injectable dissociation.

Latent-rule setting, leakage protocol, and specificity: we add a latent-rule family (rules inducible from in-context examples but not explicitly stated), a leakage-resistant protocol that separates articulation-collection contexts from execution contexts with held-out templates and counterbalanced surface forms, and specificity controls - ARR built from a different rule in the same family, from the same rule in another context, and from a semantically-matched but rule-incorrect articulation - plus a parameter-matched hidden-state steering baseline derived WITHOUT articulation. The ARR pipeline is fixed in advance (which prompt elicits the articulated rule, the token span and layer over which the representation is averaged, and how injection layers are selected on held-out items). Articulation and execution scoring metrics are specified per rule family with automatic checkers and human validation on a sample, and we report effect sizes with 95% CIs and multiple-comparison correction across rules/families with pre-registered primary endpoints. Mechanistic claims are supported by intervention at predicted rule-representation sites versus matched control sites and by mediation linking decodable-but-violated signal to ARR benefit, and are framed as representational dissociation rather than proof of separate pathways.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The say-do gap may be small or near-zero for some rules once articulation is measured carefully; we include many rule families and report the distribution, and any rules with a genuine gap suffice for the repair test. (2) Articulation scoring can be noisy (open-ended rule statements); we favor forced-choice / minimal-pair articulation where possible and use automatic compliance checkers for execution. (3) The cached articulation representation may not be cleanly transferable across the articulation→execution context shift; we test difference-in-means directions as a more robust alternative and report both. (4) ARR could improve compliance simply by generic 'follow-the-rule' pressure rather than transferring the specific rule; the incorrect-articulation and random-direction controls isolate this. (5) Explicit-rule prompting is a strong, cheap baseline that may match ARR; a finding that ARR only matches it is still informative (it shows the gap is representational and closable internally), and ARR's value is in cases where the rule cannot be conveniently prompted (implicit/self-discovered rules). (6) Effects may be model- or rule-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes. (7) A null repair result is still publishable as evidence that the say-do gap reflects a deeper execution-pathway limitation (consistent with the 'architectural split-brain' hypothesis) rather than a retrievable-knowledge dissociation.

Name: affect_labeling_debiasing
Title: Name It to Tame It: Does an LLM's Own Affect-Labeling Decouple Its Reasoning From Emotional Content?
Short Hypothesis: The human 'affect labeling' effect — putting a feeling into a compact emotion word incidentally dampens its influence on judgment — transfers to LLMs: requiring a model to first name the emotional content of an affect-laden input causally reduces the emotion's distorting pull on its subsequent reasoning (fewer affect-driven errors, better calibration on affective content), and this debiasing is mediated by a locatable affect-representation whose engagement drops after labeling and can be causally steered.
Related Work: Human affect-labeling research shows that verbally labeling an emotion incidentally (without intentional reappraisal) reduces amygdala/limbic responses and self-reported distress, distinct from and cheaper than reappraisal (Torre & Lieberman meta-analysis; Burklund et al. 2014, 116 cites; Lieberman fMRI/ERP, third-person self-talk 2017, 111 cites; Brooks et al. neuroimaging meta-analysis 2016, 128 cites), and that labeling in a second language further increases emotional distance (Morawetz et al. 2017). In LLMs, prior work studies emotion INJECTION and control — emotion vectors and steering (From Rational Answers to Emotional Resonance 2025; The Inner Sentiments of a Thought 2023), mechanistic localization of emotion inference to mid layers with appraisal-theory structure (Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference 2025), stress affecting performance (StressPrompt 2024), and emotion mediating Theory-of-Mind steering (Decomposing Theory of Mind 2025). ALL of this treats emotion as a signal to inject, detect, or amplify. NONE test the OPPOSITE, regulatory direction: whether the model's own act of labeling the emotional content of a stimulus causally REDUCES the emotion's downstream influence on reasoning/judgment (affect-labeling debiasing), whether this beats reappraisal-style prompting, or whether it is mediated by a locatable affect representation that labeling deflates. My prior proposals covered dual-process gears, foreign-language honesty, verbal overshadowing, and pragmatic enrichment, but never affect labeling as a self-regulation/debiasing mechanism. We uniquely transfer a robust human emotion-regulation finding into LLMs as a controlled label-then-judge intervention with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes clinical/moral instance. Novelty locus: the phenomenon is that a robust human emotion-regulation effect (incidental affect labeling) transfers to LLMs; the primary contribution is the CAUSAL test of the direction OPPOSITE to all prior emotion work — where that work injects, detects, or amplifies emotion, we test whether the model NAMING the emotion REDUCES its downstream influence on reasoning — together with a mechanistic mediation account. This is distinct from generic sentiment detection, which reads emotion but does not regulate it, and it is not offered as a benchmark contribution. We treat 'mediated by an affect representation' as a hypothesis adjudicated by a pre-registered mediation-plus-steering chain, not asserted as a standard probing result.
Abstract: In humans, simply putting a feeling into a word — affect labeling — incidentally weakens that feeling's grip on judgment, dampening limbic responses without any intentional attempt to reinterpret the situation. We ask whether this regulatory relationship between language and cognition transfers to large language models: does requiring a model to first name the emotional content of an affect-laden input causally reduce the emotion's distorting influence on its subsequent reasoning? We assemble tasks where affect is designed to bias judgment away from the correct answer — emotionally charged framings of factual and probability questions, morally provocative dilemmas, sentiment-loaded evaluations, and emotionally distressing clinical vignettes — each with a labeled affect-driven error lure. Holding content constant, we compare four conditions: direct judgment; AFFECT-LABEL (name the emotion present before answering); a length-matched NON-AFFECT LABEL control (describe a non-emotional attribute); and reappraisal-style prompting. We predict an affect-labeling debiasing effect: labeling the emotion reduces affect-driven errors and improves calibration relative to direct and non-affect controls, is selective to affect-biased items, and matches or exceeds costlier reappraisal — mirroring the human incidental-regulation finding. Mechanistically, we locate an affect-representation via probing, test whether it is engaged during direct judgment and DEFLATED after the model labels the emotion (mediating the behavioral debiasing), and causally steer it: subtracting it should mimic labeling's benefit, amplifying it should reinstate affect-driven errors. Across several open-weight models we quantify the effect, its selectivity, its mechanistic mediation, and a high-stakes clinical instance where emotional framing silently biases triage. Our work reframes emotion words from something LLMs express into a tool that regulates their own reasoning. If the effect holds, affect-labeling becomes a simple, general debiasing prompt wherever LLMs process emotionally framed inputs — content moderation, mental-health and crisis chat, customer-support escalation, and moral/triage decision support — changing behavior by inserting one cheap label-then-judge step instead of costlier reappraisal or fine-tuning. If it is null, that is equally informative: it would dissociate LLMs from the human incidental affect-labeling mechanism and bound how far human emotion-regulation findings transfer to machine reasoning. We release the paired affect-biased judgment battery to support replication.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Affect-labeling debiasing is real, selective, and competitive with reappraisal): Tests the behavioral core - that requiring the model to name the emotion first reduces affect-driven errors and improves calibration, selectively on affect-biased items, at or below the cost of reappraisal. Data: a constructed affect-biased judgment battery of four families, ~250 items each (~1000 total), each authored as a matched pair - an AFFECT framing carrying a labeled affect-congruent lure, and a content-identical NEUTRAL framing with the affect stripped. Families and their seed sources: (a) emotionally charged factual/probability questions re-framed from TruthfulQA-style factual claims and calibration items; (b) morally provocative dilemmas adapted from the ETHICS and Moral Stories corpora; (c) sentiment-loaded truth judgments wrapping FEVER-style claims in strongly valenced language; (d) emotionally distressing clinical vignettes adapted from MedQA/MedMCQA stems. We author rather than harvest because no existing set holds content constant while toggling only affect; 250/family keeps two-annotator verification of meaning-preservation and lure validity (target >=90% agreement) affordable while giving ~1000 paired items for adequately powered mixed-effects estimation. Ground truth and the affect-congruent lure are auto-checkable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, all open-weight and run frozen (inference only, no weights trained here); decoding at temperature 0.7, 5 samples/item, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Conditions, content held constant with output format enforced and compliance verified: (i) DIRECT; (ii) AFFECT-LABEL (name the emotion(s) present before answering); (iii) NON-AFFECT LABEL (describe a length-matched non-emotional attribute - topic/entities - before answering); (iv) REAPPRAISAL prompting; (v) SECOND-LANGUAGE AFFECT-LABEL (name the emotion in a non-dominant language). Decisive metric: affect-driven-lure rate on AFFECT items (fraction of responses equal to the labeled affect-congruent wrong answer), modeled as lure_rate ~ condition*affect_status + (1|model) + (1|item). Secondary: expected calibration error (ECE) on the factual/probability family; token cost. Convincing result: AFFECT-LABEL lowers the affect-lure rate on AFFECT items by >=8 percentage points (pp) absolute versus NON-AFFECT LABEL with the condition x affect_status interaction 95% CI excluding 0 (the drop is specific to affect items, near-zero on neutral controls), reduces ECE by >=3 pp, and lands within 2 pp of - or better than - REAPPRAISAL at lower token cost. Indecision band: a 3-8 pp lure-rate reduction, or an interaction CI that grazes 0 - a directional but underpowered effect; landing here means labeling shows the predicted sign but the debiasing is not established, and we report it as suggestive and pool across models for power. Negative result: <3 pp reduction, or no larger effect than NON-AFFECT LABEL (interaction CI centered on 0) - this dissociates LLMs from the human incidental affect-labeling mechanism, indicating emotional influence on LLM judgment is not regulated by naming. The SECOND-LANGUAGE arm is exploratory: a further reduction corroborates the L2-distancing analogue, but its absence does not by itself refute H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 - A locatable affect representation): Tests that an affect-intensity signal is linearly decodable and separable from generic content. Data: hidden states collected on the same ~1000 paired items (AFFECT vs NEUTRAL framings, and pre- vs post-label token positions), 70/30 item-disjoint train/test split so no item appears in both. Model/protocol: the same five frozen models; a logistic linear probe (L2-regularized, 3 training seeds) trained per layer to decode affect presence/intensity; a difference-in-means affect-intensity direction derived from AFFECT-minus-NEUTRAL contrasts. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC of the affect probe (chance 0.5). Convincing result: best-layer held-out AUROC >=0.80 (expected mid-network, consistent with prior emotion-inference localization), with the difference-in-means direction reproducing >=0.75 AUROC, establishing a real, generalizing affect representation. Indecision band: best-layer AUROC 0.65-0.80 - a weak signal that supports mediation/steering only tentatively. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 anywhere - no separable affect representation, undercutting the mechanistic half of the hypothesis regardless of the behavioral outcome.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Labeling deflates the affect representation and this mediates the behavioral effect): Tests that naming the emotion reduces engagement of the affect direction at the judgment position, and that this reduction predicts fewer affect-driven errors. Data/protocol: for each AFFECT item, project the judgment-position hidden state onto the Exp-2 affect direction under DIRECT, AFFECT-LABEL, and NON-AFFECT LABEL; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: paired within-item drop in affect-direction engagement (AFFECT-LABEL minus DIRECT), and the Spearman correlation between per-item engagement drop and per-item reduction in affect-driven errors. Convincing result: engagement drops significantly after AFFECT-LABEL (paired effect, 95% CI excluding 0) but not after NON-AFFECT LABEL (CI including 0), and the mediation correlation |rho| >=0.30 with CI excluding 0, with a mediation model showing the engagement drop accounts for a substantial share of the condition->accuracy effect. Indecision band: |rho| 0.15-0.30, or a drop after AFFECT-LABEL that is not reliably larger than after NON-AFFECT LABEL - engagement moves but mediation is unproven. Negative result: |rho| <0.15 or no differential drop - labeling's behavioral benefit (if any) is not carried by deflation of this affect representation, breaking the proposed mechanistic chain.

Experiment 4 (H4 - The affect representation is causally steerable): Tests that subtracting the affect direction mimics labeling's benefit and that adding it reinstates affect-driven errors. Data/protocol: activation steering along the Exp-2 affect direction at the best mediating layer during DIRECT judgment (subtract) and after AFFECT-LABEL (add), across 4 coefficients spanning a dose ladder; controls are a random-direction vector of matched norm and no-steer; same five frozen models; specificity tracked on NEUTRAL items and via output perplexity/fluency. Decisive metric: change in affect-driven-lure rate under steering versus no-steer. Convincing result: subtracting the affect direction lowers the affect-lure rate by >=6 pp on DIRECT AFFECT items with a monotonic dose-response, adding it after AFFECT-LABEL reinstates the lure by >=6 pp, the random-direction control moves it <2 pp, and NEUTRAL-item accuracy and fluency stay within a pre-set 2 pp / small-perplexity tolerance. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp steering effect, or a non-monotonic dose - a causal contribution that is present but not cleanly attributable to this direction. Negative result: <2 pp effect, or an effect no larger than the random-direction control, or one that only appears alongside broken fluency - the affect representation is not causally load-bearing for the debiasing.

Experiment 5 (H1/H4 - High-stakes clinical instance): Tests whether emotional framing biases triage and whether affect-labeling and affect-direction steering reduce that bias where it matters. Data: ~250 triage vignettes (subset/extension of family (d)) holding identical clinical facts while varying only the emotional framing of the patient/family, each with a labeled correct urgency/triage decision and a framing-driven error. Model/protocol: same five frozen models; compare DIRECT, AFFECT-LABEL, and subtract-affect-direction steering; report on the fine-distinction subset where framing and correct decision diverge; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: framing-driven triage-error rate on fine-distinction cases. Convincing result: AFFECT-LABEL and/or affect-subtraction steering cut the framing-driven error rate by >=6 pp versus DIRECT with CI excluding 0, without lowering accuracy on neutrally framed matched cases. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp reduction - a safety-relevant but modest effect warranting replication before any deployment claim. Negative result: <2 pp reduction - the regulation demonstrated in Experiments 1-4 does not transfer to a realistic high-stakes decision, bounding the practical reach of the mechanism.

Cross-experiment controls and reporting: all effects are reported as mixed-effects estimates with 95% CIs against the pre-registered effect-size thresholds stated above (and pre-registered as the confirmatory comparisons AFFECT-LABEL vs DIRECT, vs NON-AFFECT LABEL, and vs REAPPRAISAL, so a positive result cannot be read as mere 'extra deliberation helps'). We add a NEGATIVE-CONTROL condition in which emotion words are present but decision-irrelevant (the affect-congruent answer is NOT the lure), where affect-labeling should confer no benefit — establishing that any debiasing is selective to affect that actually biases the judgment rather than to the mere presence of emotion words. We report results split by task family, model family (base vs instruction-tuned), and prompt format to map robustness and boundary conditions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Affect-labeling may help simply by adding a pre-answer reasoning step / more tokens rather than via naming the emotion; mitigated by the length-matched NON-AFFECT LABEL control (equal pre-answer description, no emotion naming) and by testing the affect-specific selectivity interaction rather than raw gains. (2) Instruction-tuned models may already discount emotional framing, muting the debiasing effect (ceiling); we include harder/more vivid framings, base variants, multiple models, and measure calibration where headroom is larger. (3) 'Affect-driven lure' items may conflate emotional bias with general difficulty; matched neutral-framing controls (same content, affect removed) isolate the affect contribution, and the lure error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC affect-congruent answer) distinguishes genuine affect bias from random error. (4) The affect direction may entangle with generic content/sentiment or difficulty rather than a regulatable affect-intensity signal; mitigated by matched affect/neutral contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and neutral-item specificity checks. (5) Reappraisal is a strong, cheap prompt baseline that may match affect-labeling; a finding that labeling merely matches reappraisal at lower cost, or that a located affect direction mediates both, is still informative about the mechanism. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (labeling the emotion does not reduce affect's influence, or does so no more than non-affect labeling) is itself informative: it would dissociate LLMs from the human incidental affect-labeling mechanism, indicating emotional influence on LLM judgment is not regulated by naming. (8) The affect-labeling framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like emotional experience; clinical/moral experiments are run in controlled research settings and reported only in aggregate.

Name: verbal_overshadowing_llm
Title: Words That Blur: Does Describing an Input in Language Corrupt an LLM's Own Fine-Grained Representation?
Short Hypothesis: Like humans, a text LLM may suffer verbal overshadowing: forcing it to verbally describe a rich, hard-to-verbalize stimulus before a fine-grained recognition/discrimination judgment degrades performance relative to no-description (and non-verbal-filler / verbatim-copy) baselines. Prior LLM work already shows verbalization/CoT can hurt; our delta is a controlled describe-then-discriminate paradigm plus two specific, testable claims those results do not make: (i) the harm follows a LEXICALIZATION gradient (worst in domains the model lexicalizes poorly, where description forces lossy compression), and (ii) it is CAUSED by verbalization coarsening a recoverable internal fine-detail representation of that item (recoding interference), so patching the pre-verbalization representation back cancels the effect. We focus on text-only LLMs and treat verbal overshadowing as an operational analogy, not a claim of human-like memory.
Related Work: Verbal overshadowing (VO) is a robust human finding: verbally describing a face, taste, or object impairs subsequent non-verbal recognition (Schooler & Engstler-Schooler 1990; Meissner & Brigham 1997), with computational models attributing it to recoding interference in which verbalization strips fine-grained detail from the maintained representation (Hatano et al. 2013/2015), and recent work shows VO is STRONGER in lexically-impoverished modalities such as taste (Zhuang & Vanek 2026), directly linking the effect to poverty of vocabulary. In LLMs, interpretability work studies language bias in vision (Language-biased image classification 2022; When are Lemons Purple 2023), the binding problem (2024), and whether describing rather than seeing recovers performance (Analyzing Roles of Language and Vision 2024), and a separate overthinking/implicit-reasoning line shows that added verbal reasoning/CoT can hurt accuracy. We concede that behavioral 'verbalization can hurt' is therefore not new. Our one-sentence delta: prior work shows behavioral harm, whereas we test whether self-generated verbalization degrades a RECOVERABLE fine-detail LATENT representation of the item (a causal recoding-interference account), and whether the harm scales with a measurable lexicalization-poverty index - neither of which prior LLM work establishes. Novelty by experiment: Exp1 = the controlled paradigm and lexicalization-gradient setting, Exp2 = mechanistic correlational evidence, Exp3 = causal representation-level intervention.
Abstract: Humans who describe a face, a wine, or a suspect in words afterward recognize it worse than if they had stayed silent - verbal overshadowing - because putting a rich stimulus into language strips fine-grained, hard-to-verbalize detail from the memory that guides the later judgment. We ask whether large language models suffer the same self-inflicted damage: does forcing a model to describe an input in words before a fine-grained discrimination corrupt its own representation of that input? We study text-only LLMs and construct describe-then-discriminate tasks where a target item (a detailed textual scene/object description, a numeric/structured pattern, a code snippet, or a clinical vignette) is presented, then the model must either (a) verbalize the item in free-form words or (b) perform a non-verbal filler / verbatim copy / stay silent, and finally answer a fine-grained recognition or discrimination question separating the target from a near-neighbor distractor. We concede prior LLM work already shows verbalization/CoT can hurt; our claims are the controlled paradigm plus a lexicalization gradient and a causal recoding-interference test. We operationalize the lexicalization gradient with a pre-registered, independently-validated proxy (a nameability / vocabulary-coverage index per domain) rather than intuitive labels, and predict a verbal-overshadowing effect: self-generated description lowers fine-grained accuracy relative to no-description, filler, and copy controls, is selective to fine-grained (not gist) discrimination, and is largest in poorly-lexicalized domains. Mechanistically, we test the recoding-interference account: a probe decoding fine-grained target detail should show reduced decodability after verbalization, this blurring should predict the behavioral drop item-by-item, and patching the pre-verbalization representation back (or steering a fine-detail direction) should cancel the overshadowing. We commit to clinical differential diagnosis as the concrete high-stakes workflow, and expect uptake from CoT/overthinking, mechanistic-interpretability, faithful-explanation, and medical-AI communities. If supported, prompting and interpretability pipelines should avoid premature verbalization before fine-grained judgments; if null (verbalization is a lossless readout in LLMs), concerns about recoding interference are weakened. Across several open-weight models we quantify the VO effect, its lexical-poverty gradient, a high-stakes clinical instance, and its mechanistic mediation.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does self-generated verbalization selectively degrade fine-grained discrimination?): Tests whether forcing a verbal description before a fine-grained judgment lowers accuracy relative to no-description and non-verbal controls, selectively for fine-grained (not gist) questions, and most in poorly-lexicalized domains. Data: a describe-then-discriminate battery of ~1000 items, ~250 per domain across a lexicalization gradient - (a) richly-lexicalized textual scenes/objects, (b) structured numeric/visual-pattern descriptions (poorly lexicalized), (c) code snippets, (d) clinical vignettes (high-stakes). Each item has a target and a near-neighbor DISTRACTOR differing in one fine-grained detail, plus a matched GIST-level control question answerable from coarse features (selectivity control); ground truth is auto-checkable. Conditions (content held constant): NO-DESCRIPTION (target then question), VERBALIZE (free-form description of the target before the question), NON-VERBAL FILLER (equal-length unrelated tally task; controls delay/context length), and COPY (reproduce the target verbatim; controls re-processing without lossy re-description). We run both a target-present variant and a target-REMOVED variant (target dropped from context before the question) to match the human memory paradigm. Compliance is verified. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: the condition x question-grain interaction on accuracy, in a mixed-effects model accuracy ~ condition*grain + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: VERBALIZE lowers FINE-GRAINED accuracy below NO-DESCRIPTION, FILLER, and COPY (isolating verbalization from delay/reprocessing) with little/no effect on GIST questions (interaction 95% CI excluding zero); the VO magnitude is largest in poorly-lexicalized domains (per-domain lexicalization proxy correlates with per-domain VO magnitude, Spearman CI excluding zero); and in the clinical domain, describing a differential before choosing between two similar diagnoses raises fine-distinction error versus answering directly. Indecision band: a condition x grain interaction whose 95% CI lies within +/-2 percentage points is undecided; if the effect appears only in the target-present variant it may be a context-length artifact - the target-removed variant is the decisive one. Negative result (verbalization does not degrade fine-grained judgment, especially target-removed) would dissociate LLMs from the human recoding-interference account, indicating verbalization is a lossless readout.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Does verbalization measurably blur the internal fine-detail representation, and does that predict the behavioral drop?): Location plus mediation. Data: pre-answer hidden states from Experiment 1 under each condition (target-removed variant emphasized), 70/15/15 over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer linear probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}). Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for decoding the target's fine-grained distinguishing feature (best layer), compared across conditions. Convincing result: fine-detail decodability is lower after VERBALIZE than after NO-DESCRIPTION/COPY (representational blurring; CI excluding zero), and the per-item drop in decodability predicts the per-item accuracy drop under verbalization (Spearman rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: a verbalize-minus-baseline AUROC drop whose 95% CI is within +/-0.05, or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the recoding account undecided. Negative result (no decodability drop, or it does not track behavior) would argue any accuracy loss is not caused by representational blurring.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Can the pre-verbalization fine-detail representation be restored to cancel overshadowing, and induced to create it?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item fine-grained subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained. Patch: cache the pre-verbalization fine-detail representation and patch it back after verbalization. Steer: a difference-in-means fine-detail direction (high vs low distinguishing-feature contrast) added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: patch-back after VERBALIZE (rescue); +direction after VERBALIZE (rescue) and -direction under NO-DESCRIPTION (induce overshadowing without any description); random-direction; and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in fine-grained accuracy under patching/steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that gist accuracy and fluency are preserved. Convincing result: patching the cached representation back rescues fine-grained accuracy (detail was degraded, not deleted), +direction rescues and -direction induces overshadowing with monotone dose-response, both exceed random-direction (CIs excluding it), and gist accuracy stays within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a patch/steer effect whose 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or lacks dose-response, leaves the causal-recovery claim undecided. Negative result (patching/steering does not restore fine-grained accuracy) would mean the fine-detail direction is correlational, not the causal locus of overshadowing.

Baselines, proxy, and mechanics: we add stronger baselines - delayed no-description, paraphrase-only, an externally-provided (not self-generated) description, and short-vs-long verbalization - to separate delay, generation, and semantic compression. The lexicalization proxy is defined and validated independently rather than by intuitive domain labels. Near-neighbor distractors and gist controls are matched, with leakage from target tokens prevented, and we detail the patching mechanics: hidden states from the same forward pass, the fine-detail representation cached pre-verbalization and re-inserted at the located layer, emphasizing the target-removed variant as decisive. We pre-register effect-size thresholds for 'convincing', model-level variance handling, and multiple-comparison correction across domains, and tighten probe claims with held-out item splits, adversarial surface-token-recovery controls, cross-layer localization, and mediation linking decodability loss to behavior.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Verbalization adds tokens/delay that could impair via context length rather than recoding; mitigated by the length-matched non-verbal FILLER and verbatim-COPY controls and by testing the fine-vs-gist INTERACTION rather than raw drops. (2) Instruction-tuned models may re-access the original target tokens (still in context) and avoid overshadowing entirely, unlike humans who lose sensory access; we test both keeping and removing the target from context (a memory-maintenance variant that better matches the human paradigm) and report both — a null in the target-present variant with an effect in the target-removed variant would still cleanly confirm recoding interference. (3) The fine-detail probe may capture surface tokens rather than a maintained representation; mitigated by target-removed trials, held-out validation, matched positions, and random-direction steering controls. (4) VO effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models, domains, and report effect sizes with CIs. (5) A null result (verbalization does not degrade fine-grained judgment) is itself highly informative: it would dissociate LLMs from the human recoding-interference account, suggesting verbalization in LLMs is a lossless readout rather than a lossy recoding. (6) The verbal-overshadowing framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like memory.

Name: polarity_load_tracking
Title: Carrying the 'Not': Does Tracking Active Negations Impose a Compounding Working-Memory Load on LLM Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM represents a negated proposition as a positive proposition plus an approximately additive, separable 'polarity flag' (an operational hypothesis we test against rival encodings), so that reasoning which must hold and propagate multiple active negations across steps degrades with the NUMBER of live negations (a compounding polarity load), independent of surface length or difficulty; this polarity load is a locatable, steerable internal quantity, and errors are dominated by polarity-drop failures (silently reverting a negated fact to its positive) that can be causally reduced by amplifying the polarity signal.
Related Work: Prior negation work is overwhelmingly about single-sentence UNDERSTANDING: NLI and cloze failures on negation (MoNLI 2020; Negation/Coordination/Quantifiers 2022; CONDAQA 2022; ScoNe 2023; Pink Elephant 2025), theoretical 'strong hallucinations' from negation as a latent operator (2024), and localization of negation to early text-encoder layers (BERT attention 2020; CLIP negation 2024; NAST 2026). Reasoning-focused work shows CoT is not robust to lexical negation on single syllogisms (2023) and that symbolic cues including negation destabilize early-layer attention and drive hallucination (2026). ALL of this treats a fixed, typically small number of negations per item and studies comprehension or single-step inference. NONE frame the NUMBER of simultaneously ACTIVE negations that must be held and propagated across a multi-step reasoning chain as a graded working-memory-like LOAD with a compounding accuracy penalty, none isolate a 'polarity-drop' error mode (reverting a negated fact to positive mid-chain), and none give a Location + Causal Intervention account of a separable, additive polarity signal that can be steered to relieve the load. My prior proposals covered information-density pacing, register shift, ambiguity-branch collapse, and pragmatic enrichment, but never negation/polarity tracking as a reasoning load. We uniquely reframe negation from a comprehension deficit into a compounding, mechanistically-characterized reasoning-load phenomenon with a high-stakes clinical instance. Novelty locus: the contribution is a mechanistic package — active-negation-count scaling of a compounding load, an approximately additive polarity representation, a polarity-drop error signature, and causal rescue/induction — plus a released active-negation-load benchmark and analysis tools, not merely the observation that negation is hard. Delta versus the closest families: multi-hop cognitive-load work varies reasoning depth but never the number of live negations at fixed depth; negation-probing and negation-forgetting work study single-sentence comprehension, never a graded cross-step propagation load with a drop signature. Negation propagation also matters beyond clinical text — in legal and policy conditions, retrieval filters, and agent-planning constraints — where a dropped 'not' silently flips a decision.
Abstract: Negation is trivial to state and notoriously hard for language models, but existing work studies it as a single-sentence comprehension problem. We ask a different question central to how language bounds machine intelligence: what does it cost an LLM to CARRY negations through multi-step reasoning? We hypothesize that a model encodes a negated proposition as its positive counterpart plus a separable, additive polarity flag, so that reasoning which must simultaneously hold and propagate several live negations pays a compounding cost: accuracy falls with the number of active negations, over and above surface length and problem difficulty, and failures are dominated by 'polarity drops' in which a negated fact silently reverts to positive partway through the chain. We make three claims. First, the load is real and graded: on reasoning chains where we vary only how many propositions are negated (content and length matched), accuracy declines with negation count and errors concentrate on dropped-polarity conclusions. Second, polarity is a separable, locatable quantity: a probe decodes each proposition's live polarity from hidden states mid-chain, its decodability degrades as negation load rises, and this degradation predicts polarity-drop errors before they surface. Third, the load is causally relievable: steering along a located 'polarity' direction (or patching the pre-drop polarity representation) restores dropped negations and reduces errors, while suppressing it induces polarity drops even at low load. We evaluate across several open-weight models on logic, entailment chains, and multi-hop QA, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where a dropped 'no history of' or 'contraindicated' silently flips a decision, quantifying the compounding load, its polarity-drop signature, and mechanistic mediation. We release the negation-load battery (with matched double-negation and marker-free logically-equivalent controls) and the polarity probing/steering tools as reusable artifacts. We frame the additive-flag account as an operational hypothesis tested against rival explanations — generic difficulty, uncertainty/confidence collapse, surface 'not'-token tracking, training-frequency effects, and answer-content leakage — via matched controls and distinct predicted signatures. If confirmed, downstream reasoning evaluation and mitigation would treat negation count as a first-class load variable; if rejected, it would show negation is absorbed into content rather than carried as a separable flag.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - A compounding polarity load with a polarity-drop error signature): Tests that accuracy declines with the number of simultaneously active negations, beyond surface length and difficulty, and that errors concentrate on dropped-polarity conclusions rather than random failure. Data: a constructed negation-load battery, ~250 base items each across three families (~750 base items, ~3750 rendered): (a) deductive logic chains depth 3-6 over propositions, (b) entailment/consistency chains, (c) multi-hop QA over short passages. Each base item is rendered into a matched SET differing ONLY in how many of its propositions are negated (0/1/2/3/4 active negations) via minimal 'not'/'no' edits that preserve content, holding reasoning-step count, token length, and answer structure constant. Each item has a labeled correct answer AND a labeled POLARITY-DROP lure (the answer that follows if exactly one negated fact is treated as positive). A surface control adds equal-length non-negation modifiers. We construct because no existing set varies negation count while matching depth/length; 250 base items/family gives ~3750 rendered items for load-curve estimation and keeps entailment/human meaning-preservation checks affordable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; greedy plus temperature-0.7 sampling, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Decisive metric: accuracy as a function of negation_count, modeled as accuracy ~ negation_count + chain_depth + token_length + (1|model) + (1|item); secondary polarity-drop-rate and the polarity-drop share of errors. Convincing result: accuracy declines monotonically (and super-additively) with negation_count beyond depth/length (per-negation coefficient CI excluding 0, e.g. >=4 pp accuracy loss per added active negation), the equal-length surface-modifier control shows <1 pp/modifier decline (isolating polarity from generic modifier load), and >=50% of errors on high-load items are the specific polarity-drop lure (the diagnostic that a negation was silently dropped). Indecision band: a 1.5-4 pp/negation decline, or a polarity-drop error share of 30-50% - a real but weak or not-clearly-polarity-shaped load. Negative result: <1.5 pp/negation and lure share near chance, or a surface-modifier control that declines just as much - no specific compounding polarity load, indicating negation is absorbed into content rather than a load-bearing flag.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Flag-based additivity: double-negation and error-localization): Tests the separable-additive-flag signature - that cancelling double-negations are easier than an equal count of independent negations, and that failures localize to a specific dropped negation. Data/protocol: within the same battery, matched double-negation items (surface 'not' present but live polarity positive) versus items with the same count of independent negations; per-item error-localization tracing the wrong final answer to a specific proposition whose polarity flipped; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: accuracy gap (double-negation minus equal-count independent-negation), and the error-localization rate (fraction of errors attributable to one identifiable dropped negation). Convincing result: double-negation accuracy exceeds equal-count independent-negation accuracy by >=6 pp (CI excluding 0) - consistent with flag cancellation rather than raw 'not'-token count - and error-localization succeeds on >=60% of errors. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp double-negation advantage, or localization 40-60% - suggestive of flag structure but not decisive. Negative result: no double-negation advantage and diffuse (chance-level) localization - negation is encoded into content, not as a separable additive flag.

Experiment 3 (H2 - A locatable live-polarity representation that degrades under load): Tests that each proposition's live polarity is decodable mid-chain, that decodability degrades as load rises, and that low decodability predicts drops. Data/protocol: hidden states at each proposition-mention position (after the polarity cue) across the battery; per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) decoding negated-vs-affirmed live polarity; a difference-in-means polarity direction from content-matched negated/affirmed contrasts; same five frozen models. Double-negation items test that the probe reads live polarity, not surface 'not'. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC for live polarity (chance 0.5), and its degradation slope with negation_count. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.80 including on double-negation items (so it is live polarity, not surface tokens), decodability degrades significantly with negation_count (slope CI excluding 0), and low mid-chain decodability predicts final polarity-drop errors (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0) - and this degradation mediates the negation_count->error effect. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.80, or a prediction rho 0.15-0.30 - a polarity representation exists but its load-degradation link to errors is tentative. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or no degradation-to-error link - no separable, load-sensitive polarity representation.

Experiment 4 (H3 - The load is causally relievable by steering and patching): Tests that restoring the polarity representation rescues dropped negations and that suppressing it induces drops. Data/protocol: (a) activation patching - on trials heading toward a polarity drop, cache the correct polarity representation of the relevant proposition from an early position and patch it into the pre-drop position; specificity via cross-proposition and random-matched-vector patches. (b) steering - amplify (+) the polarity direction for the relevant proposition under high load and suppress (-) it at low load, 4 coefficients; controls random-direction and no-steer; same five frozen models; specificity tracked on zero-negation items and fluency. Decisive metric: polarity-drop rescue rate under patching (versus cross-proposition/random), and change in accuracy/drop-rate under steering. Convincing result: correct-polarity patching rescues >=30% of pre-drop trials while cross-proposition/random patches rescue <10% (so it is the polarity, not leaked answer content), +polarity steering reduces drops by >=5 pp under high load with monotonic dose-response, -polarity steering induces drops at low load, and zero-negation accuracy and fluency are preserved. Indecision band: rescue 10-30%, or a 2-5 pp steering effect - a causal contribution present but not clean. Negative result: rescue <=random, or <2 pp steering effect - polarity is not a causally load-bearing, separable quantity.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - High-stakes clinical instance): Tests that stacking negated findings drives silent decision-flipping drops and that steering/patching reduces them. Data: ~250 clinical vignettes containing a variable count of negated findings ('no history of X', 'not on anticoagulants', 'contraindicated'), each with a labeled correct diagnostic/treatment decision and a polarity-drop-induced flip; adapted from MedQA/MedMCQA stems. Protocol: same five frozen models; vary negated-finding count; compare no-steer against polarity steering/patching on fine-distinction cases; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: silent decision-flip rate as a function of negated-finding count, and its reduction under intervention. Convincing result: flip rate rises with negated-finding count (slope CI excluding 0) and polarity steering/patching cuts flips on fine-distinction cases by >=6 pp versus no-steer, without harming zero-negation matched cases. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp reduction - safety-relevant but modest. Negative result: no count-dependent flip rise, or <2 pp reduction - the polarity load does not manifest as a controllable clinical hazard, bounding its practical reach.


Rival-hypothesis controls and analysis: beyond the equal-length surface-modifier control, we include marker-free logically-equivalent reformulations (separating representational additivity from surface 'not'-familiarity), balance answer frequency, and verify that patching cannot leak answer content (single-proposition polarity patches with cross-proposition/random specificity checks). The mediation test requires that mid-chain polarity-decodability degradation temporally PRECEDES the drop error rather than merely co-occurring. Sample sizes, model comparisons, and effect-size thresholds are pre-registered with 95% CIs rather than treated as arbitrary cutoffs, and the item templates plus the two-annotator meaning-preservation protocol (target >=90% agreement) are documented in the released benchmark.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The negation-count effect could reflect general difficulty rather than a specific polarity load; mitigated by content/length/depth matching, the equal-length non-negation surface-modifier control, and the polarity-drop error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC dropped-negation answer, not random). (2) Adding negations may subtly change meaning/plausibility; we use minimal edits, verify with an entailment check and human spot-checks, and balance which propositions are negated. (3) Instruction-tuned models may handle a few negations robustly, flattening the curve at low counts; we push to higher negation counts, include harder chains, and test multiple models - a curve that only bends at high load is still informative. (4) The polarity probe may capture surface 'not' tokens rather than a maintained live-polarity representation; mitigated by probing at proposition-mention positions after the cue, held-out validation, testing on double-negation (surface has 'not' but live polarity is positive), and random-direction steering controls. (5) Patching could rescue by leaking answer content; we patch only the polarity representation of a single proposition (not the answer) and use cross-proposition/random specificity controls. (6) The polarity direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by content-matched negated/affirmed contrasts, specificity checks on zero-negation items, and the double-negation test. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (no compounding load, errors not polarity-shaped, no separable polarity signal) is itself informative: it would indicate LLMs encode negation into content rather than as a separable, load-bearing flag. (9) The 'polarity load / working memory' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like working memory; clinical experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only. (10) We treat the additive-flag claim as one of several rival representational hypotheses (additive flag vs content-entangled encoding vs uncertainty collapse vs surface-token tracking) and state which distinguishing signature each predicts, so the strongest claim is asserted only if the double-negation, marker-free, and patching-specificity tests jointly support it.

Name: associative_fan_interference
Title: The Fan Effect in LLMs: Does Associative Priming of Absent Distractors Hijack Factual Retrieval and Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: The human fan effect — retrieval of a fact slows and errs when the queried concept is linked to many competing associates — transfers to LLMs at the level of reasoning, not just next-token copying: incidentally mentioning concepts semantically associated with (but not the same as) the correct answer earlier in a prompt causes graded, associative-strength-dependent retrieval errors that pull the model toward the associated-but-wrong answer, and this retrieval-competition is a locatable, steerable internal signal distinct from literal token-copying (contextual entrainment).
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs exhibit semantic priming (Misra 2020) and structural priming (Prasad 2022), that fact retrieval can be hijacked by meaning-preserving context (Do LLMs dream of elephants, 2024), and that LMs assign higher probability to any literal context tokens via 'entrainment heads' regardless of relevance (Llama See Llama Do: Contextual Entrainment, 2025). Content-effect debiasing steers a validity-vs-plausibility direction (K-CAST, 2025). Crucially, ALL of these study either (a) next-token/lexical-decision priming, (b) hijacking by tokens or paraphrases that literally appear, or (c) copying of literal context tokens (entrainment). NONE test the human FAN EFFECT (Anderson 1974): that retrieval accuracy/latency degrades as a function of how many competing ASSOCIATES a concept has, that mentioning an ASSOCIATED-BUT-ABSENT distractor concept (never the answer token itself) causes multi-step reasoning to converge on the wrong-but-associated answer, that this scales with graded associative strength, or that a retrieval-competition representation (distinct from token-copying entrainment heads) mediates it. My prior proposals covered ambiguity-branch collapse, canonicalization, and pragmatic enrichment but never associative-fan retrieval interference. We uniquely transfer the fan effect into LLM reasoning as a graded associative-strength law with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes clinical instance. Novelty locus: the primary contribution is the behavioral phenomenon — graded, associative-strength-dependent interference from associated-but-ABSENT distractors (the answer token never appears) — sharply separated from token-copying/contextual entrainment and from paraphrase/meaning-preserving hijacking (where the answer or its paraphrase IS present); the mechanistic dissociation (a retrieval-competition signal distinct from entrainment heads) and the clinical case are secondary. Mechanistic hypothesis with a falsification criterion: retrieval competition should predict lure errors on items where NO literal answer token exists and should be separable (low head/layer overlap) from entrainment heads; if the signal instead coincides with entrainment heads or vanishes without literal presence, the retrieval-competition account is falsified and the effect reduces to entrainment.
Abstract: Human memory shows the fan effect: the more associations a concept has, the slower and more error-prone it is to retrieve any single fact about it, because associates compete during retrieval. We ask whether large language models suffer an analogous, reasoning-level failure: does incidentally mentioning concepts semantically associated with the correct answer — without ever stating the answer itself — hijack the model's factual retrieval and multi-step reasoning toward the associated-but-wrong answer? We make three claims. First, associative interference is real and graded: seeding a prompt with distractor concepts of increasing associative strength to the correct answer produces a monotonically rising rate of associated-lure errors, over and above surface difficulty, and this interference is distinct from literal token-copying because the distractors are never the answer token. Second, it follows a fan law: interference scales with the NUMBER of competing associates and their associative strength, mirroring Anderson's fan effect, and is largest exactly when the correct fact is weakly represented. Third, it is causal and steerable: a probe reads a retrieval-competition signal from hidden states that predicts lure errors before they surface, and this signal is separable from the located token-copying entrainment heads; steering along a 'retrieval-competition' direction (or ablating it) reduces associated-lure errors, while amplifying it induces them. We evaluate across several open-weight models on factual QA and multi-hop reasoning, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where mentioning an associated-but-wrong drug or diagnosis silently biases the answer. Our work reframes semantic association as a controllable retrieval-interference hazard for machine reasoning. The phenomenon bears directly on RAG, tool use, and safety-critical QA, where retrieved or in-context mentions of related-but-wrong entities could silently bias answers; if it holds, model evaluation should add an associative-robustness slice and mitigation should target the retrieval-competition signal. We treat the clinical setting as an illustrative case study of external validity, not a separate impact pillar.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Graded associative interference, selective versus non-associated distraction): Tests that mentioning concepts associated with (but never equal to) the correct answer raises associated-lure errors beyond generic distraction. Data: a fan-effect QA battery, ~300 items each for (a) single-fact retrieval (one correct entity/value; base facts sampled from TriviaQA, Natural Questions, and the LAMA probe set) and (b) 2-3 hop reasoning with a definite answer (built over the same fact sources). Per base item, generate matched prompt variants that incidentally mention DISTRACTOR concepts semantically associated with the correct answer but never the answer token itself (e.g., for answer 'aspirin', seed 'ibuprofen', 'acetaminophen'). Associative strength is set from free-association norms (USF, SWOW) plus embedding cosine, giving conditions: 0 distractors, 1 weak-associate, 1 strong-associate, and a FAN condition with 2-4 associates. Each item has a labeled correct answer and labeled associated-lure answers, plus a NON-ASSOCIATED equal-length distractor control and a LITERAL-COPY control (a distractor that IS the answer token). We construct the seeding because no existing set controls associative strength while holding the base fact fixed; 300/family covers the graded conditions with power and keeps items within well-covered association-norm vocabulary. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Decisive metric: associated-lure error rate (fraction of responses equal to the labeled associate), modeled as lure_rate ~ associative_strength + n_associates + item_difficulty + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: a strong-associate distractor raises the associated-lure rate by >=8 pp over the 0-distractor baseline AND over the equal-length non-associated control (both CIs excluding 0), with errors concentrated on the specific associate (the diagnostic that association, not generic confusion, drives failure). Indecision band: a 3-8 pp rise, or an effect not clearly separable from the non-associated control - directional but weak. Negative result: <3 pp rise or no larger than non-associated distraction - LLM retrieval is robust to associated-but-absent competitors, dissociating it from the human fan effect.

Experiment 2 (H2 - A fan law and a fan-by-fact-strength interaction): Tests that interference scales with the number and strength of associates and is largest when the correct fact is weakly represented. Data/protocol: the same battery, using the graded n_associates (0-4) and strength conditions; estimate each correct fact's representational strength via baseline solve rate / logit margin; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the slope of associated-lure rate on the number of competing associates (and on graded strength), and the fan x fact-strength interaction coefficient. Convincing result: lure rate rises monotonically with n_associates (fan slope CI excluding 0) and with associative strength, and interference is significantly larger for weakly-represented facts (interaction CI excluding 0) - mirroring Anderson's fan effect and its strength interaction. Indecision band: a positive but shallow fan slope (CI grazing 0) or an interaction that trends but is not significant - fan structure suggestive only. Negative result: flat fan slope and no strength interaction - no fan law, even if a single-associate effect exists.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Dissociation from literal-copy contextual entrainment): Tests that associated-but-absent interference is distinct from over-copying literal context tokens. Data/protocol: contrast associated-but-absent distractors versus literal-copy distractors (the answer token itself present in context); same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the associated-lure rate for associated-but-absent distractors, and whether it persists where entrainment (literal copying) cannot apply, plus the divergence in error signatures (entrainment boosts the literal token; fan interference boosts a non-present associate). Convincing result: associated-but-absent interference is substantial (>=5 pp over baseline) on items with no literal answer token in context, and the two conditions show distinct error signatures - fan interference is not reducible to entrainment. Indecision band: associated-but-absent interference present but small (2-5 pp), or signatures partly overlapping - dissociation unclear. Negative result: associated-but-absent interference vanishes without literal presence, i.e., the effect fully reduces to contextual entrainment - itself an informative reframing.

Experiment 4 (H3 - A locatable retrieval-competition signal separable from entrainment heads, with mediation): Tests that a hidden-state signal predicts lure errors and is distinct from the token-copying entrainment mechanism. Data/protocol: contrast pre-answer hidden states on interference-error vs correct trials (matched content); per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) decoding impending associated-lure error; a difference-in-means retrieval-competition direction; separately localize entrainment heads via differentiable masking and measure overlap; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC for impending lure error (chance 0.5), the Spearman correlation between per-item signal and per-item lure error, and the overlap between the retrieval-competition signal and localized entrainment heads. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.75, per-item signal predicts lure errors (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0) and mediates the associative_strength->error effect, and the signal is separable from entrainment heads (low head/layer overlap) - the key novel dissociation. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.75, mediation rho 0.15-0.30, or moderate overlap with entrainment heads - a signal that is real but not cleanly distinct. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or the signal coincides with entrainment heads - no separate retrieval-competition mechanism.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Causal steering reduces and induces associated-lure errors): Tests that the retrieval-competition direction is causally load-bearing. Data/protocol: steer -retrieval-competition (or ablate the associated distractor's attention contribution) to test error reduction, and steer +retrieval-competition to induce associated-lure errors even without distractors present; 4 coefficients; controls random-direction, no-steer, and (for contrast) ablating entrainment heads; same five frozen models; specificity tracked on no-distractor items and fluency. Decisive metric: change in associated-lure error rate under steering versus no-steer/random. Convincing result: -direction (or distractor-attention ablation) reduces associated-lure errors by >=6 pp with monotonic dose-response, +direction induces >=6 pp of lures without distractors, random-direction moves <2 pp, the intervention differs from entrainment-head ablation, and no-distractor accuracy and fluency are preserved. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp effect or a non-monotonic dose - causal but not clean. Negative result: <2 pp effect or no better than random - the retrieval-competition direction is not causally responsible for the interference.

Experiment 6 (H1/H3 - High-stakes clinical instance): Tests that associative seeding silently biases clinical answers and that intervention reduces it. Data: ~300 clinical QA/vignette items where an associated-but-wrong drug, diagnosis, or symptom (same drug class or differential) precedes the question; adapted from MedQA/MedMCQA. Protocol: same five frozen models; compare no-seed, associated-seed, and retrieval-competition steering / distractor-attention ablation on fine-distinction cases; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: associated-error rate on fine-distinction clinical cases, and its reduction under intervention. Convincing result: associative seeding raises the clinical associated-error rate by >=6 pp over no-seed, and steering/ablation cuts it by >=6 pp without harming no-seed matched cases. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp seeding effect or reduction - safety-relevant but modest. Negative result: no clinical seeding effect or <2 pp reduction - the fan interference does not manifest as a controllable clinical hazard.


Additional controls and pre-registration: Experiment 1 adds matched controls for answer frequency, prompt length, and a PARAPHRASE-HIJACK condition (a meaning-preserving mention of the answer) so that associated-but-absent interference is separated from both generic distraction and hijacking; the fan-law analysis pre-registers the fan-count x associative-strength interaction as the primary quantitative test with planned effect sizes and power, reported via mixed-effects models with 95% CIs. A precise comparison table (output variable, mechanism, observable, intervention target) positions the effect against contextual entrainment, semantic priming, and context hijacking. The mechanistic/clinical arm is scoped as a secondary extension of the primary behavioral study.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Associated-distractor interference could be generic distraction rather than semantic association; mitigated by the non-associated equal-length distractor control, the graded associative-strength dose-response, and the associated-lure error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC associate, not random). (2) The effect may overlap with contextual entrainment; we explicitly contrast associated-but-absent vs literal-copy distractors and test signal separability from located entrainment heads, so a finding of overlap is itself informative and a finding of separability is the key novel result. (3) Associative-strength norms (USF/SWOW) have limited coverage and are English-centric; we restrict items to well-covered concepts, cross-check with embedding cosine, and report robustness. (4) Instruction-tuned models may resist distraction, flattening the fan curve; we include weakly-known facts (where interference should be largest), harder multi-hop items, base variants, and multiple models — a curve that bends only for weak facts still confirms the fan-x-strength interaction. (5) The retrieval-competition direction may entangle with generic difficulty/uncertainty; mitigated by matched error/correct contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, no-distractor specificity checks, and comparison against the entrainment-head baseline. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (no graded associative interference, or it fully reduces to literal entrainment) is itself informative: it would show LLM retrieval is robust to associated-but-absent competitors, dissociating it from the human fan effect. (8) The fan-effect framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like memory; clinical experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only.

Name: grammatical_evidentiality_calibration
Title: Grammar of Knowing: Does Obligatory Evidential Marking Make LLMs Track Their Sources and Calibrate Better?
Short Hypothesis: Some human languages grammatically force speakers to mark HOW they know something (firsthand perception vs. inference vs. hearsay).
