We hypothesize that when an LLM reasons in, or is scaffolded by, an evidentiality-marking grammar, it more sharply separates the provenance of its beliefs internally and becomes better calibrated — assigning lower confidence to hearsay/inference-derived claims and higher to firsthand-supported ones — than when reasoning in a language (like English) that leaves evidence-source grammatically optional.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here but have never been connected. (1) LLM calibration/verbalized uncertainty: models can verbalize calibrated confidence (Teaching Models to Express Uncertainty, 2022), verbal uncertainty is a single linear feature only moderately aligned with semantic uncertainty (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty as a Linear Feature, 2025), verbalized confidence often mimics superficial certainty cues rather than being content-grounded (TracVC, 2026), and epistemic-modal sensitivity grows with depth (Mapping Clinical Doubt, 2025). All of this is essentially monolingual (English) and treats confidence as a scalar, ignoring information SOURCE. (2) Linguistic evidentiality: cross-linguistic studies show grammatical evidential markers change perceived certainty and psychological distance (Evidentiality & Construal Level Theory, 2014; Source vs. Stance, 2018; Perceiving Speaker's Certainty, 2025), and that grammatical (Turkish) vs. lexical (English) evidentiality is processed differently. No prior work asks whether an LLM's calibration and its internal representation of knowledge PROVENANCE depend on whether the operative grammar obligatorily encodes information source. We narrow novelty to three deltas over the closest prior work: (a) SOURCE-DECOMPOSED calibration (per-evidence-type ECE and a source-grading score) rather than the scalar verbalized uncertainty of the calibration literature; (b) a grammar-vs-reflection CAUSAL contrast that a Turkish-style trust-manipulation benchmark cannot provide, since trust manipulation changes a source's reliability but does not test whether obligatory evidential MARKING (vs. an equally long non-evidential reflection step) improves source-conditioned calibration and internal source separability; and (c) source-DIRECTION steering beyond the single linear verbal-uncertainty feature. Source-sensitivity itself is not claimed as new; the novelty is its grammatical routing and internal separability. Evidential grammar differs from ordinary prompted reflection/CoT because it obligatorily forces a source commitment before the assertion, which we isolate with a length-matched non-evidential reflection control.
Abstract: Human languages differ in whether they grammatically force speakers to mark how they came to know something: evidentiality-marking languages (e.g., Turkish, Quechua, Japanese to varying degrees) obligatorily distinguish firsthand perception, inference, and hearsay, whereas English marks this only optionally through lexical hedges. Cognitive science shows these grammatical markers systematically shift perceived certainty and psychological distance. We ask whether this feature of language shapes machine intelligence: does reasoning under an evidentiality-marking grammar make a large language model track the provenance of its own beliefs and calibrate its confidence more faithfully? We introduce a source-decomposed view of calibration in which each claim is tagged by its evidence type, and we measure whether confidence is appropriately graded by source (lower for hearsay/inference, higher for firsthand-supported). We test three conditions on identical questions: reasoning in evidentiality-marking languages, reasoning in English, and reasoning in English with an explicit evidential scaffold that requires the model to name its information source before answering. We predict that evidential grammar (native or scaffolded) yields better source-conditioned calibration, sharper internal separability of source types, and reduced overconfident hallucination on hearsay/inference claims. Mechanistically, we test whether an 'evidential-source direction' exists in representation space, whether evidentiality-marking grammars increase its use, and whether steering along it improves calibration. We tie the 'so what' to concrete failure modes - RAG answers, citation generation, and medical/legal/multilingual assistants that assert hearsay or inference with unwarranted confidence - and specify the practitioner action (adopt evidential scaffolds, source-aware calibration metrics, or source-direction steering) and a target win (reduction in confident unsupported answers at fixed accuracy). Because the English evidential scaffold is the central, deployment-ready intervention, the result is usable even in English-only systems, with the cross-lingual comparison as a supporting test. We pre-register the key prediction that source-direction steering beats the linear verbal-uncertainty baseline specifically on hearsay/inference items (not just overall calibration), and a minimum success criterion for venue-worthiness: source-conditioned calibration gains over BOTH plain English and a length-matched non-evidential reflection scaffold, plus steering gains over the linear VUF baseline on held-out tasks. A null result is itself impactful - it rules out a widely appealing linguistic route to calibration. We avoid claiming a literal 'internal provenance representation' unless the source-direction steering and separability controls jointly support it. Across several open-weight multilingual models we quantify source-conditioned calibration error, source separability, and steering controllability. Our work reframes calibration as a partly grammar-dependent capacity and offers a simple, training-free intervention grounded in linguistic typology.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Source-tagged QA construction): Prerequisite. Data: a built set of ~600 questions, each with a short context passage engineered so the answer's support is one of three evidence types - firsthand/direct (fact stated explicitly and verifiably in context), inference (must be logically derived), and hearsay/unreliable (reported only by an unreliable in-context source or absent, so the correct stance is low confidence); plus a no-context internal-knowledge variant tagged by whether the model actually knows the answer (measured via repeated sampling). Ground-truth correctness known for all items. Source categories are operationalized precisely: 'firsthand' (answer explicitly and verifiably stated in context), 'inference' (must be logically derived from context), 'hearsay-unreliable' (asserted only by an in-context unreliable source), and 'no-context internal knowledge' (tagged by whether the model actually knows, via repeated sampling); evidence source is crossed with truth status so the two are separable. Dataset design balances domain, difficulty, truth label, and source type, with an annotation protocol, adjudication, and worked examples of each item class. Multiple annotators tag evidence type. Decisive metric first: inter-annotator agreement on evidence-type tags. Convincing result: kappa >=0.6; ambiguous items dropped. Indecision band: kappa 0.4-0.6 - items adjudicated or removed. Negative result (kappa <0.4): the evidence-type construct is too unstable and items are redesigned.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Evidential grammar improves source-conditioned calibration): The central calibration test. Data: each item translated (back-translation checked) into English (optional evidentiality) and 2-3 evidentiality-marking languages (e.g., Turkish, Japanese, and Quechua or Bulgarian per model coverage), plus a fourth condition, English + Evidential Scaffold (the model must first output an evidential tag - 'I saw this stated' / 'I inferred this' / 'this is only reported/unknown' - before answering and giving confidence), a fifth control condition, English + length-matched non-evidential reflection scaffold, and scaffold ablations for content and position (source-first vs. source-after prompt, and an explicit source LABEL without evidential grammar) to localize which aspect drives any gain. Multilingual controls include native-speaker prompt validation, translation/back-translation checks, lexicalized-evidential controls, and a within-language minimal-pair manipulation where only the evidential marking changes. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B, all weights frozen; confidence is extracted by a fixed procedure - verbalized confidence normalized to a common scale across languages and log-prob confidence made comparable via per-model calibration - both elicited, 5 samples/item, seeds 0/1/2. A pre-registered power analysis sets the required sample size per cell; because 600 items stratify across five conditions and multiple models, we expand items if interaction power is insufficient. Systems compared: the five conditions. Decisive metric first: source-conditioned Expected Calibration Error (ECE computed within each evidence-type stratum, then averaged) and a Source-Grading Score = degree to which mean confidence is correctly ordered firsthand > inference > hearsay; analyzed as ECE/Source-Grading ~ condition + per_language_accuracy + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: evidentiality-marking grammar (native OR scaffolded) lowers source-conditioned ECE and raises the Source-Grading Score relative to plain English AND relative to the length-matched non-evidential reflection scaffold (95% CI on both contrasts excluding zero), after controlling for accuracy, in at least 3 of 5 models. Indecision band: the evidential-vs-control-scaffold contrast CI spanning zero - any gain is generic reflection/prompt structure, not source-marking, so grammar per se does not improve calibration. Negative result (evidential conditions worsen source-conditioned calibration): refutes the grammar-calibration link.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Evidential conditions reduce overconfident hallucination): Tests the abstention prediction. Data: the hearsay/unknown items where correct behavior is low confidence or abstention. Models: same five, frozen. Decisive metric first: confident-error rate (high-confidence wrong answers) per condition. Convincing result: evidential conditions significantly lower the confident-error rate vs. plain English and vs. the non-evidential reflection control (CI excluding zero). Indecision band: confident-error-rate difference CI spanning zero - evidential marking does not curb overconfidence. Negative result (higher confident-error rate under evidential conditions): contradicts the prediction.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Sharper internal source separability and an evidential-source direction): Mechanistic test. Data: mid/late-layer hidden states on matched items across conditions. Models: same five, frozen; trainable component is a linear probe classifying the three evidence types (seeds 0/1/2, item-disjoint split); a difference-in-means 'evidential-source direction' (firsthand vs. hearsay) is also extracted. Systems compared: source separability across conditions; magnitude of use of the evidential-source direction across conditions. Decisive metric first: probe AUROC (macro over the three evidence types) for source separability. Convincing result: evidentiality-marking grammars/scaffold significantly raise separability AUROC vs. plain English (CI excluding zero) and increase use of the evidential-source direction. Indecision band: AUROC difference CI spanning zero - grammar does not sharpen internal source representation, so the calibration effect (if any) is not mechanistically localized here. Negative result (lower separability under evidential conditions): no internal source-tracking benefit. We pre-define what counts as a genuine source direction versus a generic certainty/verbosity/sentiment artifact: the direction must classify source type on item-disjoint held-out data, survive partialling out scalar certainty and length, and its steering must move source-conditioned calibration specifically on hearsay/inference.

Experiment 5 (H4 - Steering the evidential-source direction improves calibration): Causal test. Data: 400 held-out plain-English items (item-disjoint from probe training). Models: same five, frozen; steering adds the evidential-source direction at inference in the plain-English condition; strength tuned on a dev split, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: no-steer, random-direction steering (matched norm), the linear verbalized-uncertainty-feature baseline from prior work, and evidential-source steering. Decisive metric first: change in source-conditioned ECE; secondary: confident-hallucination rate and fluency. Convincing result: evidential-source steering lowers source-conditioned ECE and confident-hallucination more than random-direction steering and the verbalized-uncertainty baseline (difference CI excluding zero) without harming fluency. Indecision band: steering effect within the random-direction control's CI - the direction is not a usable causal calibration lever. Negative result (steering worsens calibration or collapses fluency): no causal control. All calibration analyses are accuracy-stratified so improvements reflect calibration not competence; every number is planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over items, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Evidentiality-marking languages may be lower-resource for these models, confounding grammar effects with competence; mitigated by accuracy-stratified calibration metrics, back-translation checks, and by the English+scaffold condition which isolates evidential structure without changing language resource level. (2) The scaffold could improve calibration simply by adding a reflection step; we include a length-matched non-evidential reflection scaffold as a control to isolate the source-marking contribution. (3) Verbalized confidence may mimic surface certainty cues (per TracVC 2026) rather than content; we cross-check with log-prob confidence and the internal source-separability probe. (4) Constructing clean firsthand/inference/hearsay items is hard and somewhat subjective; we use multiple annotators and report robustness to item-set choices. (5) The 'evidential-source direction' may entangle with generic sentiment/certainty; random-direction controls and the linear-VUF baseline from prior work help disentangle. (6) A null result (grammar does not affect source-conditioned calibration) is still informative, showing calibration is grammar-independent and that any gains from evidential scaffolding are purely prompt-structural rather than typological.

Name: register_gated_competence
Title: Speaking Down to the Model: Does Colloquial Register Silently Lock an LLM Out of Its Own Competence?
Short Hypothesis: Holding language and semantic content constant, phrasing a problem in a low/colloquial register (slang, texting style, non-standard grammar) versus a high/formal register systematically suppresses an LLM's reasoning competence, and this register penalty is NOT explained by comprehension failure but by the model entering a 'casual/low-effort' processing mode; this mode is a locatable, steerable internal signal, so the model demonstrably possesses the competence but is locked out of it by the register of the surface form.
Related Work: Prior work on surface-form brittleness studies paraphrase robustness generically (Paraphrase and Solve/SCoP, 2024; my prior canonicalization_convergence proposal treated meaning-preserving paraphrase clusters), syntactic complexity of the INPUT (Syntactic Blind Spots, 2025), and multilingual/pivot effects on reasoning (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025). Sociolinguistic register/style is studied for detection and generation (style transfer, formality classifiers) and for bias against non-standard dialects (dialect prejudice in LLMs, 2024), but that work targets fairness/toxicity, not whether register GATES reasoning COMPETENCE. No prior work (a) isolates the high-vs-low register axis while holding language and content fixed as a reasoning-competence manipulation, (b) dissociates a register penalty from comprehension (showing competence is present but inaccessible), or (c) locates and steers a 'processing-register/effort mode' that mediates it. My prior proposals covered language choice, word order, morphology, evidentiality, tense, and paraphrase canonicalization, but never sociolinguistic register as a competence gate. This is distinct: register is orthogonal to language, meaning, and syntactic difficulty, and the claim is that a socially-coded but logically-irrelevant surface cue silently degrades reasoning. We concede that the raw low-register reasoning penalty is largely prior art (register-shift and dialect-prejudice studies, e.g. ReDial/EnDive-style evaluations); our delta is mechanistic, not a new benchmark result. Those works show non-standard phrasing lowers accuracy but never test restatement recovery, a formalize-then-solve two-step, or mediation/patching of a processing-mode representation. Novelty locus: the comprehension-vs-mode DISSOCIATION (competence present but locked out) plus CAUSAL steering/patching of a located register-mode direction. Register is defined operationally as the formal/casual style axis and separated by ablation from dialect, verbosity, slang, tokenization, and grammatical noise.
Abstract: Humans code-switch between a formal 'high' register and a casual 'low' register, and the register we hear shapes how carefully we assume the speaker is thinking. We ask whether large language models inherit an analogous, logically-unwarranted coupling: does phrasing a problem casually make the model reason worse, even though the content is identical? We hypothesize a register-gated competence effect. Holding language and semantics fixed, we rewrite reasoning problems in a high/formal register (standard grammar, precise, professional) versus a low/colloquial register (slang, texting abbreviations, non-standard grammar, filler). We predict low-register phrasing lowers reasoning accuracy relative to high-register phrasing, that this penalty is largest on genuinely hard items, and crucially that it is NOT a comprehension failure: the model can restate the low-register problem correctly and, when forced or steered into a formal processing mode, recovers the lost accuracy, demonstrating the competence was present but locked out. Mechanistically, we test whether the model carries a 'processing-register/effort' signal that low register engages: a probe reads formal-vs-casual mode from hidden states before reasoning and predicts the penalty, and steering along a located register-mode direction (or patching the formal-mode representation) rescues low-register accuracy while suppressing it induces the penalty on formally-phrased items. We evaluate on math, logic, and multi-hop QA across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where a patient's casual, colloquial description of symptoms silently degrades diagnostic accuracy relative to a clinician's formal chart phrasing of the identical facts. Our work reframes register from a stylistic surface feature into a controllable gate on machine reasoning. The settings that care most are clinical intake, tutoring, consumer support, and low-literacy or code-switched interfaces, where users naturally speak casually; we frame the result as an actionable robustness/fairness diagnostic and measure downstream consequences beyond accuracy — unsafe-advice and refusal rates and calibration error — not just a sociolinguistic curiosity. We use 'competence' only insofar as the restatement, two-step-recovery, and steering/patching dissociations support it; if register does not gate reasoning once content is controlled, the finding is a reassuring null about register-invariance.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - A register penalty, isolated from length and largest on hard items): Tests that low/colloquial register lowers reasoning accuracy versus high/formal register when content and answer are held constant. Data: a register-paired battery, ~250 items each across three families (~750): multi-step arithmetic/GSM-style (adapted from GSM8K), deductive logic chains depth 2-6 (built), and 2WikiMultiHop-style multi-hop QA (sampled). For each item a HIGH-register rendering (standard formal English) and a LOW-register rendering (colloquial: slang, texting abbreviations 'u/ur/gonna', dropped articles, filler 'like/basically', non-standard grammar) preserve exact content and answer, generated via templated transforms plus an LLM stylizer and VERIFIED meaning-preserving by back-translation, an entailment check, and human spot-checks. An INTERMEDIATE register and a length-matched padded-formal control separate register from length. We construct because no existing set pairs identical reasoning content across a controlled register axis; 250/family keeps meaning-preservation verification affordable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Decisive metric: accuracy, modeled as accuracy ~ register * item_difficulty + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: LOW register lowers accuracy versus HIGH by >=5 pp (main-effect CI excluding 0), the gap widens on harder items (register x difficulty interaction CI excluding 0), and the padded-formal control shows <2 pp change (isolating register from length/verbosity). Indecision band: a 2-5 pp register gap, or an interaction CI grazing 0 - a directional penalty that is not established. Negative result: <2 pp gap, or a padded-formal control that shows the same drop - reasoning is register-invariant (any behavioral penalty is length/tokenization, not register).

Experiment 2 (H1 - Comprehension dissociation and two-step recovery): The key claim that the penalty is a processing-mode gate, not a comprehension failure - the competence is present but locked out. Data/protocol: on the same LOW-register items, measure (a) whether the model can accurately RESTATE/formalize the problem (comprehension check) and (b) on items it restates correctly but answers wrong, whether failure is register-driven rather than misunderstanding; add a TWO-STEP prompt (first formalize, then solve) and test recovery; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the gap between restatement accuracy and answer accuracy on LOW-register items, and the fraction of the register penalty recovered by the two-step prompt. Convincing result: high restatement accuracy (>=90% of HIGH-register answer accuracy) coexists with low LOW-register answer accuracy - competence present, access blocked - and the two-step formalize-then-solve prompt recovers >=60% of the register penalty (CI excluding 0), pinning the effect on processing mode rather than understanding. Indecision band: partial dissociation (restatement only modestly above answer accuracy) or 30-60% two-step recovery - the comprehension-vs-mode account is not clean. Negative result: restatement accuracy tracks answer accuracy (both low) and two-step gives little recovery - the penalty is genuine comprehension difficulty, refuting the locked-out-competence claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 - A locatable processing-register/effort mode that mediates the penalty): Tests that a formal-vs-casual mode is decodable before reasoning and predicts the per-item penalty. Data/protocol: contrast pre-answer hidden states on HIGH vs LOW renderings (matched content); per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) decoding formal-vs-casual mode; a difference-in-means formal-mode direction; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC for formal-vs-casual mode (chance 0.5), and the Spearman correlation between per-item casual-mode engagement and per-item accuracy drop. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.80, low register engages a distinct casual mode, and mode engagement predicts the per-item penalty (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0), mediating register->accuracy. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.80 or mediation rho 0.15-0.30 - a mode representation exists but its link to the penalty is tentative. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or no engagement-penalty link - no locatable processing-mode signal to explain a behavioral penalty.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Causal rescue via steering and patching): Tests that manipulating the formal-mode representation rescues low-register accuracy and induces the penalty on formal items, holding content fixed. Data/protocol: (a) steering - +formal-mode on LOW-register items and -formal-mode on HIGH-register items, 4 coefficients; controls random-direction and no-steer. (b) patching - cache the pre-reasoning representation from the HIGH-register version and patch it into the LOW-register forward pass before any solution content; specificity via cross-item and random-matched patches. Same five frozen models; specificity tracked on HIGH-register accuracy and fluency. Decisive metric: change in LOW-register accuracy under +formal-mode steering and under HIGH->LOW patching, versus no-steer/random. Convincing result: +formal-mode steering raises LOW-register accuracy toward the HIGH-register level by >=4 pp (monotonic dose-response), -formal-mode induces the penalty on HIGH-register items, HIGH->LOW patching rescues LOW-register accuracy while cross-item/random patches do not (<1.5 pp), random-direction moves <2 pp, and HIGH-register accuracy and fluency are preserved. Indecision band: a 2-4 pp rescue or patching that partly overlaps the random control - causal contribution present but not clean. Negative result: <2 pp rescue or no better than random - the formal-mode direction is not causally responsible for the penalty.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - High-stakes clinical instance): Tests that colloquial patient phrasing silently degrades diagnosis and that formal-mode intervention reduces misdiagnosis. Data: ~250 register-paired clinical vignettes where identical diagnostic facts are phrased colloquially (patient-reported, casual) vs formally (clinician chart); adapted from MedQA/MedMCQA stems, meaning-preservation verified. Protocol: same five frozen models; compare colloquial vs formal phrasing and formal-mode steering/patching on fine-distinction cases; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: diagnostic misdiagnosis rate on fine-distinction cases as a function of register, and its reduction under intervention. Convincing result: colloquial phrasing raises misdiagnosis by >=6 pp over formal phrasing of identical facts, and formal-mode steering/patching cuts the colloquial misdiagnosis rate by >=6 pp without harming formal-phrasing matched cases. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp register effect or reduction - safety-relevant but modest. Negative result: no register effect on diagnosis, or <2 pp reduction - the register gate does not manifest as a controllable clinical hazard, bounding its practical reach.


Register-isolation ablations and downstream measures: Experiment 1 adds controls separating register from length, sentiment/politeness, lexical rarity, punctuation, dialect, and instruction tone (each varied independently while holding content fixed), with semantic equivalence validated by back-translation, entailment, and human spot-checks on all paired prompts; the mediation test and its falsification condition (no engagement-penalty link) are pre-registered; and Experiment 5 additionally reports refusal rate, unsafe-advice rate, and calibration under colloquial versus formal phrasing so the clinical stakes are quantified beyond raw accuracy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Low-register renderings may not be perfectly meaning-preserving, confounding register with subtle content change; mitigated by back-translation, entailment checks, human spot-checks, and templated minimal transforms. (2) The penalty could reflect genuine comprehension difficulty rather than a processing-mode gate; the comprehension/restatement dissociation, the two-step (formalize-then-solve) recovery, and the causal formal-mode steering/patching (which hold content fixed) are designed precisely to distinguish these. (3) Register may confound with token length or tokenization of slang; addressed by the length-matched padded-formal control and by testing that the effect tracks register, not length. (4) Instruction-tuned models may be robust to register, flattening the effect (ceiling); we include harder items, base variants, an intermediate register, and multiple models - a penalty concentrated on hard items is still informative. (5) The formal-mode direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence rather than register per se; mitigated by content-matched high/low contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and high-register specificity checks. (6) Patching could rescue by leaking answer content; we patch only the pre-reasoning problem representation (no solution tokens) with cross-item/random specificity controls. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (register does not gate competence once content is controlled) is itself informative, showing LLM reasoning is register-invariant and that any behavioral penalty is pure comprehension. (9) The register/diglossia framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like sociolinguistic cognition; clinical experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only.

Name: pragmatic_enrichment_default
Title: Reading Between the Lines When You Shouldn't: A Pragmatic-Enrichment Default as a Hidden Reasoning Failure Mode in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs, like humans, apply a pragmatic-enrichment default — spontaneously upgrading literal meaning with Gricean inferences (scalar implicature 'some'→'not all', exhaustivity, relevance-driven additions) — and this default is beneficial for cooperative dialogue but silently corrupts tasks that require the strict literal reading (formal logic, contracts, statutes, clinical instructions). This enrichment is a locatable, steerable internal 'pragmatic-mode' signal that fires by default; suppressing it at literal-mode tasks reduces enrichment errors, while amplifying it induces them even on cases where the literal reading is required. We narrow to one crisp primary contribution: a LITERAL-REQUIRED failure mode of pragmatic enrichment that is causally reducible by steering a probeable pragmatic-enrichment direction. We treat 'pragmatic-mode' as an operationally defined, probeable latent direction, not a claimed new mechanistic entity, and we do not weight the behavioral, probe, and steering claims equally.
Related Work: Existing LLM pragmatics work is behavioral or competence-oriented: LLMs partly detect implicatures and improve with Gricean CoT prompting (Is the Pope Catholic? 2023), fall short of humans on implicature/presupposition/speech acts (Pragmatic Competence Without Embodiment 2025; Manner Implicatures 2024; Are BabyLMs Deaf to Gricean Maxims 2025), and neural encoders predict scalar-inference strength from linguistic features (Harnessing the Linguistic Signal 2020). Ambiguity work locates sparse Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons that steer answering vs abstention (Sparse Neurons 2025), and loophole work shows models exploit scalar implicature (LLMs Identify Ambiguities and Exploit Loopholes 2025). ALL of this treats pragmatic enrichment as a capacity to be measured or improved. NONE frame enrichment as a DEFAULT that mis-fires as a reasoning FAILURE MODE on literal-required tasks, isolate a controllable literal-vs-enriched internal mode, test whether it causally CAUSES errors on formal/legal/clinical text, or provide a Location + Causal Intervention account with a suppression fix. My prior proposals covered ambiguity-branch collapse, evidentiality, counterfactual mood, and canonicalization but never pragmatic enrichment / the Quantity maxim as a default reasoning liability. We uniquely flip pragmatics from a desired competence into a diagnosable, steerable hazard. Sharper contrast with recent literalist-bias findings: some 2025 results report LLMs can be overly literal on figurative or implicature-laden inputs; our claim is compatible and complementary -- on tasks that REQUIRE the strict literal reading (formal logic, contracts, statutes, clinical instructions), models over-enrich, and our matched literal-vs-enriched pairs are designed to expose exactly this regime and to refine, not merely restate, the literalist-bias picture. The reusable matched-pair protocol (literal-required vs enrichment-correct items with a labeled enrichment lure) is itself a dataset/task contribution.
Abstract: Cooperative communication depends on going beyond literal meaning: when a speaker says 'some students passed,' listeners infer 'not all.' Large language models reproduce these pragmatic enrichments, and prior work treats this as a competence to celebrate. We argue the opposite is also true: pragmatic enrichment is a DEFAULT that silently corrupts reasoning whenever the task actually requires the strict literal reading — formal logic, contracts, statutes, and clinical instructions, where 'some' must mean 'at least one', an unstated condition must not be assumed, and only what is written counts. We hypothesize that an LLM carries a controllable internal 'pragmatic-mode' signal governing whether it computes literal or enriched meaning, that this mode is engaged by default, and that it is a proximal cause of systematic errors on literal-required tasks. We make three claims. First, the enrichment default is real and harmful: on matched items differing only in whether the correct answer needs the literal or the enriched reading, models over-enrich, producing characteristic errors (treating 'some' as 'not all' in a valid syllogism, importing unstated exceptions into a contract clause). Second, mode is diagnostic: a probe reads literal-vs-enriched processing from hidden states and predicts these errors before they surface. Third, mode is causal and fixable: steering down a located pragmatic-enrichment direction reduces literal-task errors, while steering it up induces enrichment even where the literal reading is required. We evaluate across several open-weight models on logic, contract, and clinical-instruction tasks, plus a high-stakes medical instance where over-reading a literal dosing instruction is dangerous, quantifying the default, its mechanistic mediation, and steering controllability. We frame the contribution as a safety/robustness issue for legal and clinical deployment, quantify how often the failure occurs in naturally occurring prompts/documents (not only synthetic matched pairs), and compare against existing guardrails/literal-instruction prompting so the practical value is explicit. If effects are modest, the phenomenon value stands: it reveals that fluent, cooperative enrichment is a default that silently violates literal constraints. We separate three hypotheses (behavioral default, probe predictivity, causal steering), pre-register the primary endpoint, and add a failure-mode analysis for cases where the probe predicts but steering does not help.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). "Pragmatic enrichment" is upgrading literal meaning with Gricean inference (scalar "some" -> "not all", exhaustivity, unstated conditions); the "enrichment lure" is the answer obtained if the enriched (rather than literal) reading is applied where the literal reading is required.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- The enrichment default is real and harmful on literal-required tasks): Tests over-enrichment on matched pairs. Data: a literal-versus-enriched matched battery of 250 items per domain -- (a) scalar implicature in logic (syllogisms/entailments where treating "some" as "not all" or "or" as exclusive flips validity), (b) exhaustivity/presupposition in contracts (clauses where importing an unstated exception or reading a list as exhaustive changes the answer), (c) clinical instructions (directives where enriching a literal statement changes the action) -- each in matched pairs differing ONLY in whether the LITERAL or the ENRICHED reading is correct, with a labeled enrichment lure, plus matched cooperative-dialogue controls where enrichment IS correct (selectivity); items are constructed from templated scalar/exhaustivity/instruction schemas with auto-checkable ground truth and expert spot-checks, 750 core items plus 250 cooperative controls. 250/domain supports stable required_mode x domain estimates within budget. Decisive metric first: enrichment-lure rate (and accuracy) on LITERAL-required versus ENRICHED-required items from mixed-effects regression lure_rate ~ required_mode * domain + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: whether errors concentrate on the specific enrichment lure (the diagnostic of reading in an unstated inference), and whether explicit "interpret literally" prompting only partially closes the gap. Convincing result: models show a reliably higher enrichment-lure rate on literal-required items than on enriched-required items (CI excludes 0), with errors concentrated on the enrichment lure, cooperative controls staying accurate, and literal-prompting closing less than half the gap (default persists). Indecision band: a literal-versus-enriched lure-rate difference within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) means no default is detectable. Negative result: no over-enrichment, or literal-required errors that are not enrichment-shaped, means pragmatic inference is contextually gated rather than a default liability, refuting H1.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Enrichment errors are not generic difficulty): Tests the matched-pair and lure-signature controls. Data: the same battery. Decisive metric first: the accuracy gap between the literal and enriched member of each matched pair (same surface content), attributable to interpretation mode rather than difficulty; secondary: fraction of literal-item errors equal to the exact enriched reading versus random wrong answers. Convincing result: the within-pair gap is reliable (CI excludes 0) and literal-item errors are predominantly the enriched reading (>= 60%), not random. Indecision band: a within-pair gap within +/-2 points, or an enriched-error fraction near chance, means the effect cannot be separated from difficulty. Negative result: errors unrelated to the enriched reading refute the enrichment interpretation of H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- A locatable pragmatic-mode signal is engaged by default and predicts errors): Tests the internal mode. Data: matched-pair items and enrichment-correct-versus-enrichment-error trials, split 70/30 by item; a linear probe (only probe trainable) on hidden states decodes enriched-versus-literal mode (per-layer held-out AUROC), and we derive a difference-in-means "pragmatic-enrichment" direction. Decisive metric first: held-out mode-decoding AUROC and the baseline projection onto the enrichment direction on literal-required items (is enrichment engaged by default?); secondary: whether per-item enrichment-mode projection predicts literal-task error and mediates required_mode -> error (Spearman). Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.70, a positive default enrichment projection on literal-required items, and enrichment projection predicts error (rho >= 0.2, CI excludes 0) and mediates the mode effect. Indecision band: AUROC 0.55-0.65 or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 means the mode signal is weak or not error-linked. Negative result: chance AUROC means no locatable pragmatic-mode signal, refuting H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Steering the enrichment direction reduces and induces enrichment errors, with preserved cooperative competence): Tests causality and specificity. Data: the enrichment direction from Experiment 3. Systems: minus-enrichment steering on literal-required items (reduce errors), plus-enrichment steering on literal-required and cooperative-control items (induce errors), random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: enrichment-lure error reduction on literal-required items under minus-direction steering versus random-direction; secondary: plus-direction induced errors, dose-response, and the crucial specificity test that minus-direction steering does NOT harm cooperative-control accuracy (a generic push would hurt it), plus fluency preserved. Convincing result: minus-direction steering cuts literal-task enrichment errors by >= 3 points over random-direction (CI excludes 0) with monotonic dose-response, plus-direction induces enrichment errors even where the literal reading is required, and cooperative-control accuracy stays within 1 point (mode switch, not capacity removal). Indecision band: steering effects within +/-2 points of random-direction, or a cooperative-control drop that makes the effect look generic, leave the direction unproven. Negative result: no steerable, specific effect means the pragmatic-mode direction is not a causal, controllable switch.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests unsafe over-reading of literal dosing instructions. Data: 300 dosing/instruction vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) and constructed instruction cases where the safe action requires the literal reading (do exactly what is written, do not infer unstated conditions); 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Systems: no-intervention and minus-enrichment steering. Decisive metric first: unsafe-action rate (enriched over-reading producing an unsafe action) on fine-distinction cases under no-intervention versus minus-direction steering; secondary: preserved accuracy on cases where enrichment is appropriate. Convincing result: the enrichment default produces unsafe over-reading at baseline and minus-direction steering reduces the unsafe-action rate by >= 5 points (CI excludes 0) without harming enrichment-appropriate items. Indecision band: an unsafe-action reduction within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no unsafe over-reading, or no steering benefit, bounds the claim to benign benchmarks.

Experiment 6 (H3 -- Robustness across implicature types and scale): Tests generality. Data: the battery re-partitioned by implicature type (scalar, exhaustivity, manner). Decisive metric first: whether the enrichment direction derived on one implicature type transfers (reduces errors) to the others; secondary: the default's dependence on model scale (7B versus 14B). Convincing result: the direction generalizes across implicature types (reliable cross-type error reduction, CI excludes 0) and the default is present across scales. Indecision band: cross-type transfer within +/-2 points leaves generality open without affecting the within-type results. Negative result: no cross-type transfer means the mode signal is implicature-specific rather than a unified pragmatic-mode axis.

Experiment 7 (Protocol, baselines, and specificity ablations): We specify the exact item-generation and annotation protocol for literal-required vs enrichment-correct pairs, including adjudication of ambiguous cases and inter-annotator agreement, and pre-register the primary endpoint (the literal-vs-enriched within-pair enrichment-lure gap) with separated hypotheses for behavior, probe, and steering. Baselines include generic difficulty, instruction-following, and confidence-calibration controls plus a random-direction steering control. Steering-specificity ablations test whether minus-enrichment steering changes PRAGMATICS specifically versus overall verbosity, conservatism, or refusal behavior (measured on neutral and cooperative items). We add a prevalence analysis estimating how often over-enrichment arises in naturally occurring legal/clinical/logical text, a comparison against literal-instruction prompting and guardrails, and a failure-mode analysis for the probe-predicts-but-steering-fails case. The clinical dosing section is tightened to a vetted-benchmark subset with clear literal ground truth, or downscoped to a motivating instance if such ground truth is unavailable.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Errors on literal-required items could stem from general difficulty rather than genuine pragmatic enrichment; mitigated by matched literal/enriched pairs (same surface content), the enrichment-lure error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC enriched reading, not random), and the cooperative-dialogue selectivity control. (2) Instruction-tuned models may already read literally when in a formal register, muting the default; we include base variants, harder items, and test whether 'interpret literally' prompting only partially closes the gap. (3) The enrichment direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by matched literal/enriched contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and the crucial specificity test that suppression preserves cooperative-control accuracy (a generic push would hurt it). (4) Suppressing enrichment could globally flatten pragmatic ability; we explicitly measure and require preserved performance on enrichment-correct items, framing the goal as a controllable mode switch, not permanent removal. (5) Legal/clinical ground truth can be contestable; we use items with clear literal-correct answers and expert spot-checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (no enrichment default, or literal errors are not enrichment-shaped) is itself informative — it would show LLM pragmatic inference is contextually gated rather than a default liability. (8) The Gricean/pragmatics framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like communicative intent. (9) We reduce overclaiming around 'default' and 'cause': the causal-default language is asserted only where the within-pair gap, lure-signature, probe mediation, and steering specificity jointly hold; otherwise we report the weaker correlational finding.

Name: morphological_role_scaffolding
Title: Case Closed: Does Overt Morphological Role-Marking Scaffold an LLM's Relational Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: A language's morphological role-marking (e.g., explicit case marking that tags each argument's role directly on the word) acts as a built-in scaffold for an LLM's relational reasoning: reasoning about role-sensitive problems framed in a morphologically transparent, case-marking language yields more robust argument-role binding, better resistance to word-order perturbation, and fewer role-confusion errors than the same content in a morphologically poor, word-order-reliant language like English, and this benefit is mediated by a locatable, steerable role-binding representation. Primary novelty: a representational scramble-invariance signature of role binding under overt case marking that is not implied by linguistic typology alone; the cross-lingual behavioral advantage and the steering result are subordinate. The decisive endpoint is the language-type-by-scramble interaction (Experiment 2).
Related Work: Prior work characterizes morphological complexity information-theoretically (Productivity and Predictability, 2019; Processing-Oriented Inflectional Complexity, 2019), shows LLMs encode morphology in middle layers and that irregular-morphology languages benefit from more data (Tokenization and Morphology, 2024; LINSPECTOR, 2020), and shows LLMs reuse shared syntactic circuits across languages but add language-specific components for language-specific morphology (The Same But Different, 2024). Separately, 'When Less Language is More' (2025) shows ablating language-specific components improves multilingual reasoning, treating morphology/language as noise. My prior proposals covered word-order typology (answer-commitment), tokenization granularity, lexical gaps, evidentiality, tense, and counterfactual mood, but NONE address morphological role-marking (case) as a functional scaffold for relational reasoning. No prior work asks whether overt morphological role-marking causally improves argument-role binding and relational-reasoning robustness, tests whether it makes reasoning resistant to word-order scrambling, or links this to a locatable role-binding representation. We uniquely reframe morphology from a modeling nuisance into a controllable reasoning resource, with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes clinical instance. Closest baselines, claim-by-claim delta: multilingual morphology-as-noise work (When Less Language is More 2025) treats morphology/language-specific components as removable noise, whereas we test morphology as a FUNCTIONAL scaffold; relational-binding/SRL work localizes role representations but not their morphology-dependent scramble-invariance; prior word-order studies do not test case-marked scramble robustness. Why the scramble result is more than restating typology: linguistics predicts case-marked sentences remain interpretable under scrambling, but it does not predict that an LLM's INTERNAL role-binding representation is more scramble-invariant under case marking, nor that steering a located role-binding direction rescues scrambled English -- these are model-level, representational predictions.
Abstract: Human languages divide labor between word order and morphology to signal who did what to whom: English relies on word order ('the dog bit the man'), while case-marking languages tag each argument's role directly on the word, freeing word order. We ask whether this typological choice shapes machine intelligence: does overt morphological role-marking act as a built-in scaffold that makes an LLM's relational reasoning more robust? We construct role-sensitive reasoning problems (agent/patient tracking, multi-participant event chains, transitive relational inference) and render each, with content held constant, in a morphologically poor, word-order-reliant language (English) versus morphologically transparent, case-marking languages (e.g., Turkish, Russian, Finnish). Our central prediction is a morphology-scaffolding effect: role-marked framing yields fewer role-confusion errors and, critically, greater robustness to word-order scrambling that would break a purely order-based reasoner, whereas English framing collapses under scrambling. We further predict the benefit is largest exactly when role assignment is hard (many participants, non-canonical order). Mechanistically, we test whether overt case-marking strengthens a locatable role-binding representation: a probe decoding which entity fills which role should be more accurate and more scramble-invariant under case-marking, this representational robustness should mediate the behavioral gain item-by-item, and steering a located role-binding direction should induce or cancel the scaffolding effect. We evaluate across several open-weight multilingual models, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where scrambled or morphologically ambiguous phrasing of 'drug X interacts with drug Y' silently flips the reasoned direction. Our work reframes morphology from a modeling nuisance into a controllable scaffold for relational intelligence. To show the effect is specifically about morphological role marking rather than any explicit cueing, we add a non-case control that preserves overt role cues without rich case morphology -- English augmented with explicit role labels/paraphrastic role markers -- and within-language minimal pairs where only case morphology changes. The rendering protocol is specified rigorously (native-speaker validation, ambiguity checks, and lexical/morphological frequency matched across languages). Practical stakes and adopters: if morphology scaffolds role binding, then language choice and prompt framing systematically change relational reliability in information extraction, legal/medical causal statements, multilingual agents, and translation robustness; under a positive result practitioners would adopt language-conditioned prompting or morphology-aware evaluation, and under a null they would treat relational reasoning as order-agnostic and content-driven.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight multilingual models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). All cross-lingual analyses are accuracy-stratified so that the morphology effect is separated from a language's general resource competence. "Role-confusion lure" is the answer obtained if agent/patient (or an asymmetric relation's direction) is swapped.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Overt case-marking lowers role-confusion errors, most when role assignment is hard): Tests the core scaffolding effect with content held constant. Data: a role-sensitive battery of 250 items per family -- (a) agent/patient tracking over 2-5 participants, (b) multi-participant event chains (A gave B to C, C passed it to D... query final holder), (c) transitive relational inference over asymmetric relations -- 750 items, plus 250 matched role-symmetric controls (relations where role order does not matter) for selectivity; each item has a labeled correct answer and a labeled role-confusion lure. Each item is rendered, content held constant and back-translation-checked, in English (morphologically poor, order-reliant) and in Turkish, Russian, and Finnish (overt case marking). 250/family supports stable language_type x difficulty estimates within budget. Decisive metric first: role-confusion lure rate (and accuracy) under case-marking versus English from mixed-effects regression lure_rate ~ language_type * difficulty + (1|model)+(1|item), accuracy-stratified; secondary: the widening of the gap as role-assignment difficulty rises (more participants, non-canonical order). Convincing result: case-marking framing lowers the role-confusion lure rate relative to English by a reliable margin (CI excludes 0) that grows with difficulty, holding at matched competence. Indecision band: a language_type effect within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) after accuracy-stratification means no morphology advantage is detectable above resource differences. Negative result: no case-marking advantage means relational reasoning is order-agnostic and content-driven, refuting H1 and dissociating LLMs from the human labor-division account.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Case-marking gives robustness to word-order scrambling that English lacks): The sharpest test. Data: the same items; we permute the surface order of arguments within each item. Under case marking the morphology still uniquely determines roles (meaning preserved, native-speaker-verified on a sample), while English scrambling destroys or flips role cues. Decisive metric first: the language_type x scramble interaction on accuracy from mixed-effects regression accuracy ~ language_type * scramble + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: where scrambling errors concentrate (should be on the role-confusion lure in English). Convincing result: case-marking framing shows a small accuracy drop under scrambling (<= 5 points) while English collapses (>= 15-point drop), yielding a large, reliable interaction (CI excludes 0) with English errors concentrated on the role-confusion lure. Indecision band: an interaction whose CI corresponds to a between-language drop difference within +/-3 points means scrambling robustness is not distinguishable between framings. Negative result: equal collapse under scrambling in both framings means overt morphology does not scaffold role binding, refuting H2 (the central novel claim).

Experiment 3 (H1/H2 -- High-stakes clinical direction-flip instance): Tests whether English non-canonical/scrambled phrasing silently flips a clinical causal direction. Data: 300 drug-interaction / causal-direction vignettes ("drug X potentiates drug Y", dosage-adjustment directionality) adapted from a curated drug-interaction knowledge base and constructed cases where the reasoned direction matters; rendered in English and case-marking languages, with 2-5 interacting entities; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Decisive metric first: direction-flip rate (inferred direction reversed from ground truth) under English scrambled/non-canonical phrasing versus case-marked framing; secondary: scaling of the flip rate with number of interacting entities. Convincing result: English scrambled phrasing raises the direction-flip rate while case-marked framing preserves direction, a reliable gap (CI excludes 0) that grows with entity count. Indecision band: a flip-rate gap within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no flip-rate difference bounds the scaffolding claim to benign benchmarks.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- A locatable role-binding representation is stronger and more scramble-invariant under case-marking): Tests the mechanism's representational side. Data: the battery from Experiments 1-2, split 70/30 by item. A linear probe (only probe trainable) on mid-layer hidden states at the query position decodes which entity fills the queried role (per-layer held-out AUROC). Decisive metric first: probe role-decoding AUROC under case-marking versus English, and its scramble-invariance (AUROC drop under scrambling); secondary: per-item mediation -- whether probe role-decodability and its scramble-invariance predict per-item accuracy/lure-rate (Spearman). Convincing result: role-decoding AUROC is higher and markedly more scramble-invariant under case-marking (AUROC-drop difference CI excludes 0), and per-item decodability predicts accuracy (rho >= 0.2, CI excludes 0). Indecision band: an AUROC-invariance difference within +/-0.03 means the representation is not demonstrably more robust under morphology. Negative result: equal probe robustness across framings means the behavioral effect (if any) is not carried by a morphology-strengthened role-binding representation.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- Steering the role-binding direction rescues and induces role confusion): Tests causality. Data: a difference-in-means "role-binding" direction from correct-role-bound-minus-role-confused contrasts at the best probe layer. Systems: plus-direction steering under scrambled English (rescue), minus-direction under case-marking framing (induce confusion despite morphology), random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: accuracy recovery under plus-direction steering of scrambled English versus random-direction; secondary: induced lure-rate increase under minus-direction on case-marked items, dose-response, and specificity (role-symmetric-control accuracy within 1 point, fluency preserved). Convincing result: plus-direction steering recovers scrambled-English accuracy toward case-marking levels (>= 3-point gain over random-direction, CI excludes 0), minus-direction induces role confusion despite overt case marking, both with monotonic dose-response and preserved role-symmetric-control accuracy. Indecision band: steering effects within +/-2 points of random-direction leave the direction unproven; the behavioral scrambling test (Experiment 2) then stands alone. Negative result: no steerable rescue/induction means the role-binding direction is not causal.

Experiment 6 (Cue-explicitness control, minimal pairs, and mechanistic negative controls): We add two control arms to isolate morphology from mere cue explicitness: (a) English augmented with explicit role labels or paraphrastic role markers (overt cues, no case morphology), and (b) within-single-language minimal pairs where only case morphology is added/removed with content fixed. If the case-marking advantage exceeds the explicit-role-label arm, the effect is morphology-specific rather than general explicit annotation. For the mechanism we add negative controls: the role-binding probe/direction must NOT decode matched non-role features, alternative steering directions of matched norm must not rescue scrambling, and role-symmetric controls must be unaffected representationally as well as behaviorally. We distinguish correlational mediation (per-item probe-decodability predicts accuracy) from interventional evidence (steering), and use causal language only for the intervention. We designate Experiment 2 (the language-type-by-scramble interaction) as the decisive test if others are mixed, and report a power/effect-size justification for the 300-item clinical set.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Case-marking languages may be lower-resource for these models, confounding morphology with competence; mitigated by accuracy-stratified metrics, back-translation checks, and the content-matched steering intervention that isolates the role-binding representation from language. (2) Tokenization may fragment case suffixes, weakening the morphological signal; we test multiple case-marking languages/models and report robustness, and the within-English scramble test (which needs no cross-lingual comparison) is a clean primary probe of the word-order-reliance failure mode. (3) The scrambling stress test requires that scrambled case-marked sentences stay unambiguous and English scrambling genuinely disrupts roles; we validate both with native speakers on a sample and design canonical/non-canonical orders carefully. (4) Instruction-tuned models may reason robustly regardless of framing, yielding ceiling effects; we increase participant count, use non-canonical orders, and calibrate difficulty to mid-range. (5) The role-binding direction may entangle with generic difficulty rather than role assignment per se; mitigated by matched role-bound vs role-confused contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and role-symmetric-control specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model/language-specific; we test multiple models and languages and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (morphological role-marking gives no robustness advantage) is itself informative: it would show LLM relational reasoning is order-agnostic and content-driven rather than scaffolded by surface morphology, dissociating LLMs from the human labor-division account. (8) The morphology-as-scaffold framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like processing. (9) We keep the mediation and intervention claims separate: per-item probe-decodability is treated as correlational evidence, and only the steering rescue/induction (Experiment 5) supports the causal role-binding claim; broad 'morphology as a reasoning resource' language is tempered until the cue-explicitness and minimal-pair controls rule out simpler explanations.

Name: linguistic_cost_of_thought
Title: The Linguistic Cost of Thought: Difficulty-Gated Language-Agnostic Steering for Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: As an LLM reasons through harder sub-steps, it dynamically suppresses surface-language identity in favor of a language-agnostic representation; the momentary degree of this suppression is a readable, causal signal of reasoning difficulty and correctness, and selectively increasing suppression only at high-difficulty steps improves reasoning more than blanket language-component ablation.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs develop a compact language-agnostic core (Emergence of Abstract Thought, 2025), route reasoning through English-shaped space (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025), and that static, blanket ablation of language-specific activations improves multilingual reasoning (When Less Language is More, 2025). Others study language mixing as a latent-preference symptom (Language Mixing in Reasoning LMs, 2025) and knowledge-free reasoning transfer (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners, 2024). All existing interventions are static/global: they remove or preserve language components uniformly across a generation. Our proposal is distinct in three ways: (1) we treat language-agnosticism as a time-varying per-step signal (a 'linguistic cost' meter) rather than a fixed property; (2) we causally test whether difficulty predicts this signal via truncation and error-injection at the step level; and (3) we introduce a difficulty-gated steering intervention that increases language-agnosticism only at hard steps, contrasting it head-to-head with blanket ablation. No prior work links the dynamics of language suppression to step-level difficulty or uses it as an adaptive controller. Recent 'shared difficulty geometry' and hidden-state correctness-probe work identifies a static difficulty/correctness direction read once per generation; we differ by testing the temporal dynamics of language-shedding across steps and by causally gating an intervention on it, not merely reading a fixed difficulty direction. In one sentence, our novelty claim is: per-step, difficulty-gated language-agnostic steering improves multilingual reasoning more than static blanket ablation under matched compute and intervention budget.
Abstract: Recent interpretability work reveals that large language models (LLMs) maintain a compact language-agnostic representational core underlying cross-lingual generalization, and that suppressing surface-language components can improve multilingual reasoning. However, these interventions are static, applying uniform treatment across an entire generation. We hypothesize that language-agnosticism is instead dynamic: an LLM temporarily 'sheds' its surface language when a reasoning sub-step becomes hard, and this momentary shedding is a readable and causal signal of reasoning difficulty and correctness. We define a per-step Language-Agnosticism Score (LAS) from the projection of hidden states onto a language-identity subspace estimated from parallel data. First, we characterize the dynamics of LAS across chain-of-thought steps and test whether it rises with step-level difficulty using truncation and controlled error-injection probes. Second, as a secondary result in service of the controller (not as a standalone monitor competing with existing high-AUROC correctness probes), we test whether LAS at intermediate steps flags high-difficulty steps well enough to drive the gate. Third, we introduce Difficulty-Gated Language-Agnostic Steering (DG-LAS), which increases language-agnosticism only at steps flagged as high-difficulty, and compare it against blanket ablation and no-intervention baselines on multilingual math and commonsense reasoning across typologically diverse languages and several open-weight models. We expect DG-LAS to match or exceed blanket ablation while preserving fluency and reducing the fluency degradation that global ablation causes on easy steps. The concrete deployment payoff is a multilingual assistant that preserves native-language fluency and token cost on easy content yet matches the accuracy of blanket ablation on hard multilingual math/commonsense steps; we pre-register the tradeoff threshold that would make practitioners switch from static ablation, namely that gating preserves easy-step fluency while its accuracy 95% CI lower bound meets blanket ablation. Our work reframes language suppression from a static property to a dynamic, controllable resource, offering both an interpretable difficulty meter and a training-free intervention.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Language-identity subspace construction and validation): This prerequisite builds the meter the rest of the study reads. Data: FLORES-200 (an existing professionally-translated parallel corpus; 997 sentences in its dev split are available in every language), used as is; we take all ~997 dev sentences in 8 typologically diverse languages (English, Spanish, French, German, Russian, Chinese, Japanese, Swahili), ~7,976 sentence instances. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Aya-23-8B, all pretrained weights frozen; we fit only an external linear classifier. For each layer we extract the final-token residual-stream vector and fit an 8-way L2-regularized logistic-regression language classifier (5-fold cross-validation, seeds 0/1/2); its top three directions define the language-identity subspace, and LAS(token,layer)=1 minus the L2-normalized projection magnitude of the hidden state onto that subspace (higher = more language-agnostic). Systems compared: per-layer classifier vs. a shuffled-label control; and, to establish LAS is not a relabeling of simpler quantities, we regress LAS against token entropy, the classifier's language-ID confidence, and residual-stream layer-norm magnitude and require LAS to retain independent variance (partial correlation controlling for all three) before any downstream use. Decisive metric first: held-out language-classification accuracy (chance = 12.5%); then transfer accuracy on 500 held-out Tatoeba parallel sentences. Convincing result: at least one middle layer reaches >=85% held-out accuracy and >=80% Tatoeba transfer while the shuffled control stays at chance, establishing a content-orthogonal identity subspace. Indecision band: 40-85% held-out accuracy - the subspace only weakly separates languages, LAS becomes a noisy meter, and we would restrict every downstream analysis to the single best layer and report reduced power. Negative result (<40%, or no layer beating the shuffled control): no readable language-identity subspace exists, LAS is undefined, and the dynamic-shedding hypothesis cannot be tested as framed.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Reasoning difficulty raises momentary language-shedding): Tests the claim that LAS rises with step-level difficulty. Data: MGSM (existing; 250 GSM-style problems per language, human-translated) across the 8 languages above = 2,000 problems, and XCOPA (existing; 500 validation items per language) for the commonsense arm across its overlapping languages; used as is. We segment each generated chain-of-thought into steps by newline/sentence and arithmetic-operation boundaries. Models: same three, frozen; greedy decoding plus 5 samples/problem (temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2) for stability. Systems compared: per-step LAS regressed on two difficulty proxies - token surprisal under the same model, and operation complexity (operand count/carries for math). Decisive metric first: the standardized regression coefficient of step difficulty on step LAS in a mixed-effects model (LAS ~ difficulty + step_position + (1|problem) + (1|model)); secondary: Spearman correlation per model. Convincing result: a positive difficulty coefficient with 95% bootstrap CI excluding zero in at least 2 of 3 models, robust to controlling for step position and length. Indecision band: standardized coefficient in [-0.05, 0.05] with CI spanning zero - difficulty does not measurably move LAS, so the 'linguistic cost' meter is not difficulty-sensitive and H1 is unsupported at this resolution. Negative result (significant negative coefficient): the model becomes MORE language-anchored on hard steps, contradicting the shedding hypothesis. Evidence is planned, not measured.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Causal difficulty manipulation): Isolates difficulty from confounds by intervening on it; the causal identification contrasts the error-injection arm (raises genuine sub-step difficulty while holding remaining length fixed) against a length-only truncation control (truncates without raising sub-step difficulty), so a LAS spike specific to the error-injection arm and absent in the length-only control identifies difficulty rather than truncation or position. Data: a built set of 300 MGSM-derived items (drawn from the 2,000 above) each rendered in two forms - (a) truncated CoT fed back so the model must complete a genuinely hard remaining step, and (b) a single interior step corrupted by a controlled arithmetic error requiring recovery - plus matched easy-step controls; ~1,200 constructed trials. Models: same three, frozen. Systems compared: LAS at the manipulated hard/error-recovery step vs. matched easy step, within item. Decisive metric first: within-item LAS difference (hard minus easy), tested with a paired bootstrap. Convincing result: mean LAS spike at genuinely hard/error-recovery steps with 95% CI excluding zero and effect size (Cohen's d) >=0.3 in at least 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: |d|<0.15 with CI crossing zero - the causal manipulation does not reliably move LAS, meaning any correlation in Experiment 2 is likely driven by uncontrolled length/position rather than difficulty per se. Negative result (LAS drops at manipulated hard steps): shedding is not caused by difficulty.

Experiment 4 (H2 - LAS predicts final correctness): Tests that intermediate-step LAS is a readable self-monitoring signal. Data: the 2,000 MGSM problems, each with 8 sampled trajectories labeled correct/incorrect by exact match = ~16,000 labeled trajectories; we hold out 30% of problems for testing (no problem overlap). Models: same three, frozen; the only trainable component is a lightweight logistic probe on aggregated intermediate-step LAS features (mean/max/slope), seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: LAS probe vs. baselines - answer-token confidence, predictive entropy, and logit-lens English-routing degree. Decisive metric first: AUROC for predicting final correctness on held-out problems. Convincing result: LAS-probe AUROC >=0.65 and statistically above the confidence/entropy baselines (DeLong test, 95% CI on the AUROC gap excluding zero) in at least 2 of 3 models. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65] or overlapping the baselines' CIs - LAS carries weak, non-additive correctness information and is not a useful monitor on its own. Negative result (AUROC <=0.55): LAS does not predict correctness, refuting the self-monitoring claim.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Difficulty-Gated Language-Agnostic Steering beats blanket ablation): Tests the central intervention claim. Data: a held-out MGSM split of 800 problems across the 8 languages (kept separate from probe training). Models: same three, frozen; steering adds -alpha times the language-identity component to the residual stream in middle layers only at flagged steps; alpha and gate threshold tuned on a 200-item dev split, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared, four conditions: (i) no intervention, (ii) blanket ablation (prior state of the art; language component removed at every step), (iii) random-gated steering matched for number of intervened steps, tokens, and steering strength (a matched-budget control isolating the gating contribution), and (iv) DG-LAS (steer only at steps flagged high-difficulty by surprisal threshold or the Experiment-4 probe). Decisive metric first: exact-match accuracy per language (macro-averaged); secondary: output fluency (perplexity under an external LM plus a GPT-judge rating on a 200-sample subset) and answer-in-target-language rate. Convincing result: DG-LAS matches or exceeds blanket ablation on accuracy (its 95% bootstrap CI lower bound at or above blanket ablation) AND shows higher fluency / lower easy-step degradation than blanket ablation, while beating random-gated steering by >=1 accuracy point. Indecision band: DG-LAS within +/-1.0 accuracy point of blanket ablation with overlapping fluency CIs - difficulty-gating yields no measurable advantage over blanket treatment, so the adaptive-controller motivation is not supported even if the meter is real. Negative result (DG-LAS below no-intervention or below random-gated): selective language-shedding does not help and may hurt.

Experiment 6 (Robustness - ablations): Data/models as above. We sweep layer choice, gating threshold, and steering strength alpha; test alternative difficulty proxies for gating (operation complexity, probe-flagged difficulty, and surprisal); add a null model that steers on random time-varying gates drawn from the same marginal LAS distribution (matched intervention rate and strength) to confirm any gain comes from WHERE we gate, not merely from time-varying perturbation; add one user-facing arm beyond benchmark QA (multilingual open-ended instruction-following graded by an LM judge for accuracy and native-language fluency); and test cross-language generalization of the identity subspace (fit on 6 languages, evaluate LAS and DG-LAS on 2 held-out languages). Decisive metric: stability of the Experiment-2 difficulty coefficient and the Experiment-5 accuracy gap across settings. Convincing result: the sign and significance of both hold across a majority of layer/threshold settings and transfer to held-out languages. Indecision band: results flip sign across reasonable settings - findings are setting-specific and we report them as such. Negative result: effects vanish off the tuned operating point, indicating overfitting rather than a robust mechanism. All quantities above are planned evidence, not measured outcomes.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The language-identity subspace may entangle content with language, confounding LAS; we mitigate with parallel-data controls and orthogonalization. Step segmentation is noisy for languages with weak CoT structure. Difficulty proxies (surprisal) may not reflect true reasoning difficulty. Difficulty-gated steering could destabilize generation or reduce fluency if applied too aggressively; strength/threshold tuning is required. Gains may be model- or language-specific and small on high-resource languages. Causal claims from steering are correlational unless carefully controlled, so we include random-gated and blanket baselines to isolate the difficulty-gating contribution.

Name: codeswitch_executive_control
Title: Code-Switching as a Cognitive Tool: Does Inducing Language Mixing Boost an LLM's Inhibitory Control?
Short Hypothesis: In humans, code-switching transiently boosts executive control (inhibition and conflict monitoring), with different switch types (insertion vs. alternation vs. dense) modulating different control modes. We hypothesize the same functional relationship holds inside LLMs, but our specific, testable contribution is NOT the coarse claim that language mixing helps reasoning (prior 2025 work already shows monolingual enforcement can hurt math): it is the finer-grained law that (i) deliberately inducing code-switching in the reasoning trace improves conflict/inhibition performance beyond length-matched monolingual reasoning, (ii) the beneficial switch TYPE dissociates by control demand - alternation aiding reactive (transient-distractor) control and dense switching aiding proactive (sustained-monitoring) control - and (iii) this benefit is mediated by a locatable conflict-monitoring component whose engagement rises under induced switching and whose steering reproduces or cancels the effect. 'Executive control' is treated as an operational analogy, not a claim of human-like cognition.
