Related Work: Recent LLM work treats language mixing largely as a symptom of latent pivot-language preferences to be controlled away: 'Language Mixing in Reasoning LMs' (2025) shows mixing increases with difficulty and that forcing a Latin/Han script can help; 'When Less Language is More' (2025) and MRRE (2025) improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing/aligning language-specific components; 'Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners' (2024) shows reasoning transfers across languages. These results establish only an aggregate accuracy relationship (and a remedy), and already pre-empt the coarse claim that mixing helps reasoning. Separately, a large human cross-domain literature shows the opposite valence: code-switching trains executive control (inhibition, goal-monitoring; e.g., Language athletes 2023; Training in Language Switching 2019), and switch TYPE selectively modulates reactive vs. proactive control via a dual-control-mode account (2020), with fast context effects on non-verbal conflict tasks (2013). Our delta is exactly what the 2025 mixing papers do not imply: (1) a switch-type-by-control-mode crossover (alternation to reactive, dense to proactive), and (2) a causal, steerable conflict-monitoring mediator located inside the model. We thus reframe language mixing from a symptom-to-suppress into a controllable executive-control resource and give it a mechanistic (Location + Causal Intervention) test; the novelty is a new behavioral law plus its mechanism, not a new benchmark.
Abstract: Multilingual interpretability work treats an LLM's tendency to mix languages while reasoning as a nuisance symptom of its internal pivot language, best suppressed. Yet decades of bilingualism research show the reverse for humans: code-switching trains and transiently boosts executive control, sharpening inhibition and conflict monitoring, with distinct switch types tuning distinct control modes. We ask whether this functional relationship transfers to LLMs: can deliberately inducing code-switching in a model's chain-of-thought act as a cognitive tool that improves performance on tasks demanding inhibition and conflict resolution? We assemble a battery of conflict/inhibition-heavy reasoning tasks (linguistic-Stroop-style distractor items, misleading-premise math, cognitive-reflection lures, and irrelevant-context word problems) and compare monolingual reasoning against three induced switch regimes drawn from the psycholinguistic taxonomy: insertion (single foreign content words), alternation (whole-clause switches between languages), and dense switching (frequent intra-sentence switching). Crucially we control for confounds by matching reasoning length and adding a same-language 'switch-token' scramble control, so any gain reflects switching rather than extra tokens or translation. We predict induced switching improves conflict-resolution accuracy over length-matched monolingual reasoning, that alternation aids reactive (distractor) control while dense switching aids proactive (sustained-monitoring) control, mirroring the human dual-control dissociation, and that these gains dissociate from ordinary (non-conflict) reasoning. Mechanistically, we locate a conflict-monitoring direction/component (via probing on high- vs low-conflict trials) and test whether induced switching raises its engagement and whether steering it reproduces the switching benefit. Our contribution is not the coarse claim that mixing helps reasoning (already pre-empted), but a switch-type-by-control-mode behavioral law plus its conflict-monitoring mediator: if confirmed, switch type becomes a cheap inference-time knob for reasoning under conflict (e.g., choosing alternation for distractor-heavy multilingual QA, or dense switching for agentic prompts that must sustain monitoring against misleading context); if null, it cleanly separates LLM mixing from the human executive-control finding and tells practitioners that language identity in the trace is safe to normalize away. Across several open-weight models we quantify the switching-benefit effect, its type-by-control-mode dissociation, and mechanistic mediation.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does induced code-switching cut conflict errors beyond length-matched monolingual reasoning?): Tests whether deliberately inducing code-switching in the chain-of-thought improves performance on inhibition/conflict tasks over monolingual reasoning of equal length, and whether the benefit is specific to conflict rather than ordinary reasoning. Data: a conflict battery of ~1000 items, 250 per family - (a) linguistic-Stroop distractor items (constructed; a salient distractor word/number must be suppressed), (b) misleading-premise math sampled and adapted from GSM-IC (Shi et al. 2023, ~58k released problems) by tagging the tempting irrelevant number as the labeled lure, (c) Cognitive-Reflection-Test-style lures (only ~7 canonical CRT items exist, so we template 250 items preserving the intuitive-lure structure), (d) irrelevant-context word problems drawn directly from GSM-IC; plus a matched NON-CONFLICT control set of 250 plain arithmetic/logic items of equal surface difficulty. We use 250 per family rather than the full GSM-IC pool to balance families and keep 5 models x 5 regimes x 4 decoding passes within a single-lab compute budget. Each conflict item carries a labeled correct answer AND a labeled lure answer so lure-error rate is scorable. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models spanning families/scales - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Mistral-7B-Instruct; inference only, no weights trained; decoding at temperature 0.7 with sampling seeds {0,1,2} plus one greedy pass (four traces per item). Regimes, all length-matched to the same reasoning-token budget and format-enforced: monolingual baseline; insertion; alternation; dense switching; a same-language switch-token scramble control (foreign-looking nonce tokens injected at the switch positions); and a pure-translation control (reason fully in the second language). The second language is one of each model's strong languages (English<->Chinese or English<->Spanish). We verify switch compliance and analyze only compliant traces. Decisive metric: lure-error rate on conflict items (fraction of responses equal to the labeled lure), in a mixed-effects model lure_error ~ regime*conflict_level + (1|model) + (1|item); secondary: accuracy. Convincing result: alternation and/or dense switching lower lure-error rate versus both length-matched monolingual and the switch-token scramble control with 95% bootstrap CIs excluding zero, AND a regime x conflict interaction showing the reduction is larger on conflict than on non-conflict items. Indecision band: if the switching-minus-monolingual lure-error difference has a 95% CI contained within +/-2 percentage points (thus overlapping zero), or the regime x conflict interaction CI lies within +/-2 pp, the measurement cannot decide and H1 is treated as unsupported at this power. Negative result (switching no better, or worse, than length-matched monolingual and scramble) would mean LLM language mixing is a nuisance symptom rather than an executive-control tool, cleanly separating LLMs from the human bilingualism finding.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Does switch TYPE dissociate by control mode, alternation for reactive and dense for proactive?): Tests the predicted crossover between switch type and control demand. Data: the same conflict battery re-labeled by control demand - reactive (transient single-distractor suppression: linguistic-Stroop and CRT items, ~500) vs proactive (sustained monitoring across distractor-laden context: irrelevant-context and misleading-premise word problems, ~500). Models, seeds and decoding as Experiment 1, restricted to monolingual, alternation and dense regimes. Decisive metric: the regime x control_mode interaction coefficient on accuracy (and, secondarily, lure-error rate) in the mixed-effects model. Convincing result: a crossover in which alternation's advantage over monolingual is larger on reactive items while dense switching's advantage is larger on proactive items, with the interaction's 95% CI excluding zero and the two simple effects ordered as predicted. Indecision band: if the interaction coefficient's 95% CI lies within +/-2 pp of zero, the type-by-mode dissociation is undecided and we retreat to the weaker claim that switching helps without dissociating by mode. Negative result (no crossover, or the reverse ordering) leaves H1 intact but refutes the human dual-control-mode analogy for LLMs.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Is there a locatable conflict-monitoring component whose engagement rises under induced switching?): Location plus mediation. Data: hidden states cached from the monolingual runs of Experiment 1 on the conflict battery, split into high-conflict vs low-conflict (and lure-resolved vs lure-failed) trials, with a 70/15/15 train/validation/test split over items. Model: the same five models, frozen; the only trainable parameters are per-layer logistic-regression linear probes trained with 5-fold cross-validation over seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for high- vs low-conflict trials (per layer; report best-layer AUROC). Then mediation: the Spearman correlation between the per-item increase in projection onto the conflict-monitoring direction (switching minus monolingual, at the critical resolution step) and the per-item accuracy gain. Convincing result: best-layer held-out AUROC clears 0.70 and generalizes to held-out items, induced switching raises the projection onto this direction versus monolingual, and the projection-gain-to-accuracy-gain Spearman rho is positive with a 95% CI excluding zero. Indecision band: probe AUROC in [0.55, 0.65] means no reliable conflict-monitoring direction was located; a mediation rho whose 95% CI lies within +/-0.1 of zero means engagement change does not track behavior. Either leaves the mechanism undecided. Negative result (no decodable direction, or switching does not raise its engagement, or engagement does not predict benefit) would show any behavioral benefit from Experiment 1 is not mediated by a conflict-monitoring component, undercutting the mechanistic half of the hypothesis while leaving the behavioral claim standing.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Does steering the conflict-monitoring direction reproduce and cancel the switching benefit?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item conflict subset disjoint from the probe-training items of Experiment 3. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; the difference-in-means conflict-monitoring direction from Experiment 3 is added or subtracted at the located layer across a dose sweep (coefficients spanning 0 to a few times the natural projection norm), each over seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: +direction during monolingual reasoning; -direction during dense-switch reasoning; random-direction steering; and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in lure-error rate (and accuracy) under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check on the non-conflict control set. Convincing result: +direction under monolingual reproduces at least 50% of the alternation/dense switching benefit from Experiment 1 with a monotone dose-response, -direction under dense switching cancels it, both exceed the random-direction control (95% CIs excluding it), and off-target non-conflict accuracy stays within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: if the steering effect's 95% CI overlaps the random-direction control, or reproduces less than 25% of the behavioral benefit with no dose-response, the causal claim is undecided. Negative result (steering does not shift behavior, or is indistinguishable from random) would mean the conflict-monitoring direction is correlational at best, not the causal mediator the hypothesis requires.

Pre-registration and analysis: we pre-register the three hypotheses (H1 behavioral effect, H2 type-by-mode dissociation, H3 mechanism) with the distinct acceptance and indecision criteria stated above, correct for multiple comparisons across families/regimes with Benjamini-Hochberg, and report standardized effect sizes with 95% bootstrap CIs. The operational definitions of insertion (a single foreign content word), alternation (a whole-clause switch), and dense switching (frequent intra-sentence switching) are fixed in advance and compliance-verified, so the regimes are clearly distinct from prior aggregate language-mixing setups. The novelty is a new behavioral law plus its mechanism, not a new benchmark.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Induced switching may simply add tokens/'thinking time'; mitigated by strict length-matching, the switch-token scramble control, and testing the conflict-vs-non-conflict INTERACTION rather than raw gains. (2) Switching may degrade fluency or cause the model to lose the thread, hurting rather than helping; a null or negative result is still informative (it would show LLM language mixing is a symptom, not a tool, cleanly separating LLMs from the human executive-control literature). (3) The second-language choice confounds switching with translation quality; the pure-translation and random-direction controls plus multiple language pairs isolate switching per se. (4) The 'conflict-monitoring' direction may entangle with generic difficulty rather than genuine inhibition; mitigated by matched high/low-conflict contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering controls, and specificity checks on non-conflict tasks. (5) Reactive/proactive task labels are hypotheses; a flat (non-crossover) result would still test the core switching-benefit claim and is publishable. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) The human-cognition framing (executive control, dual control modes) is an operationalized analogy, not a claim of human-like cognition; all findings are framed behaviorally and mechanistically.

Name: reasoning_register_shift
Title: Simpler Sentences, Deeper Thought: Do LLMs Downshift Their Own Syntax When Reasoning Gets Hard?
Short Hypothesis: When reasoning becomes difficult, an LLM spontaneously reduces the syntactic complexity of its own generated language (a 'register downshift'), reallocating capacity from fluent surface form to computation; this downshift is a readable, per-step signal of reasoning difficulty and impending error, and causally forcing high-syntactic-complexity output at hard steps degrades reasoning while inducing simpler output syntax at hard steps improves it. We pre-register a single gold-standard syntactic metric (Dependency-Locality-Theory integration cost) and one backup (dependency-tree depth), both defined on the model's OWN generated tokens and explicitly residualized against step length and token entropy so the claim is about dependency structure, not brevity. Primary claim: difficulty-driven downshift (H1) plus its causal counterpart (forcing elaborate syntax at hard steps hurts, H3); the diagnostic probe and steering are secondary.
Related Work: Prior work links syntactic complexity to reasoning only for the INPUT or TRAINING data. 'Syntactic Blind Spots' (2025) shows higher Dependency-Locality-Theory (DLT) complexity of the PROBLEM STATEMENT raises math-error rates, and rephrasing to simpler syntax fixes errors. CIRS / 'When Do Program-of-Thoughts Work' (2023/2024) find an optimal AST/cyclomatic complexity of code TRAINING data for reasoning gains. 'Understanding Syntax in LLMs' (2025) and ID-of-representation work (2026) characterize how models process complex syntax, and 'Reasoning in LLMs: A Geometric Perspective' (2024) links intrinsic dimension to reasoning. Multi-dimensional gCoT-quality studies (2026) measure trace quality but not self-generated syntactic complexity as a function of difficulty. Critically, NO prior work studies the syntactic complexity of the model's OWN generated reasoning trace as a dynamic, self-regulated variable, tests whether it downshifts with difficulty, uses it as a difficulty/error signal, or causally intervenes on output-syntax complexity at the step level. My own prior proposals covered information-density pacing (bits per step), private-speech length dynamics, and tokenization granularity, but none address the syntactic (dependency-structure) complexity of self-generated language or a register-downshift-under-load account. We uniquely flip the direction from input-syntax->reasoning to reasoning-difficulty->output-syntax, and add a Location + Causal Intervention mechanism. One-sentence delta: prior work (Syntactic Blind Spots 2025; CIRS 2023/2024) manipulates INPUT or TRAINING-DATA syntax, whereas we study the syntactic complexity of the model's OWN generated reasoning as a dynamic, self-regulated, step-level variable with a causal intervention. Contrast along three axes -- locus (input vs training vs output), causality (correlational vs interventional), and measurability (static vs per-step) -- output-reasoning-syntax occupies the empty cell. If the effect turns out to be merely a correlate of shorter chains-of-thought or lower token entropy, then generic CoT-compression/short-CoT findings would already subsume it; our length- and entropy-matched controls and the generic-shortening baseline exist precisely to exclude that reading.
Abstract: Existing work shows that syntactically complex problem statements make LLMs reason worse, and that there is an optimal syntactic complexity in reasoning-oriented training data. We ask a complementary, unexplored question: what governs the syntactic complexity of the language an LLM PRODUCES while it reasons, and does it matter? Drawing on the human observation that speakers simplify their syntax under cognitive load, we hypothesize a reasoning register shift: as a reasoning sub-step becomes hard, the model spontaneously downshifts the syntactic complexity of its own generated tokens, trading fluent surface form for computational capacity. We make three claims. First, downshift is real and graded: per-step syntactic complexity of a model's chain-of-thought (measured by dependency-tree depth, Dependency-Locality-Theory integration cost, and clause embedding) drops at genuinely hard steps, and its magnitude tracks step difficulty. Second, downshift is diagnostic: per-step output-syntax complexity predicts step-level errors and final-answer correctness, providing a lightweight, decode-only self-monitoring signal that complements confidence and entropy. Third, downshift is causal, not incidental: forcing the model to emit high-complexity (elaborate, deeply-embedded) syntax at hard steps degrades reasoning, while inducing simpler syntax at hard steps improves it, and these effects are mediated by a locatable internal 'syntactic-elaboration' signal that can be steered to move the register up or down. We test these on multilingual math, logic, and multi-hop QA across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical-reasoning instance where syntactically elaborate self-generated reasoning silently raises diagnostic error. Our work reframes an LLM's own linguistic form as a controllable resource that competes with, and can sabotage, its reasoning. We narrow the paper to one primary hypothesis (difficulty-driven register downshift and its causal effect on reasoning) and one secondary mechanistic hypothesis (a readable, steerable syntactic-elaboration signal), rather than weighting downshift, diagnosis, and steering equally. The one-line practical payoff is a low-cost, decode-only online signal for when a model is about to fail and when to simplify its own reasoning trace; likely adopters are reasoning-benchmark, monitoring/interpretability, adaptive-decoding, and clinical-decision-support researchers. We are explicit that this primarily enables a post-hoc analysis signal and an inference-time control policy (not retraining), and we include a failure-mode analysis showing why it matters even if accuracy gains are modest -- e.g., as a safety-monitoring flag for silently over-elaborated reasoning.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for the primary condition and temperature 0.7 for any sampled condition, each such run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). Traces are segmented into steps at sentence/newline boundaries. For each step's generated text we compute a Syntactic Complexity Score (SCS) from an off-the-shelf dependency parser (Stanza, with UDPipe as a second parser for robustness): mean dependency-tree depth, Dependency-Locality-Theory integration cost, clause-embedding/subordination ratio, and mean dependency length; parsers are validated on each target language and results reported across all four metrics. Tasks are rendered in 3-4 typologically diverse languages (English, Spanish, Turkish, Chinese).

Experiment 1 (H1 -- The model spontaneously downshifts its own output syntax as difficulty rises): Tests whether per-step SCS drops at harder steps. Data: 500 items from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), 500 from the MATH test split (5,000 available, level-stratified), 400 synthetic deductive-logic chains we construct (depth 2-6, auto-checkable), and 400 items from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), 1,800 base items each rendered in each language; these sizes give a few hundred items/task/language for stable step-level estimates within a single-GPU-week budget. Difficulty proxies per step: per-step surprisal, operation complexity for math, and hop index for QA. Decisive metric first: the step_difficulty coefficient in mixed-effects regression SCS ~ step_difficulty + step_position + (1|model)+(1|item), pooled across parsers and languages; secondary: robustness of the sign across the four SCS metrics and across parsers. Convincing result: a negative, statistically reliable difficulty coefficient (CI excludes 0) consistent in sign across >= 3 of 4 SCS metrics and both parsers, with a position control ruling out that SCS merely tracks step index. Indecision band: a standardized difficulty coefficient whose CI lies within +/-0.05 is treated as no downshift. Negative result: a null or positive coefficient means the model does not simplify its own syntax under load, refuting H1 and dissociating LLMs from the human load-induced-simplification account.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Downshift tracks genuine difficulty, not step length or position): Tests that SCS drops at genuine hard/error-recovery steps beyond position and length confounds. Data: the same 1,800 items; on items solved correctly under free reasoning, we inject a controlled error or truncate at a step to create genuine error-recovery/hard steps, matched to easy steps at the same position and length. Decisive metric first: within-item SCS difference at error-recovery/hard steps minus matched easy steps at equal position and length; secondary: token-length-matched re-analysis. Convincing result: SCS is lower at genuine hard steps by a reliable margin (CI excludes 0) after matching position and length. Indecision band: a matched SCS difference within +/-0.05 standardized units is uninformative. Negative result: no SCS drop after matching means the Experiment-1 effect was a length/position artifact.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Per-step output-syntax complexity is diagnostic of errors): Tests whether SCS predicts step-level and final errors. Data: the traces above, split 70/30 by item. A lightweight probe (only probe trainable) is trained on per-step SCS features to predict step-level error and final correctness. Baselines: token entropy, verbalized confidence, per-step surprisal, and the information-density burst signal (density above within-trace running median). Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC for final-correctness prediction from SCS features; secondary: step-level error AUROC and delta-AUROC over each baseline. Convincing result: SCS-based AUROC >= 0.65 and exceeds the best baseline by >= 0.05 (CI excludes 0). Indecision band: AUROC in 0.55-0.62 or a delta over baselines within +/-0.03 means SCS carries no diagnostic value beyond existing signals. Negative result: AUROC ~ 0.5 refutes H2's diagnostic claim.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Forcing high-complexity syntax at hard steps degrades reasoning; simpler syntax helps): Tests the causal, content-matched syntax effect. Data: the same 1,800 items. Via strict-format prompting, each step is forced into HIGH-complexity syntax (elaborate, deeply embedded, subordinated), LOW-complexity syntax (short, flat, coordinated), or FREE baseline, with reasoning content held constant (same operations required) and SCS verified to actually differ; a length-matched control equalizes token count across conditions. Decisive metric first: the syntax_condition x step_difficulty interaction on accuracy from mixed-effects logistic regression accuracy ~ syntax_condition * step_difficulty + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: main effects at hard versus easy steps. Convincing result: HIGH-complexity syntax lowers accuracy disproportionately at hard steps (>= 4 points below FREE, CI excludes 0) and LOW-complexity helps at hard steps (>= 3 points above FREE), while both are within 2 points of FREE on easy steps, and the effect survives length-matching (isolating syntactic form from verbosity). Indecision band: interaction effects within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) mean output-syntax form does not modulate reasoning. Negative result: no interaction, or equal effects on easy and hard steps, refutes H3's causal syntax claim; only compliant, content-preserving trials are analyzed.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- Difficulty-gated simplification beats blanket and random-gated simplification): Tests that where you simplify matters. Data: the same items. Systems at matched token budget: no-intervention; blanket simplification (every step); random-gated simplification (matched intervention count at random steps); and Register-Gated Simplification (induce LOW-complexity syntax only at steps flagged hard by a surprisal threshold or the Experiment-3 probe). Decisive metric first: accuracy at matched token cost, primary contrast Register-Gated minus random-gated; secondary: Register-Gated versus blanket at equal cost. Convincing result: Register-Gated matches or exceeds blanket at lower cost and beats random-gated by >= 3 points (CI excludes 0). Indecision band: within +/-2 points of random-gated means placement is not load-bearing. Negative result: no gain over no-intervention refutes the practical value of H3.

Experiment 6 (H3 -- A locatable, steerable syntactic-elaboration signal mediates downshift): Tests the mechanism. Data: matched high-SCS-minus-low-SCS content-matched generation contrasts yield a difference-in-means "syntactic-elaboration" direction (per-layer probe AUROC, held-out validated). Systems: minus-direction steering at hard steps (predict accuracy gain), plus-direction (predict degradation), random-direction of matched norm, and no-steer. Decisive metric first: accuracy change from minus-direction steering at hard steps versus random-direction; secondary: whether the elaboration signal engages more at easy than hard steps (mediating downshift), per-item elaboration-signal-to-SCS/error Spearman correlation, dose-response, and specificity (easy-item accuracy within 1 point, fluency preserved). Convincing result: minus-direction steering raises hard-step accuracy by >= 3 points over random-direction (CI excludes 0) with monotonic dose-response and preserved easy-item accuracy, and the signal is higher at easy steps. Indecision band: steering effects within +/-2 points of random-direction leave the direction unproven; behavioral Experiments 4-5 then stand alone. Negative result: no steerable effect means the elaboration direction is not causal.

Experiment 7 (H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests whether elaborate self-generated reasoning raises misdiagnosis and register-gated simplification mitigates it. Data: 300 differential-diagnosis vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) fine-distinction items; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Systems: FREE, forced HIGH-complexity syntax, and Register-Gated Simplification. Decisive metric first: confident-misdiagnosis rate on fine-distinction cases under HIGH-complexity versus FREE; secondary: mitigation under Register-Gated. Convincing result: HIGH-complexity raises confident misdiagnosis and Register-Gated lowers it by >= 5 points (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: gaps within +/-2 points are inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no effect bounds the claim to benign benchmarks.

Experiment 8 (Uniform controls, generic-compression baseline, and cross-model/language steering ablation): For EVERY syntax intervention (Experiments 4-6) we attach both a length-matched and a token-entropy-matched control, and we add a generic CoT-shortening/compression baseline (shorten the step without targeting dependency structure) to show the effect is syntactic rather than merely shorter or lower-entropy. Compliance for forced-syntax prompts is checked by verifying the SCS actually shifts in the intended direction with operations preserved; non-compliant trials are excluded a priori by a fixed rule and their fraction reported. We then ablate the steering direction across all five models and all four languages to test whether the syntactic-elaboration direction generalizes or is confined to a single model family/language.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) SCS may be confounded with step length and difficulty (hard steps are shorter/simpler for many reasons); mitigated by length-matched controls, testing the syntax x difficulty INTERACTION rather than raw drops, position controls, and the content-matched forced-syntax and steering interventions that isolate syntactic form from content. (2) Dependency parsers are imperfect on model-generated and multilingual text; we use multiple complexity metrics and parsers, validate on the target languages, and report robustness. (3) Forcing high/low syntax via prompting may be non-compliant or covertly change content; we verify SCS actually shifts, hold operations constant, and analyze only compliant trials. (4) Instruction-tuned models may resist syntactic manipulation or already reason robustly, flattening effects; we include base variants, calibrate difficulty to mid-range, and test multiple models. (5) The elaboration direction may entangle with generic difficulty/verbosity rather than syntax per se; mitigated by content-matched high/low-SCS contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and easy-item specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-/language-specific; we report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (output-syntax complexity does not affect reasoning, or does not downshift under load) is itself informative: it would show an LLM's self-generated linguistic form is decoupled from its reasoning, dissociating LLMs from the human load-induced-simplification account. (8) The 'register shift under cognitive load' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like processing limits.

Name: endogenous_filler_buffer
Title: Um, Let Me Think: Is an LLM's Spontaneous Verbal Filler a Self-Allocated Computation Buffer?
Short Hypothesis: The semantically-empty verbal padding an LLM spontaneously emits during free generation (hedges, restatements, 'let me think', discourse fillers) is not noise but self-allocated serial computation buffer: the model adaptively increases spontaneous filler at exactly the reasoning points where extra computation is needed, this endogenous filler carries genuine hidden computation (unlike most padding elsewhere), and a locatable internal 'buffer-request' signal governs where filler is emitted, so it is a self-regulated resource rather than only an externally-injectable one.
Related Work: A cluster of work shows externally-INJECTED filler/pause tokens can buy computation: transformers solve algorithmic tasks with meaningless filler ('Let's Think Dot by Dot', 2024; 'Pause Tokens Strictly Increase Expressivity', 2025), inference-time inserted fillers help smaller models ('Expanding Computation Spaces', 2025), the effect works via activation redistribution ('Meaningless Tokens, Meaningful Gains', 2025), hidden computation over filler is decodable from the residual stream ('Reading Between the Dots', 2026; 'Understanding Hidden Computations', 2024), and frontier models exploit filler for invisible reasoning ('Not All LLM Reasoning is Visible', 2026). Separately, content-vs-length debates show verbose CoT helps mainly via content, not raw length ('Does Verbose Chain-of-Thought Really Help?', 2026), and stopwords/punctuation carry high context ('LLM-Microscope', 2025). Crucially, ALL of this studies filler that is INJECTED by the experimenter, or trained-in special tokens, or the content-vs-length of substantive CoT. NONE ask whether an LLM's OWN spontaneously-emitted, semantically-empty verbal padding in natural generation functions as an ADAPTIVE, self-allocated buffer — whether the model raises spontaneous filler precisely where computation is needed (a just-in-time allocation law), whether endogenous filler carries hidden computation while matched substantive padding does not, or whether a locatable 'buffer-request' signal causally gates where filler is emitted. My prior proposals covered information-density pacing, private-speech length, and register shift, but none isolate endogenous semantic-filler as a self-regulated computation resource. We uniquely transfer the human 'disfluency/filler under cognitive load' finding into LLMs as an adaptive-allocation phenomenon with a Location + Causal Intervention account. Novelty locus and what is new versus inherited: prior work establishes that EXPERIMENTER-INJECTED or trained-in filler can buy hidden computation; inherited from it is only that filler CAN be load-bearing. New here is that an LLM's OWN spontaneously-emitted filler is ADAPTIVELY allocated (a just-in-time law), that endogenous filler is load-bearing while length-matched substantive or neutral padding is not, and that a locatable 'buffer-request' direction governs where filler appears and can be steered — a self-regulated resource, contrasted point-by-point against each injected-filler baseline rather than conflated with it.
Abstract: When people hit a hard point in speaking they stall with 'um', 'well', 'let me think' — verbal filler that buys processing time. Large language models likewise pepper their outputs with semantically-empty padding: hedges, restatements, meta-comments, and discourse fillers. Prior interpretability work shows that filler tokens INJECTED by an experimenter can buy hidden computation, but no work asks whether an LLM's OWN spontaneously-produced filler serves this function adaptively. We hypothesize that endogenous filler is a self-allocated computation buffer: the model increases spontaneous filler at exactly the reasoning points where extra serial computation is needed, this naturally-emitted filler carries genuine hidden computation, and a locatable internal 'buffer-request' signal governs where it appears. We make three claims. First, adaptive allocation: across difficulty-graded reasoning, the rate and placement of spontaneous semantically-empty filler rise with local step difficulty, concentrating just before hard sub-computations — a just-in-time allocation law, not uniform verbosity. Second, functional load-bearing: endogenous filler spans carry decodable hidden computation (the answer becomes more decodable after them, and corrupting/deleting them hurts accuracy) whereas length-matched substantive-restatement spans do not, dissociating buffer-filler from mere tokens. Third, a controllable signal: a probe reads a 'buffer-request' signal from hidden states that predicts where filler will be emitted and predicts errors when the model fails to allocate, and steering this signal induces or suppresses filler and moves accuracy accordingly. We test these on math, logic, and multi-hop QA across several open-weight models, quantifying the allocation law, the buffer-vs-substantive dissociation, and mechanistic controllability, reframing an LLM's own filler from stylistic noise into a self-regulated computational resource. The buffer-request signal is defined concretely as a difference-in-means direction over about-to-emit-filler versus about-to-emit-substantive step-boundary states, read by a probe and manipulated by steering/patching. We pre-register a dissociation from generic long-form CoT length and from surprisal/entropy so the effect is not mere verbosity, and we test settings where spontaneous filler occurs WITHOUT permissive prompting to show the behavior is native, not prompt-induced. Practically, a buffer-request probe enables adaptive inference-time compute (spend extra tokens only where the model requests buffer) and CoT-safety monitoring of hidden computation; we benchmark the buffer-gated controller against uncertainty-triggered extra-token and repeated-sampling/test-time-scaling baselines, not only random gating.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Spontaneous filler follows a just-in-time allocation law): Tests that the model raises its own semantically-empty filler at exactly the reasoning points where extra computation is needed, concentrating just before hard sub-computations rather than uniformly. Data: free-form generations over difficulty-graded tasks - a GSM8K/MATH subset (~300 items) selected across operand/step-count difficulty, deductive logic chains depth 2-6 (~300 built), and 2WikiMultiHop-style multi-hop QA (~300 sampled); ~900 items total. Traces are segmented into spans, each auto-classified as SEMANTICALLY-EMPTY FILLER (hedges 'well/hmm/let me think', pure restatements, meta-commentary, contentless discourse connectives) vs SUBSTANTIVE (introduces a new fact/operation/value), using a rubric plus an entailment-based information-gain check, validated against human labels on a 300-span sample (target agreement >=0.8). We use existing task items but must construct the span-level filler annotation because none exists. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Decisive metric: per-step spontaneous filler rate as a function of local step difficulty, modeled as filler_rate ~ local_step_difficulty + step_position + trace_length + (1|model) + (1|item), where difficulty is proxied by per-step surprisal, operation complexity, and hop index; plus a lead-lag test (does filler at step t predict a hard computation at t+1?). Convincing result: filler rate rises with local step difficulty (coefficient CI excluding 0) beyond length/position, and the lead-lag test shows filler significantly precedes hard sub-computations (CI excluding 0) - a just-in-time allocation signature, not uniform verbosity. Indecision band: a positive but weak difficulty coefficient (CI grazing 0), or filler that co-occurs with but does not lead hard steps - allocation is suggestive only. Negative result: no difficulty dependence or no lead-lag structure - spontaneous filler is uniform stylistic noise, not adaptive allocation.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Causal difficulty check): Tests that injecting a hard sub-step makes the model spontaneously emit more filler just before it. Data/protocol: on items solved correctly under free generation, prompt-inject a controlled hard sub-step vs a matched easy sub-step at a fixed point; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: difference in spontaneous filler emitted immediately before the injected hard vs easy sub-step. Convincing result: the model emits significantly more filler before the hard sub-step than the easy one (paired difference CI excluding 0), establishing difficulty causes allocation rather than merely correlating with it. Indecision band: a small positive difference (CI grazing 0) - weak causal evidence. Negative result: no difference - difficulty does not drive spontaneous filler emission.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Endogenous filler is load-bearing, dissociated from substantive and neutral padding): Tests that the model's own filler carries hidden computation whereas length-matched substantive or neutral padding does not. Data/protocol: (a) answer-emergence - train logit-lens/linear probes to track when the answer becomes decodable across the trace and test whether decodability jumps ACROSS endogenous filler spans more than across length-matched substantive spans; (b) deletion/corruption - remove or scramble the model's own filler spans and re-run continuation from that point, versus removing equal-length substantive-restatement spans, plus a NEUTRAL-FILLER SWAP (replace emitted filler with generic '...' of equal length) to separate specific filler content from mere buffer length; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: accuracy drop when buffer-filler is removed at hard steps, contrasted with the drop from removing matched substantive spans and from the neutral-'...' swap; plus the answer-emergence jump across filler vs substantive spans. Convincing result: removing endogenous filler at hard steps lowers accuracy by >=5 pp more than removing equal-length substantive spans (CI excluding 0), the answer becomes more decodable specifically across filler spans, and the neutral-'...' swap recovers a substantial share of the accuracy (showing buffer length matters) while the model's specific filler adds further benefit. Indecision band: a 2-5 pp differential deletion effect, or an ambiguous neutral-swap result - filler is weakly or non-specifically load-bearing. Negative result: filler deletion hurts no more than substantive-span deletion, and neutral-'...' fully substitutes - endogenous filler carries no special computation, and any buffer benefit is generic to injected padding, dissociating LLMs from the human load-driven-disfluency account.

Experiment 4 (H3 - A locatable buffer-request signal that predicts filler and under-allocation errors, with mediation): Tests that a hidden-state signal governs where filler is emitted. Data/protocol: contrast step-boundary hidden states where the model is about-to-emit filler vs about-to-emit substantive content; per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) predicting impending filler emission; a difference-in-means buffer-request direction; baselines token entropy and surprisal; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC for impending filler emission (chance 0.5), whether the signal fires more at hard steps, and whether low buffer-request signal at hard steps predicts errors (under-allocation), beyond entropy/surprisal. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.75 with incremental value over entropy/surprisal, the signal is elevated at hard steps, low signal at hard steps predicts errors (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0), and per-item signal predicts filler placement which in turn predicts correctness (mediation). Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.75 or mediation rho 0.15-0.30, or no advantage over surprisal - a signal that is real but not distinctly a buffer-request. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or fully explained by surprisal - no locatable buffer-request signal.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Causal steering and a buffer-gated efficiency controller): Tests that steering the buffer-request signal moves filler and accuracy, and that gating filler by the signal is efficient. Data/protocol: steer +buffer-request at hard steps to induce filler and -buffer-request to suppress it, 4 coefficients; controls random-direction, no-steer, and blanket injected-'...'; then build a Buffer-Gated Generation controller that allows filler only at probe-flagged hard steps and compare accuracy-vs-token-cost against free generation, blanket 'think step by step', and random-gated filler; same five frozen models; specificity tracked on easy-step accuracy and fluency. Decisive metric: accuracy change under +/- buffer-request steering versus no-steer/random, and the accuracy-per-token curve of Buffer-Gated Generation versus baselines. Convincing result: +buffer-request steering at hard steps raises accuracy by >=4 pp (monotonic dose-response), -buffer-request lowers it, random-direction and blanket-'...' move <2 pp, easy-step accuracy and fluency are preserved, and Buffer-Gated Generation matches free-generation accuracy at strictly lower token cost (or higher accuracy at equal cost) versus random-gating. Indecision band: a 2-4 pp steering effect, or a controller that only ties (not beats) random-gating - causal/efficiency signal present but weak. Negative result: <2 pp steering effect or no controller advantage over random-gating - the buffer-request signal is not causally load-bearing and self-buffering confers no controllable benefit.


Adaptive-compute baselines and power: Experiment 5's Buffer-Gated Generation is compared against uncertainty-triggered extra-token allocation and standard repeated-sampling/test-time-scaling at matched token budgets (in addition to random-gating and blanket '...'); all experiments pre-register sample sizes per task/model, primary endpoints, and multiple-comparison correction, and auto-classified filler spans are human-validated as semantically empty (not covert planning text). We report base-vs-instruction-tuned failure cases and keep the two narratives separate — a behavioral allocation law and a candidate mechanistic signal — rather than presenting either as established by the other's evidence.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Classifying spans as semantically-empty filler vs substantive is hard and noisy; mitigated by a rubric + entailment-based information-gain check, human validation on a sample, and multiple detectors, plus reliance on the DELETION and answer-emergence causal tests that do not depend on perfect labels. (2) The adaptive-allocation correlation could be an artifact: hard steps are surprising, and surprisal drives both filler and difficulty; mitigated by the lead-lag test (filler PRECEDES the hard computation), the causal hard-step-injection test, and controlling for length/position. (3) Endogenous filler may simply co-occur with more thinking without being load-bearing; the buffer-vs-substantive and neutral-'...'-swap dissociations, plus deletion/corruption, isolate whether the model's specific filler carries computation. (4) Instruction-tuned models may emit little spontaneous filler (trained toward concise CoT), flattening the effect; we include base variants, less-aligned models, permissive prompts, and tasks where filler naturally appears — low spontaneous filler with a still-present buffer-request signal is itself informative. (5) The buffer-request direction may entangle with generic difficulty/verbosity rather than a specific allocation signal; mitigated by matched about-to-filler/about-to-substantive contrasts, held-out validation, random-direction steering, and easy-step specificity checks. (6) Deletion/re-run changes context and could hurt for trivial reasons; we use matched substantive-span deletion and neutral-swap controls to isolate the buffer-specific effect. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (spontaneous filler is uniform, non-load-bearing, or indistinguishable from injected filler) is itself informative — it would show LLM filler is stylistic noise and that the computation-buffer benefit only exists for experimenter-injected tokens, dissociating LLMs from the human load-driven-disfluency account. (9) The 'self-allocated buffer / disfluency under load' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like processing.

Name: self_translation_drift
Title: Lost in Self-Translation: Does an LLM Corrupt Its Own Intermediate Conclusions When Forced to Re-Express Them in Another Language?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is made to restate its own intermediate reasoning conclusions in a different language mid-trace (self-translation), the semantic content of those conclusions systematically drifts away from the original, this drift compounds across a multi-step trace and causes downstream errors, is larger for concepts lacking clean cross-lingual equivalents, and is mediated by a locatable 'meaning-preservation' representation that can be causally steered to reduce drift. The central novelty is the CONTROLLED intra-trace self-translation paradigm together with the same-language-paraphrase contrast (which isolates cross-lingual re-expression from restatement per se), not the broad observation that cross-lingual drift exists. Primary contribution: this causal paradigm and finding; the internal decodable meaning-retention state is a secondary mechanistic contribution.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work shows LLMs route reasoning through an English-shaped pivot (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025; Beyond English-Centric, 2024), that latent-language consistency is not always necessary because models re-align near output layers (Do LLMs Need to Think in One Language?, 2025), that language mixing rises with difficulty and reflects internal preferences (Language Mixing in Reasoning LMs, 2025), and that ablating language-specific components improves multilingual reasoning (When Less Language is More, 2025). Translation-mechanism work (Exploring the Translation Mechanism, 2025) localizes sparse heads for word-level translation. ALL of this studies where reasoning is routed or how surface translation works; none studies what happens to the CONTENT of a model's OWN intermediate conclusions when it is forced to re-express them in another language partway through reasoning, whether such self-translation induces compounding semantic drift, whether drift concentrates on cross-lingually mismatched concepts, or whether a meaning-preservation signal mediates it. Human bilingual research (self-translation cost, interpretation load; fMRI of Simultaneous Interpretation, 2014) shows re-expression across languages taxes control and can distort meaning. We uniquely transfer this into LLMs as a controlled intra-trace self-translation manipulation with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes clinical instance. Three-to-four closest papers with one-sentence deltas: 'Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?' (2025) and 'Beyond English-Centric' (2024) show NATURAL pivot routing, not forced self-restatement; 'Language Mixing in Reasoning LMs' (2025) studies spontaneous mixing, not a controlled manipulation with a same-language control; 'Exploring the Translation Mechanism' (2025) localizes word-level translation heads, not intermediate-conclusion drift. Our delta is a controlled intra-trace manipulation with same-language-paraphrase and external-translation controls that isolates a causal effect on the model's OWN conclusions.
Abstract: Bilingual humans who translate their own thoughts on the fly pay a cost: meaning can distort as an idea is re-expressed in another language, especially for concepts that do not map cleanly between languages. Large language models increasingly reason across languages, mixing scripts and routing through an English-shaped pivot, yet no work asks whether re-expressing their own intermediate conclusions in a different language corrupts the content of those conclusions. We introduce a controlled self-translation paradigm: partway through a multi-step reasoning trace, the model is required to restate an intermediate conclusion it just derived in a target language, then continue reasoning from the re-expressed version. We test three claims. First, self-translation induces semantic drift: the re-expressed conclusion measurably diverges in meaning from the original, and this drift compounds across successive self-translations, degrading final accuracy relative to same-language paraphrase and no-restatement controls. Second, drift is content-selective: it is larger for reasoning steps whose key concepts lack clean cross-lingual equivalents (lexical gaps, culturally specific terms) than for steps built on cross-lingually stable concepts. Third, drift is causally mediated by a locatable meaning-preservation representation: a probe reading whether the re-expressed conclusion still encodes the original meaning predicts downstream error, and steering along a located preservation direction (or patching the pre-translation conclusion representation) reduces drift and rescues accuracy. We evaluate on multilingual math, multi-hop QA, and logic across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where re-expressing a partial diagnosis in another language silently flips the conclusion. Our work reframes multilingual reasoning as vulnerable to self-inflicted meaning loss and offers an interpretable failure signal and a training-free mitigation. We align the title and abstract around one primary claim (a controlled self-translation paradigm that causally induces conclusion drift) and one secondary mechanistic claim (a decodable meaning-retention state that mediates it). We add an external-translation control (a separate module translates the conclusion) and a copy-preserve-semantic-content baseline to show the effect is not reducible to code-switching or translation noise. Concrete deployment pathways where models are forced to re-express intermediate content across languages include cross-lingual agent hand-offs, multilingual RAG (retrieve in one language, reason in another), translate-then-reason pipelines, localized tool-call arguments, and multilingual summarization; if confirmed, practitioners would add prompting rules against mid-trace cross-lingual restatement, safeguard RAG hand-offs, or apply representation-level mitigation, and we define success by practical-significance thresholds (not only statistical significance) for these settings.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight multilingual models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). "Self-translation" means the model is required, at a defined insertion point, to restate an intermediate conclusion it just derived in a target language different from the reasoning language, then continue reasoning from the re-expressed version. Target languages are drawn from each model's stronger and weaker languages and are back-translation-checked.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Self-translation induces semantic drift that compounds and degrades accuracy): Tests the core effect against restatement controls. Data: a battery of 250 items each for (a) multi-step arithmetic sampled from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), (b) multi-hop QA (3-5 hops) sampled from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), and (c) synthetic deductive-logic chains (depth 2-6, auto-checkable), 750 items, each with defined insertion points where an intermediate conclusion has just been derived and with known intermediate-conclusion ground truth; 250/task supports stable condition contrasts within budget. Conditions, content held constant, format-enforced and compliance-verified: (i) NO-RESTATE baseline; (ii) SAME-LANGUAGE PARAPHRASE (restate then continue, controlling for the act of restating); (iii) SELF-TRANSLATE (restate in a different language, continue from it); (iv) COMPOUNDING SELF-TRANSLATE (translate at 2-3 successive insertion points). Decisive metric first: final-answer accuracy of SELF-TRANSLATE versus SAME-LANGUAGE PARAPHRASE and NO-RESTATE from mixed-effects logistic regression accuracy ~ condition + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: a dose-response drop with number of self-translations, and error-localization (does the final error follow from the drifted conclusion?). Convincing result: SELF-TRANSLATE falls below SAME-LANGUAGE PARAPHRASE by >= 4 points (CI excludes 0, isolating cross-lingual re-expression from restatement per se), COMPOUNDING degrades further monotonically, and errors localize to the re-expressed step. Indecision band: a SELF-TRANSLATE-minus-PARAPHRASE gap within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) means cross-lingual re-expression is not separable from restatement. Negative result: no gap beyond paraphrase means self-translation is lossless, refuting H1 and dissociating LLMs from the human self-translation cost; only compliant trials (restated conclusion actually used downstream) are analyzed.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Drift measures are valid and agree): Tests that drift is measurable two independent ways. Data: the same traces. Drift between original and re-expressed conclusion is quantified by (a) round-trip semantic equivalence (back-translate, compare to the original via an NLI/entailment model and exact-answer match for numeric conclusions) and (b) representational distance between hidden-state encodings of the original versus re-expressed conclusion at matched positions. Decisive metric first: rank correlation between the NLI-based and representational drift measures; secondary: whether either drift measure separates error from correct trials. Convincing result: the two drift measures agree at Spearman rho >= 0.4 (CI excludes 0) and higher drift accompanies errors. Indecision band: agreement rho 0.2-0.35 means the drift construct is only weakly cross-validated and downstream mediation is treated cautiously. Negative result: no agreement (rho ~ 0) means "drift" is measurement noise, undermining the mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Drift is content-selective, larger for cross-lingually mismatched concepts): Tests selectivity. Data: the same intermediate conclusions, each tagged by whether its key concept has a clean target-language equivalent (using cross-lingual dictionaries and lexical-gap / culturally-specific term lists) versus a cross-lingually stable concept, controlling for concept frequency and step difficulty. Decisive metric first: the concept_gap coefficient on drift and on accuracy loss from mixed-effects regression drift ~ concept_gap_status + concept_frequency + step_difficulty + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: the accuracy-loss interaction. Convincing result: gap/mismatched concepts show reliably larger drift and accuracy loss (CI excludes 0) after controlling for frequency and difficulty. Indecision band: a concept_gap coefficient CI within +/-0.05 standardized units means selectivity is not detectable. Negative result: no gap effect means drift is uniform across concept types, refuting H2.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- A locatable meaning-preservation representation mediates drift): Tests the representational locus. Data: the traces, split 70/30 by item. At the post-self-translation position a linear probe (only probe trainable) decodes whether the original meaning/answer of the intermediate conclusion is still encoded (per-layer held-out AUROC). Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC for original-meaning decodability, and whether low decodability predicts downstream error; secondary: per-item mediation of the condition-to-error effect (Spearman). Convincing result: AUROC >= 0.70, low decodability predicts error (rho >= 0.2, CI excludes 0), and probe-decodable drift mediates the condition effect. Indecision band: AUROC 0.55-0.65 means a weak preservation signal that cannot anchor the mediation claim. Negative result: chance AUROC means no locatable preservation representation, refuting H3's mechanism.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- Patching and steering reduce drift and rescue accuracy): Tests causality. Data: (a) Patching -- cache the pre-self-translation conclusion representation and patch it into the post-translation forward pass; controls are patching from a different item's conclusion and a random-matched representation, and we patch only the intermediate-conclusion representation (before the final answer) to rule out answer-leakage. (b) Steering -- a difference-in-means "meaning-preservation" direction from preserved-minus-drifted conclusion contrasts; plus-direction steering after self-translation, minus-direction under same-language paraphrase, random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: accuracy rescue on failed self-translate items under same-item patching versus no-patch, and under plus-direction steering versus random-direction; secondary: specificity (cross-item/random patching does not rescue; NO-RESTATE accuracy within 1 point; fluency preserved), dose-response. Convincing result: same-item patching and plus-direction steering each recover accuracy by >= 5 points over their controls (CIs exclude 0) while cross-item/random controls do not, with monotonic steering dose-response. Indecision band: rescue within +/-3 points of controls means the intervention is not selective. Negative result: no selective rescue means meaning-preservation is not a causal lever.

Experiment 6 (H3 -- High-stakes clinical hand-off instance): Tests whether self-translation flips a diagnosis and mitigation reduces it. Data: 300 clinical vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) and constructed bilingual hand-off cases where a partial diagnostic conclusion must be re-expressed in another language mid-reasoning; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Systems: NO-RESTATE, SELF-TRANSLATE, and SELF-TRANSLATE with preservation-direction steering or conclusion patching. Decisive metric first: diagnosis-flip rate on fine-distinction cases under SELF-TRANSLATE versus NO-RESTATE; secondary: flip-rate reduction under steering/patching. Convincing result: self-translation raises the diagnosis-flip rate and the mitigations cut it by >= 5 points (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: gaps within +/-2 points are inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no flip effect bounds the claim to benign benchmarks.

Experiment 7 (Ground-truth, downstream-use, and localization rigor): We define intermediate-conclusion ground truth per dataset (numeric value for GSM8K, the resolved entity/fact for 2WikiMultiHopQA, the derived proposition for logic chains) and verify insertion points are semantically comparable across tasks. We add a direct test that the translated conclusion is causally used downstream -- contradiction injection into the re-expressed conclusion and masked-context probes -- not just format compliance. Localization of probing/patching/steering (layer, token, site) is pre-registered on held-out data. Answer-leakage and generic-denoising controls are strengthened with within-item WRONG-conclusion patches and orthogonalized steering directions, plus no-translation baselines. The concept-gap labeling protocol is specified with multiple resources, inter-annotator agreement, and a human bilingual evaluation on a stratified subset to validate the NLI/back-translation drift metrics. We report a power/effect-size analysis for the per-condition splits and add a naturally-occurring agent/RAG setting to show the phenomenon beyond the forced-restatement protocol.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Self-translation may degrade accuracy simply by adding tokens/steps rather than via meaning drift; mitigated by the SAME-LANGUAGE PARAPHRASE control (equal added steps, no cross-lingual re-expression) and by requiring the drift measures to mediate the accuracy loss. (2) Instruction-tuned models may re-align near output layers (per Do LLMs Need to Think in One Language?, 2025) and avoid drift entirely, muting effects; a null in easy conditions with an effect in COMPOUNDING/gap-concept conditions is still informative, and we include harder items and multiple models. (3) Compliance risk - the model may ignore the self-translation instruction or covertly keep the original-language conclusion in context; we enforce format, verify the restated conclusion is used downstream, and analyze only compliant trials. (4) Drift measures may be confounded by NLI-model or tokenizer noise; we cross-validate NLI-based and representational drift and use exact-answer match for numeric conclusions. (5) Patching could rescue by leaking the answer rather than restoring meaning; we patch only the intermediate-conclusion representation (before the final answer) and use cross-item/random patching specificity controls. (6) The preservation direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; mitigated by matched preserved/drifted contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and NO-RESTATE specificity checks. (7) Concept-gap tagging is fuzzy; we use multiple resources and annotators and control for frequency/difficulty. (8) Effects may be small or model/language-specific; we test multiple models and languages and report effect sizes with CIs. (9) A null result (self-translation preserves meaning) is itself informative, showing LLM cross-lingual re-expression is lossless unlike the human self-translation cost. (10) The self-translation framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like bilingual cognition. (11) We temper the mechanistic language: the 'meaning-preservation representation' is described as an operationally defined, decodable meaning-retention STATE unless the stricter causal localization (within-item wrong-conclusion patches, orthogonalized steering) holds, and the clinical hand-off is scoped as one bounded high-stakes instance with expert spot-checks, not a clinical-grade evaluation.

Name: doubt_marker_gating
Title: A Word for Doubt: Do Metacognitive Discourse Markers Causally Gate an LLM's Error Correction, or Are They Just Surface Style?
Short Hypothesis: The specific metacognitive discourse markers an LLM emits mid-reasoning ('wait', 'actually', 'but', 'hmm', 'however') are not interchangeable stylistic decorations: each marker's lexical identity causally recruits a distinct error-monitoring/revision computation, so that (a) forcing an appropriate doubt marker at a hidden error step triggers correction the model would otherwise skip, (b) marker identity carries graded information about whether and how the model will revise, and (c) suppressing the model's own emitted marker aborts an in-progress correction. In short, the model needs a word for doubt to enact doubt. Primary contribution (single, crisp): the LEXICAL IDENTITY of a metacognitive marker causally gates error correction, tested by two decisive experiments -- a sufficiency test (forcing the appropriate marker at a hidden-error step triggers correction that a length-matched neutral filler and a mismatched marker do not) and a necessity test (suppressing the model's own emitted marker aborts an in-progress correction). Marker-type granularity, internal separability, mediation, and the clinical instance are subordinate analyses.
Related Work: Recent interpretability work extracts a single holistic 'reflection direction' and steers reflection frequency (ReflCtrl 2025; From Emergence to Control 2025), traces layer-wise reflection onset through discourse-cue competition (From Latent Signals to Reflection Behavior 2026), shows reflection correlates with internal uncertainty (ReflCtrl 2025), and that error-detection is decodable from activations (Probing for Arithmetic Errors 2025; The Validation Gap 2025). Self-correction studies (Dissociation of Faithful/Unfaithful Reasoning 2024; Understanding the Dark Side 2024; Accuracy-Correction Paradox 2025) show correction is brittle and sometimes causes answer-wavering. Crucially, ALL of this treats reflection as a single latent behavior/direction and treats the surface discourse markers as an epiphenomenal readout of an underlying decision. NONE ask whether the LEXICAL IDENTITY of the emitted marker is itself causally functional — whether different doubt words ('wait' vs 'actually' vs 'but') recruit different revision computations, whether inserting the RIGHT marker (vs a wrong or generic one) at a hidden error step gates correction, or whether the marker is a linguistic tool the model needs to enact revision rather than a byproduct of an already-made revision decision. This reframes the language<->intelligence question at the level of individual metacognitive words and distinguishes us from holistic reflection-vector and error-probe work. Distinguished from known marker-type correlations (e.g., Wait/Hmm vs But/However co-occurring with different revisions): those are observational associations under a single holistic 'reflection direction', whereas our new CAUSAL prediction is that only the semantically APPROPRIATE marker, not a mismatched or neutral filler of equal length, changes revision at a hidden-error step -- and that suppressing the emitted marker aborts correction. The delta over each prior result is that marker identity is a functional linguistic tool, not an epiphenomenal readout.
Abstract: When people catch themselves making a mistake they often say 'wait' or 'actually' — self-directed words that mark and license a correction. Large language models sprinkle the same markers through their chains of thought, and prior interpretability work treats these markers as surface readouts of an underlying, holistic 'reflection' decision. We test the opposite, stronger claim: that the specific metacognitive discourse marker is a causally functional linguistic tool, and that the model needs the right word for doubt in order to enact doubt. We make three claims. First, marker identity is informative and distinct: different doubt markers ('wait', 'actually', 'but', 'however', 'hmm') precede systematically different revision outcomes (full backtrack vs local edit vs no change), and are carried by partly distinct internal signals rather than one reflection direction. Second, markers causally gate correction: at reasoning steps containing a hidden, latent error the model is about to propagate, forcing the appropriate doubt marker triggers correction the model would otherwise skip, while forcing a mismatched or a neutral filler marker does not — isolating lexical content from mere token insertion. Third, markers are necessary, not epiphenomenal: suppressing the model's own spontaneously emitted marker (via constrained decoding or activation intervention) aborts an in-progress correction, driving the model to propagate the error. We evaluate on math, logic, and multi-hop QA with injected latent errors across several open-weight reasoning models, and add a high-stakes clinical-reasoning instance where the absence of a doubt word lets a wrong provisional diagnosis stand. Our work reframes metacognitive markers from stylistic residue into causal, language-borne machinery for machine self-correction. We reduce the paper to one primary hypothesis and two decisive, pre-registered experiments (sufficiency and necessity), with informativeness, internal separability, mediation, and clinical transfer as secondary analyses. Downstream uses include prompt-level control of self-correction, interpretability of metacognition, calibration, safety monitoring, and practical debugging of reasoning failures; the communities most likely to build on it are mechanistic interpretability, reasoning, alignment, and evaluation. Both outcomes matter: a positive result yields a controllable linguistic gate on correction, while a null sharpens the view that markers are pre-lexical readouts -- the explicit weaker finding being 'marker identity predicts but does not cause revision'.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and its reasoning variant, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled/forced-continuation run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). "Metacognitive discourse markers" are the emitted words wait, actually, but, however, hmm, "let me reconsider", "hold on"; "revision outcome" is one of no change / local numeric-or-fact edit / full backtrack-and-restart, labeled by ground-truth-anchored diff of the pre- and post-marker reasoning.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Marker identity is informative about revision outcome beyond position and difficulty): Tests whether different doubt words precede different revision types. Data: natural chains of thought on 500 items from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), 300 synthetic deductive-logic chains (depth 2-6, auto-checkable), and 300 from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), 1,100 items; traces are segmented into steps and marker occurrences detected, with each occurrence labeled by downstream revision outcome via automatic diff against ground truth (multiple thresholds plus human spot-checks on a 10% sample). 1,100 items yield enough marker occurrences for a stable multinomial fit within budget. Decisive metric first: whether marker_identity predicts revision_type beyond step position and difficulty, from multinomial mixed-effects regression revision_type ~ marker_identity + step_difficulty + step_position + (1|model)+(1|item), reported as the likelihood-ratio improvement over a marker-free model; secondary: the per-marker revision-type distribution. Convincing result: marker identity reliably improves revision-type prediction over the marker-free baseline (CI on the improvement excludes 0) with distinct per-marker profiles. Indecision band: a likelihood-ratio improvement whose CI overlaps 0, or near-identical per-marker distributions, means markers are not differentially informative. Negative result: no predictive gain means markers are interchangeable surface style, refuting H1's distinctness claim.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Forcing the appropriate doubt marker at a hidden-error step gates correction): The central sufficiency test. Data: a latent-error-injection benchmark built from the same 1,100 items -- on items the model solves correctly under free reasoning, inject a controlled error into a specified step (wrong intermediate value / invalid inference) and truncate just after it, yielding matched hidden-error steps where correction is warranted. At the post-error continuation point the next tokens are forced to be (i) an APPROPRIATE doubt marker ("wait," / "actually,"), (ii) a MISMATCHED marker implying agreement ("therefore," / "so,"), (iii) a NEUTRAL FILLER of equal length ("okay," / a nonce-but-fluent phrase), or (iv) FREE continuation baseline. Decisive metric first: correction rate (model fixes the injected error and reaches the right answer) under the appropriate doubt marker versus the neutral-filler and mismatched controls, from mixed-effects logistic regression corrected ~ marker_condition + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: dose (single versus repeated marker) and specificity on NO-error control items (forcing a doubt marker should not spuriously break correct reasoning). Convincing result: appropriate doubt markers raise correction by >= 5 points over both the neutral-filler and mismatched controls (CIs exclude 0), isolating lexical content from mere token insertion, with a dose effect and <= 2-point spurious breakage on no-error controls. Indecision band: an appropriate-minus-neutral-filler gap within +/-2 points means lexical content is not separable from "more tokens". Negative result: no advantage over neutral filler means the marker's identity does not gate correction, refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- Specific markers selectively induce specific revision types): Tests marker granularity. Data: the matched hidden-error steps from Experiment 2. Decisive metric first: the revision-type distribution each forced marker produces (e.g., does "wait" yield more full backtracks and "actually" more local edits?), tested as a marker-by-revision-type association; secondary: effect consistency across models. Convincing result: forced markers produce reliably different revision-type distributions (association CI excludes independence), matching a backtrack-versus-local-edit split. Indecision band: distributions differing within a small association effect (CI overlapping independence) mean granularity is not established though gating (Experiment 2) may still hold. Negative result: identical distributions across markers refute the fine-grained selectivity part of H1.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 -- Distinct markers have partly separable internal signals, not one reflection axis): Tests the locational claim. Data: hidden states at pre-marker positions on will-revise-versus-won't-revise trials, split 70/30 by item; linear probes (only probe trainable) predict (a) whether a revision is impending and (b) which marker is about to be emitted (per-layer held-out AUROC). Decisive metric first: pairwise linear separability (held-out AUROC) between marker-specific directions, compared against a single-reflection-direction baseline for predicting correction; secondary: impending-revision AUROC. Convincing result: distinct markers are pairwise separable (AUROC >= 0.65) and a marker-specific probe beats the single-reflection-direction baseline for predicting correction by >= 0.05 AUROC (CI excludes 0). Indecision band: pairwise AUROC 0.55-0.62, or a marker-specific-versus-holistic delta within +/-0.03, means markers may collapse onto one reflection axis. Negative result: markers not separable beyond one reflection direction means the lexical distinctions are epiphenomenal, refuting the distinct-signal part of H1.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- Suppressing the model's own emitted marker aborts an in-progress correction): The necessity test. Data: trials where the model SPONTANEOUSLY emits a doubt marker and then corrects. We suppress the marker two ways -- (a) constrained decoding banning the full doubt-marker synonym set at that position, and (b) subtracting the located marker direction from the residual stream at that position -- against a random-token-ban control and a random-direction control of matched norm. Decisive metric first: correction-abort rate (error propagated to the final answer) under marker suppression versus the random controls; secondary: agreement between the two suppression methods and whether per-item marker-probe strength predicts correction. Convincing result: suppressing the model's own doubt marker aborts correction, raising the error-propagation rate by >= 5 points over random controls (CIs exclude 0) under both suppression methods. Indecision band: an abort-rate increase within +/-2 points of the random controls means necessity is not demonstrated (suppression may merely reroute to a synonym, which the full-synonym ban is designed to prevent). Negative result: no increase in error propagation means the marker is a pure readout of an already-made revision decision, refuting H3 and cleanly dissociating the enactment of revision from the word that names it.
