Experiment 6 (H2/H3 -- Mediation): Tests that the marker direction carries the causal effect. Data: the forced-marker and suppression trials. Decisive metric first: whether forced-marker-induced correction gain is mediated by increased engagement of the located marker direction (Spearman between induced direction-engagement and correction gain); secondary: whether per-item marker-probe strength predicts correction. Convincing result: the correction gain is mediated by marker-direction engagement (rho >= 0.2, CI excludes 0). Indecision band: a mediation rho within +/-0.1 leaves the causal path underdetermined while the behavioral gating (Experiment 2) stands. Negative result: no mediation dissociates the behavioral effect from the located direction.

Experiment 7 (H2/H3 -- High-stakes clinical instance): Tests whether an absent doubt word lets a wrong provisional diagnosis stand. Data: 300 differential-diagnosis vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) and constructed cases where a plausible-but-wrong provisional diagnosis is injected mid-reasoning; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Systems: FREE continuation, forced appropriate doubt marker at that step, and neutral-filler control. Decisive metric first: confident-misdiagnosis rate when no doubt marker is forced versus when an appropriate marker is forced; secondary: neutral-filler comparison. Convincing result: absence of a doubt marker lets the wrong diagnosis stand and forcing an appropriate marker rescues the correct diagnosis by >= 5 points over the neutral-filler control on fine-distinction cases (CI excludes 0). Indecision band: a rescue within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no rescue bounds the gating claim to benign benchmarks.

Experiment 8 (Pre-registration, lexical-isolation controls, and naturalism): We pre-register Experiment 2 (sufficiency) and Experiment 5 (necessity) as the two decisive tests, with primary endpoints (correction-rate gain over neutral filler AND mismatched marker for sufficiency; correction-abort-rate increase over random controls under both suppression methods for necessity), effect-size targets, and explicit failure criteria. Additional controls isolate lexical semantics from token count, punctuation, and position (equal-length fillers, punctuation-matched insertions, position-matched insertion points). We verify the latent-error injection preserves naturalism -- injected errors are validated as plausible continuations so markers are not made artificially useful by conspicuous errors. The mediation analysis (Experiment 6) is explicitly marked secondary, and the clinical vignette (Experiment 7) is scoped as a bounded high-stakes demonstration rather than part of the core decisive claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Forcing a doubt marker may help simply by adding a pause/extra tokens rather than via lexical meaning; mitigated by the length-matched NEUTRAL FILLER and MISMATCHED-marker controls and by testing marker-specific revision-type selectivity (a generic 'more tokens' account predicts no marker-type differentiation). (2) Reasoning-tuned models may correct robustly regardless of marker, yielding ceiling effects; we use latent-error injection to create genuine hidden-error steps, include base/non-reasoning variants, and calibrate error difficulty. (3) Suppression via token-banning may push probability onto a synonymous marker, masking necessity; we ban the full doubt-marker synonym set and cross-check with the activation-subtraction suppression and random-token/random-direction controls. (4) Automatic labeling of revision type (backtrack vs local edit) is noisy; we use ground-truth-anchored diffs, multiple thresholds, and human spot-checks on a sample. (5) Marker directions may entangle with generic uncertainty rather than marker identity; mitigated by matched will-revise/won't-revise contrasts, pairwise-separability tests against a single-reflection-direction baseline, held-out probe validation, and specificity controls. (6) Effects may be model-specific; we test several models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result — markers are interchangeable surface style, forcing/suppressing them does not gate correction — is itself highly informative, showing LLM self-correction is decided pre-lexically and the discourse marker is a pure readout, cleanly dissociating the enactment of revision from the language that names it. (8) The 'word for doubt' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like metacognitive experience.

Name: linguistic_cognitive_gear
Title: Language as a Cognitive Gear: Does Prompt Language Shift LLMs Between Intuitive and Reflective Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: The surface language of a prompt does not merely change an LLM's accuracy; it shifts the model along an intuition-vs-reflection axis, changing WHICH decision strategy it deploys on identical problems. We frame this as an LLM-native multilingual strategy-routing phenomenon, not a literal import of the contested human Foreign Language Effect: on semantically identical items, the prompt's surface language systematically shifts the model's susceptibility to intuitive lures (belief bias, base-rate neglect, CRT traps) beyond what per-language accuracy or resource level explain, and this shift is a locatable, steerable internal direction. The human FLE is cited only as motivating analogy, not as the claim under test.
Related Work: Cognitive-science work documents a 'Foreign Language Effect': people show altered belief-bias and cognitive-effort allocation when reasoning in a foreign language (Thinking in a Foreign Language Distorts Allocation of Cognitive Effort, 2019). In LLMs, prior work shows (i) reasoning is routed through English latent space (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025; Beyond English-Centric, 2024), (ii) language shapes causal-order biases (Under the Shadow of Babel / BICAUSE, 2025), (iii) accuracy gaps stem from understanding failures (Why Do Multilingual Reasoning Gaps Emerge?, 2025), and (iv) ablating language components boosts multilingual reasoning (When Less Language is More, 2025). All of these treat language as affecting ACCURACY, latent-routing, or a single bias type. None test whether surface language systematically changes the model's position on the general intuition-vs-reflection (System-1 vs System-2) axis across a battery of dual-process cognitive-bias tasks, whether such shifts are dissociable from accuracy and resource level, or whether the 'cognitive gear' is a locatable and steerable internal direction. The three closest prior families are (i) multilingual reasoning-accuracy papers (differences framed as competence), (ii) single-bias language-effect papers (one bias at a time, e.g. causal-order), and (iii) System-1/2 probing and steering papers (monolingual). Our delta is a language-conditioned, multi-bias intuition-vs-reflection axis measured on semantically identical items and dissociated from accuracy, plus a causal internal direction. We add conditions not covered by prior bias batteries: tightly controlled same-semantic-content cross-language switches within model and item, and cross-script/code-switch conditions, to separate language identity from comprehension and resource effects. We treat the dual-process (System-1/System-2) vocabulary as a behavioral abstraction, not a claim of human-like cognition, and we do not rely on the contested human FLE as evidence.
Abstract: Does an LLM reason with the same cognitive style regardless of the language it is prompted in? Cognitive science shows that humans reasoning in a foreign language allocate cognitive effort differently, altering their susceptibility to intuitive-but-wrong answers. We hypothesize an analogous phenomenon in LLMs: the surface language of a prompt acts as a 'cognitive gear,' shifting the model between fast intuitive answering and slow reflective reasoning on identical problems. Crucially, this is a claim about reasoning STRATEGY, not just accuracy. We assemble a multilingual battery of dual-process items where the intuitive answer diverges from the correct answer: belief-bias syllogisms, base-rate-neglect scenarios, Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) traps, and conjunction-fallacy items, each semantically matched and translated across typologically diverse languages. For each item we measure not just accuracy but the intuitive-response rate (rate of giving the tempting-but-wrong lure) and reflection engagement (spontaneous multi-step reasoning). We test whether the same model gives more intuitive-lure responses in some languages than others even when accuracy is controlled, and whether this dissociates from language resource level. We then probe mechanism: using a linear probe on hidden states we identify a 'reflection direction' separating intuitive-lure from reflective trajectories, test whether prompt language moves representations along it, and causally steer along it to override language-induced intuitive answering. We pre-register a primary hypothesis (H1: prompt language shifts the intuitive-lure rate on identical items after controlling per-language accuracy and resource level) and secondary mechanistic and causal hypotheses (H2 probe, H3 steering), and we add a higher-stakes applied arm (medical-triage and policy/risk vignettes carrying an intuitive lure) to test relevance beyond classic cognitive-bias items. We narrow the contribution to what the design can establish, namely behavioral dissociation plus causal-intervention evidence for a language-conditioned strategy axis, not literal System-1/System-2 cognition. Confirmed or null, the result tells benchmark designers, localization teams, and safety evaluators whether multilingual evaluation must control for strategy shifts and not just accuracy. Our study reframes multilingualism from an accuracy problem to a cognitive-style problem, offering the first dual-process, mechanistically-grounded account of how language shapes reasoning strategy in AI.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Multilingual dual-process battery): Prerequisite dataset. Data: a built battery of ~200 items per family across 4 families - belief-bias syllogisms (valid/invalid x believable/unbelievable), base-rate-neglect scenarios with a stereotype lure, expanded CRT-style traps, and conjunction-fallacy (Linda-style) items - 800 English source items, each with a labeled correct answer AND a labeled intuitive-lure answer, calibrated to mid-range difficulty. Translated into 8 typologically diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Japanese) using independent human translations with back-translation checks, translationese/adequacy detection, within-language paraphrase controls, item-level semantic-invariance checks, cross-language difficulty calibration, and bilingual-speaker validation on a sample, giving 6,400 language-item instances. Decisive metric first: back-translation match rate and human-judged adequacy. Convincing result: >=90% items pass adequacy in all languages; items failing are dropped and regenerated. Indecision band: 70-90% adequacy in some language - we retain only passing items and flag that language's reduced item count. Negative result (<70% in a language): that language is excluded to avoid confounding translation noise with strategy shifts.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Language shifts intuitive responding beyond accuracy): The central strategy-vs-accuracy test. Data: the 6,400 instances above, used as is. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Mistral-7B, all weights frozen; 5 samples/item at temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: the same model across the 8 languages, plus baselines that separate language identity from comprehension - translate-to-English-then-answer, hidden-chain language controls, script-transliterated variants, and code-switched prompts. A pre-registered power analysis targets the minimum detectable language variance component per model; because 800 source items stratify by task, model, and language, we pre-register the required per-cell n and expand items if power falls short. Decisive metric first: the Intuition Index = intuitive-lure response rate among errors (fraction of wrong answers matching the labeled lure vs. other wrong answers); we additionally report a richer error taxonomy (lure-selection rate, confidence/calibration, token-budget/latency proxies, and answer distribution conditional on correctness) so the strategy claim does not rest on a single scalar. The primary index is analyzed in a mixed-effects model (lure_rate ~ language + per_language_accuracy + resource_level + (1|model) + (1|item)). Convincing result: language retains a significant effect on lure responding after controlling for per-language accuracy and a corpus-based resource-level covariate (likelihood-ratio test p and 95% CI on the language variance component excluding the accuracy-only model), replicated in at least 3 of 4 models. Indecision band: the language term explains <2% additional variance beyond accuracy with a CI touching zero - language differences are essentially accuracy-driven, so the cognitive-gear claim reduces to competence. Negative result (no language effect once accuracy is controlled): surface language does not move the intuition axis, refuting the hypothesis.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Reflection responsiveness by language): Tests the Foreign-Language-Effect analog that some languages carry more residual intuitive responding that reflection must correct. Data/models as Experiment 2. Systems compared: direct-answer vs. chain-of-thought prompting within each language. Decisive metric first: reflection responsiveness = reduction in lure rate from direct to CoT prompting, per language. Convincing result: languages differ significantly in residual (post-CoT) lure rate (mixed-effects language term CI excluding zero), mirroring cross-language effort differences. Indecision band: cross-language spread in residual lure rate < 3 points - reflection erases language differences, so any gear effect is superficial. Negative result: no language differences in reflection responsiveness.

Experiment 4 (H2 - A reflection direction exists and language moves representations along it): Tests the mechanistic locatability claim. Data: hidden states collected on items where the model answered intuitive-lure vs. reflective-correct (matched items, differing only in lure salience), from the 6,400 instances. Models: same four, frozen; trainable component is a per-layer linear probe (logistic, L2, seeds 0/1/2) separating lure from reflective trajectories; 70/30 item-disjoint train/test split. Systems compared: probe direction vs. random directions; adversarial controls confirming the direction is not merely language-ID, correctness, or token-length/difficulty (the reflection probe must beat probes trained to predict those nuisances and retain variance after partialling them out) and cross-task and cross-model transfer of the direction; and the projection of a fixed item's representation under different prompt languages. Decisive metric first: probe AUROC for lure-vs-reflective on held-out items; secondary: correlation between the per-item projection shift when switching prompt language and the per-item behavioral lure shift. Convincing result: probe AUROC >=0.70 at some layer AND a positive projection-shift-to-behavior correlation (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55,0.70] or projection-behavior correlation CI spanning zero - the 'reflection direction' is weak or not the axis language moves, so mechanism is unclear. Negative result (AUROC <=0.55): no linear reflection axis, undermining the mechanistic account.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Causal steering reduces language-induced intuitive answering): Tests the steerability claim. Data: 800 held-out items (item-disjoint from probe training) in the languages showing highest intuitive responding in Experiment 2. Models: same four, frozen; steering adds +beta times the reflection direction in mid layers; beta tuned on a 200-item dev split, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: no-steer, multiple sham controls (random-direction matched-norm, off-target-layer steering, and sign-flipped reflection-direction steering), reflection-direction steering, and, to quantify collateral damage, evaluation on non-bias tasks (general QA/fluency) alongside the bias items. Decisive metric first: change in Intuition Index; secondary: fluency (external-LM perplexity) and answer-language fidelity. Convincing result: reflection-direction steering lowers the lure rate significantly more than random-direction steering (95% CI on the difference excluding zero) without degrading fluency (perplexity within 5% of no-steer) or answer-language fidelity (>=95%). Indecision band: steering effect within 1 point of the random-direction control - steering does not causally isolate reflection. Negative result (no reduction, or fluency collapse): the direction is not a usable causal lever. Ablations (Experiment 6): layer/strength sweeps and cross-lingual generalization of the direction (train the probe on English, test cross-lingually); convincing if the English-trained direction still reduces lure rate in other languages, indecisive if it transfers only within language family, negative if it fails to transfer. All numbers are planned evidence.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Translation artifacts could create item difficulty differences that masquerade as strategy shifts; mitigated by back-translation checks, human verification on a sample, and controlling for per-language accuracy in the dissociation analysis. (2) Intuitive-lure rate among errors can be noisy if accuracy is very high or very low in some languages; we design items calibrated to mid-range difficulty and report confidence intervals. (3) The 'reflection direction' may entangle with content or difficulty rather than a genuine strategy axis; mitigated with matched-item contrasts (same problem, differing only in lure salience) and random-direction controls. (4) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes. (5) The System-1/System-2 framing is a useful abstraction, not a literal claim about LLM cognition; we frame findings behaviorally and mechanistically rather than as evidence of human-like dual processing. (6) A null result (language does not shift the intuition axis beyond accuracy) is still informative, showing multilingual differences are purely competence-driven.

Name: translation_crutch_grammar_induction
Title: Grammar Book or Bilingual Dictionary? Testing Whether LLMs Learn a Novel Language In-Context by Building a Grammar or Leaning on a Translation Crutch
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is given a novel language in-context (a mini grammar plus examples), it does not induce a genuine standalone grammar; instead it leans on a 'translation crutch,' covertly mapping each construction back to a pivot language and generating via that pivot. The strength of this crutch grows with typological distance from the model's training languages, causally bounds how well the model generalizes to unseen constructions, and is a locatable, steerable internal signal: suppressing the crutch forces (and, for near-typology languages, improves) genuine grammar use, while amplifying it induces pivot-shaped errors. We define the constructs operationally: 'genuine standalone grammar induction' = generalization to held-out construction types that is invariant to typological distance from the model's dominant language and shows no pivot-shaped error concentration; 'pivot-mediated generation' = generalization that degrades with typological distance and produces pivot-shaped errors with decodable pivot glosses. Primary contribution: this mechanistic dissociation with a causal near-vs-far typology crossover.
Related Work: Recent work shows LLMs can do some explicit in-context language learning from grammar-book explanations ('Explicit Learning and the LLM in MT', 2025) and that learnability degrades with typological implausibility both in pretraining ('Can LMs Learn Typologically Implausible Languages?', 2025) and constructed-language studies (Culbertson & Kirby 2011). In-context language learning has been mechanistically tied to n-gram/induction heads ('In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms', 2024), and multilingual work shows shared cross-lingual syntactic circuits with a language-independent pivot direction ('The Same But Different', 2024; 'On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages', 2024) and English-shaped pivot routing. All of this either (a) measures behavioral learnability without asking HOW the model represents the novel language, or (b) studies pivot routing only for KNOWN languages present in training. None ask whether in-context learning of a genuinely novel language is a real grammar induction or a covert translation-to-pivot process, whether that crutch scales with typological distance, whether it causally caps generalization to unseen constructions, or whether it is a locatable/steerable component. We uniquely reframe in-context language learning as a translation-crutch-vs-native-grammar dissociation with a Location + Causal Intervention account. Closest baselines and what they cannot explain: behavioral in-context-language-learning work (Explicit Learning and the LLM in MT 2025; Can LMs Learn Typologically Implausible Languages 2025) measures learnability but not HOW the novel language is represented, and known-language pivot-routing work (The Same But Different 2024) studies pivots only for languages seen in training; neither can explain whether novel-language ICL is covert translation nor predict a suppression-induced near-vs-far crossover. We pre-register the causal estimand for the 'translation crutch' (the effect of subtracting the pivot-translation direction on pivot-incompatible generalization) as distinct from generic latent-semantic or instruction-following states.
Abstract: Give a large language model a short grammar and a handful of examples of a language it has never seen, and it will often produce plausible new sentences. But is it inducing a genuine grammar, or is it quietly translating every construction back to a language it already knows and generating through that crutch? We propose the translation-crutch hypothesis: in-context learning of a novel language proceeds largely by covert mapping to a pivot (typically English-shaped) representation rather than by building a standalone grammar, that reliance on this crutch grows with the novel language's typological distance from the model's training languages, and that the crutch causally limits generalization to constructions not derivable by pivot-style word-for-word mapping (e.g., non-canonical word order, agreement, and morphology absent from the pivot). We construct controlled artificial languages that systematically vary typological distance from English (word order, case marking, agreement, morphological richness), each presented in-context via a mini grammar plus examples, and test generalization to held-out construction types. Behaviorally, we predict a distance-graded generalization cliff concentrated on pivot-incompatible constructions, with characteristic pivot-shaped errors (e.g., defaulting to English word order or dropping agreement). Mechanistically, we locate a 'pivot-translation' representation via probing (can the pivot-language gloss be decoded from hidden states during novel-language generation?) and test causally: suppressing this component should force genuine grammar use and improve near-typology generalization while hurting far-typology output, and amplifying it should induce pivot-shaped errors. Across several open-weight models we quantify the crutch, its typological-distance scaling, its causal cap on generalization, and steering controllability, reframing in-context language learning as translation rather than acquisition. We replace the hand-designed distance metric with a FACTORIAL design that isolates word order, case, agreement, and morphology as separate manipulable factors, and we validate each model's 'dominant training language' EMPIRICALLY (e.g., via pivot-gloss decodability and per-language competence) rather than assuming English. To show the contribution is not only about artificial languages, we add a semi-natural held-out setting: a real low-resource language the model saw little of, presented grammar-book style, testing the same pivot-shaped-error prediction. Concrete downstream implications: for low-resource MT, language documentation, and prompt-based adaptation, grammar-book prompting should be trusted only for pivot-compatible constructions, and a pivot-gloss-decodability check offers a deployable detector of crutch failure; under a null (distance-independent generalization) researchers would credit genuine in-context grammar induction.
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights on frozen hidden states. The novel language is supplied entirely in-context (a compact grammar-book plus example pairs); no fine-tuning occurs. Decoding is greedy for primary conditions and temperature 0.7 for sampled conditions, each sampled run over seeds 0, 1, 2. Effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap CIs over 1000 item-level resamples; behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts (1|model)+(1|item). The "pivot" is the model's dominant training language (English by default); a "pivot-shaped error" is one that defaults to pivot structure (e.g., English word order or dropped agreement).

Experiment 1 (H1 -- In-context novel-language learning shows a typological-distance-graded generalization cliff on pivot-incompatible constructions): Tests the behavioral crutch signature. Data: a controlled artificial-language suite we construct -- 6-8 synthetic languages sharing a fixed nonce lexicon and a small function-word inventory but varying along typological axes graded from English: word order (SVO -> SOV -> VSO -> free order with case), overt case marking (none -> nominative/accusative suffixes), subject-verb and adjective-noun agreement (none -> gender/number), and morphological richness (isolating -> agglutinative suffix stacking); each language ships a compact in-context grammar-book (rules stated in English) plus 15-30 example sentence pairs, and a per-language typological-distance score is the count/type of features diverging from English. For each language we hold out entire construction TYPES from the in-context examples (show declaratives, test questions; show singular agreement, test plural; show intransitives, test ditransitives) and test roughly 200 held-out items per language via translation-into and translation-out-of the novel language plus grammaticality judgments over minimal pairs, auto-graded against the ground-truth generative grammar; 6-8 languages x ~200 items spans the distance axis with stable estimates within budget. Decisive metric first: the typological_distance x construction_pivot_compatibility interaction on accuracy from mixed-effects regression accuracy ~ typological_distance * pivot_compatibility + (1|model)+(1|item); secondary: the pivot-shaped error rate on pivot-incompatible held-out constructions. Convincing result: accuracy on pivot-INCOMPATIBLE held-out constructions falls steeply with typological distance (reliable negative distance slope, CI excludes 0) while pivot-compatible constructions stay high, and errors are predominantly pivot-shaped (>= 50% of errors). Indecision band: a distance x compatibility interaction whose CI corresponds to an accuracy-slope difference within +/-3 points across the distance range means no differential cliff is detectable. Negative result: distance-independent generalization with no pivot-shaped error concentration means the model performs genuine in-context grammar induction, a strong positive result refuting the crutch hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- A locatable pivot-translation representation rises with distance and on errors): Tests the internal crutch. Data: during novel-language generation (with in-context English glosses REMOVED at test time to avoid a shortcut), we extract hidden states at content and function-word positions, split 70/30 by item, and train linear probes (only probe trainable) to decode (i) the corresponding English gloss token and (ii) a pivot-translating-versus-native-generating state from near-typology-versus-far-typology contrasts (per-layer held-out AUROC). Decisive metric first: pivot-gloss decoding AUROC and its scaling with typological distance; secondary: whether pivot-gloss decodability is higher on error trials. Convincing result: pivot-gloss decodability is well above chance (AUROC >= 0.65), rises reliably with typological distance (positive slope, CI excludes 0), and is higher on error trials. Indecision band: AUROC 0.55-0.62 or a distance slope CI overlapping 0 means the pivot representation is not clearly present or not distance-scaled. Negative result: chance decodability (with glosses removed) means no covert pivot-translation step, supporting genuine acquisition and refuting H2.

Experiment 3 (H1/H2 -- The pivot representation mediates the behavioral cliff): Tests the link. Data: the same items. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation between per-item pivot-gloss decodability and per-item generalization error on pivot-incompatible constructions; secondary: whether decodability adds predictive power over typological distance alone. Convincing result: per-item decodability predicts pivot-incompatible error at rho >= 0.2 (CI excludes 0) and improves prediction beyond distance. Indecision band: rho within +/-0.1 means the crutch representation and the behavioral cliff are not linked at our power. Negative result: no correlation dissociates the representation from behavior.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- Suppressing the crutch dissociates near- from far-typology; amplifying induces pivot-shaped errors): Tests causality via the predicted dissociation. Data: a difference-in-means "pivot-translation" direction from pivot-translating-minus-native-generating contrasts at the best probe layer. Systems: SUPPRESS (subtract the direction during generation), AMPLIFY (add it), random-direction of matched norm, no-steer. Decisive metric first: the interaction of steering (suppress versus no-steer) with typological distance on accuracy -- suppression should HELP near-typology and HURT far-typology (a dissociation, not a uniform effect); secondary: amplification-induced pivot-shaped error rate on well-learned constructions, dose-response, and specificity (lexical accuracy and fluency preserved). Convincing result: suppression improves near-typology pivot-compatible/agreement/word-order compliance by >= 3 points while reducing far-typology accuracy (a reliable crossover interaction, CI excludes 0), and amplification induces pivot-shaped errors (English word order / dropped morphology) even on well-learned constructions, both beyond random-direction controls. Indecision band: a suppression x distance interaction whose CI corresponds to a differential within +/-2 points means the dissociation is not demonstrated (a uniform degradation would be ambiguous). Negative result: uniform or null steering effects, or effects indistinguishable from random-direction, mean the pivot direction is not a causal route.

Experiment 5 (H1 -- Grammar-book versus examples, and pivot-tracks-the-model's-dominant-language crossover): Tests robustness and ties the crutch to the model's own pivot. Data: the same suite. We vary whether in-context material is rule-based (explicit grammar) versus example-only, vary the number of examples and lexicon overlap, and for a model with a non-English dominant language test whether the crutch tracks THAT language's typology rather than English. Decisive metric first: crutch reliance (pivot-shaped error rate and pivot-gloss decodability) under rule-based versus example-only material; secondary: whether the distance axis realigns to a non-English pivot for the non-English-dominant model. Convincing result: explicit rules reduce crutch reliance (or only improve pivot-compatible constructions) reliably, and for the non-English-dominant model the cliff and pivot-decodability realign to that language's typology (CI excludes 0), directly tying the effect to the model's dominant language. Indecision band: rule-versus-example differences within +/-2 points, or an ambiguous pivot realignment, leave these refinements open without affecting Experiments 1-4. Negative result: no realignment to the model's own pivot would undercut the claim that the crutch is the dominant training language specifically.

Experiment 6 (Empirical pivot, probe/steering controls, and human adjudication): We determine each model's dominant language empirically and repeat the distance axis relative to THAT language. Probe controls include shuffled gloss targets, alternative non-pivot label sets, matched layer/time positions, and an explicit test against simple lexical memorization of in-context examples. Steering directions are learned on held-out contrasts and validated against equal-norm random directions, unrelated semantic directions, and a global-degradation check, with the predicted near-vs-far DISSOCIATION (not a uniform effect) as the decisive signature. We add difficulty-matched constructions that break pivot-translatability and adversarial constructions where pivot and grammar predict different outputs at equal surface complexity. Free-generation outputs are adjudicated by humans on a stratified subset (beyond auto-grading), and we report power/item counts per condition to justify detecting the interaction and crossover.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Artificial languages may be too easy or too hard, flattening the distance-graded cliff; we calibrate feature counts and example numbers to mid-range difficulty and report the full distance sweep. (2) A pivot-gloss probe decoding English during generation could reflect the in-context English glosses still present in context rather than a genuine internal translation step; we mitigate by removing glosses from context at test time, probing at matched positions, and using near-vs-far typology contrasts and the causal steering test (which manipulates the representation, not the prompt). (3) Suppressing the crutch may broadly degrade generation, confounding the near-typology improvement claim; we use random-direction and matched-magnitude controls and test the predicted DISSOCIATION (helps near-typology, hurts far-typology) rather than a uniform effect. (4) 'Typological distance from training languages' is approximate and model-specific; the non-English-pivot crossover test and per-model distance scoring address this. (5) Instruction-tuned models may already do robust in-context grammar induction, muting the crutch; we include base variants, harder morphology, and multiple models, and report effect sizes. (6) Auto-grading against a generative grammar may miss acceptable variation; we use minimal-pair grammaticality judgments and human spot-checks. (7) A null result (no translation crutch; generalization independent of typological distance and pivot-decodability) is itself highly informative: it would show LLMs perform genuine in-context grammar induction rather than covert translation, a strong positive claim about language-learning ability. (8) The 'crutch/acquisition' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim about human-like language acquisition. (9) The main claim is narrowed to a behavioral dissociation supported by probe evidence PLUS the causal near-vs-far crossover; if steering yields only uniform degradation we retain the behavioral and probe results and do not overclaim causal localization.

Name: lexical_gap_resolution
Title: Mind the Gap: Do Lexicalization Gaps in the Latent Pivot Language Blur an LLM's Concepts?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs route non-English inputs through a largely English-shaped 'concept space.' We hypothesize that a concept's internal representational resolution is bottlenecked by whether it is *lexicalized* (has a compact, single-/few-token word) in the model's latent pivot language: concepts that fall in a lexical gap of the pivot language are represented more diffusely, are harder to separate from neighbors, and yield systematically worse fine-grained reasoning — and providing an ad-hoc lexicalization (a coined single token/name) in-context sharpens both the geometry and the behavior.
Related Work: A cluster of work establishes that multilingual LLMs form a shared, largely English-pivoted concept space in middle layers (Semantic Hub Hypothesis 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Separating Tongue from Thought 2024; Tracing Multilingual Representations with Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025; When Meanings Meet 2026). These works show a shared space *exists* and can be causally patched, and that averaging concept representations across languages helps translation. Concept Space Alignment (2024) and High-Dimensional Interlingual Representations (2025) show alignment quality varies by typology and abstractness. XCOMPS (2025) shows conceptual understanding degrades for low-resource and morphologically complex languages. Crucially, all this work treats concepts holistically or averages across languages; none isolates *lexicalization gaps* — concepts that are compactly lexicalized in some languages but not the pivot — as a natural, controllable experiment on whether the pivot language's vocabulary sets a resolution limit on non-linguistic conceptual discrimination and reasoning. We differentiate from the closest prior probing of gap representations (which reports that gap concepts have weaker or more holistic representations) in a dedicated way: our novel claim is not 'gaps are weaker' but a PIVOT-LANGUAGE resolution-bottleneck MECHANISM with a causal intervention and behavioral consequences. We name the new elements: (1) a sharper mechanistic prediction that the penalty tracks lexicalization in the model's PIVOT language specifically - not source-language lexicalization, raw token length, or dictionary-definition length; (2) a causal, training-free ad-hoc-lexicalization vs. forced de-lexicalization intervention holding the concept fixed; (3) behavioral fine-grained discrimination consequences with a mediation test; and (4) a reusable, carefully annotated lexical-gap/control benchmark across languages that others can adopt. We contrast the penalty with frequency, abstractness, and other confounds throughout.
Abstract: Multilingual language models process the world through a shared internal concept space that is disproportionately shaped by their dominant (often English) latent pivot language. We ask a simple question with deep implications for how language bounds machine intelligence: does the *vocabulary* of the pivot language set a resolution limit on what the model can finely discriminate and reason about? Human languages differ in which concepts they lexicalize — some have a single compact word for a notion (e.g., a specific kinship relation, an emotion, a color category, a shade of taste) that other languages must express periphrastically. We hypothesize a lexicalization-gap penalty: concepts that lack a compact lexicalization in the pivot language are represented more diffusely (lower cluster tightness, poorer separability from neighbors) and are correspondingly harder for the model to reason about at fine grain, even when the content is expressed identically. We assemble concept sets that are lexicalized in some languages but constitute lexical gaps in English, matched to lexicalized controls on frequency and abstractness, and measure (i) representational resolution via probing and cluster geometry across layers, and (ii) fine-grained behavioral discrimination and relational reasoning. We then test causality two ways: introducing an ad-hoc single-token lexicalization (a coined name) in-context should sharpen geometry and improve reasoning about gap concepts, while artificially 'de-lexicalizing' control concepts (forcing periphrastic reference) should blur them. We make the pivot-language crossover test (does the penalty relocate with a model's own pivot vocabulary?) a central, not optional, novelty-bearing experiment, with concrete candidate non-English-pivot models and a pre-specified fallback. We narrow the behavioral claim to FINE-GRAINED concept discrimination under matched descriptions rather than broad 'reasoning,' and we include application-facing case studies (culturally specific emotion terms, kinship, legal/social concepts, and safety-critical translation categories). Across several open-weight models we quantify the gap penalty, its dissociation from frequency, abstractness, and other confounds, the effectiveness of ad-hoc lexicalization (with a mediation test of whether representational sharpening mediates behavioral gains), and pre-registered effect-size thresholds that would make the findings actionable for multilingual training, prompting, and evaluation. We release the annotated gap/control benchmark as a reusable metric suite. A positive result implies pivot-vocabulary-aware training/evaluation and prompt-time lexicalization; a null implies the shared concept space is genuinely vocabulary-independent. Our work reframes the shared concept space from a uniform interlingua into a vocabulary-limited one, revealing a concrete channel by which language shapes AI intelligence.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Lexicalization-gap concept sets with matched controls): Prerequisite. Data: a built set of ~120 target concepts that are compactly lexicalized in at least one non-English language but are English lexical gaps requiring periphrasis (e.g., Portuguese 'saudade', German 'Schadenfreude', fine kinship distinctions, specific color/material/taste/texture and social-relation terms), each paired with a control concept that IS compactly lexicalized in English, matched on estimated corpus frequency (from a reference corpus) and on human abstractness rating; each concept supplied with a cross-lingual definition (English plus 2-3 other languages, back-translation checked) and a set of minimally-different neighbor concepts. Gap status set by a pre-registered protocol with multiple annotators, expert adjudication, explicit inclusion criteria, and cross-linguistic dictionaries; controls are matched not only on corpus frequency and abstractness but also on token length, definitional length, familiarity, concreteness, cultural salience, and estimated training-data prevalence. Decisive metric first: inter-annotator agreement on gap status and match quality across all these covariates. Convincing result: strong agreement (target kappa >=0.7 with adjudication) and no significant target/control difference on any matched covariate. Indecision band: kappa 0.4-0.6 - ambiguous items are dropped. Negative result (targets and controls differ on frequency/abstractness): the confound is unresolvable and sets are rebuilt.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Lexicalization-gap penalty on representational resolution): Central representational test. Data: for each concept, multiple paraphrased descriptions in English and 2-3 other languages (back-translation checked); representation extraction is fully specified - prompt templates, layer set (middle layers, swept), pooling over the concept-description span, paraphrase count, and language conditions - and geometry is measured both within-language and cross-language. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Aya-23-8B, all weights frozen; trainable component is a linear neighbor-discrimination probe (seeds 0/1/2). Systems compared: gap concepts vs. matched controls. Decisive metric first: per-concept representational resolution measured three ways - cluster tightness (within-concept variance across paraphrases), neighbor separability (silhouette vs. minimally-different neighbors), and probe AUROC distinguishing the concept from neighbors - entered as resolution ~ lexical_gap_status + frequency + abstractness + language + (1|model). Convincing result: a significant negative lexical_gap coefficient (resolution lower for gap concepts) with 95% CI excluding zero beyond frequency and abstractness, consistent across the three resolution measures and in at least 3 of 4 models. Indecision band: lexical_gap coefficient CI spanning zero once frequency/abstractness are controlled - any raw gap penalty is a frequency/abstractness artifact, so pivot-vocabulary does not set a resolution limit. Negative result (gap concepts show higher resolution): refutes the lexicalization-gap penalty.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Behavioral fine-grained penalty that tracks representational resolution): Tests downstream consequences. Data: for each concept, built discrimination and relational items - odd-one-out among near-neighbors, 'does description X match the concept better than its neighbor?', and analogy/relational-ordering - all expressed via descriptions so the surface never contains a compact English word; ~5 items/concept. Models: same four, frozen; 5 samples/item, seeds 0/1/2. Decisive metric first: accuracy with the lexical_gap coefficient controlling for frequency/abstractness; secondary: per-concept Spearman correlation between the behavioral penalty and the Experiment-2 resolution penalty. Convincing result: a significant behavioral gap penalty (coefficient CI excluding zero) that correlates with the representational penalty (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: behavioral-penalty CI spanning zero - representational diffuseness, if any, does not reach behavior. Negative result (no penalty or negative resolution-behavior correlation): the resolution limit does not affect reasoning.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Ad-hoc lexicalization sharpens, forced de-lexicalization blurs): Causal test holding the concept fixed. Data: for gap concepts, an in-context coined single-token name ('Let X = <definition>') then the same discrimination/relational items using X, vs. a no-name baseline, a matched-length inert-preamble control, a random-name control, semantically meaningless but equally salient labels reused across different concepts, a delayed-label condition, and tokenization-matched pseudo-words - together separating a genuine lexicalization/anchoring effect from a generic salient-token effect; conversely, for control concepts, forced periphrastic reference (never the compact word, only its definition). We additionally run a mediation analysis testing whether representational sharpening mediates the behavioral gain rather than only co-occurring with it. Models: same four, frozen; seeds 0/1/2. Decisive metric first: change in accuracy for gap concepts under naming (and change in cluster tightness/separability); secondary: change for control concepts under de-lexicalization. Convincing result: naming significantly improves gap-concept accuracy and sharpens geometry beyond the inert-preamble and random-name controls (difference CI excluding zero), and forced de-lexicalization degrades control-concept resolution/accuracy toward gap levels. Indecision band: naming effect within the inert-preamble control's CI - any benefit is a generic anchor-token effect, not lexicalization per se, leaving causality unestablished. Negative result (naming does not help or de-lexicalization does not hurt): lexicalization is not the causal factor.

Experiment 5 (H1 - Pivot-language crossover): Directly ties the penalty to the pivot language's vocabulary. Data: the concept sets re-scored for lexicalization in a non-English pivot language. Models: an available non-English-pivot model (e.g., a Japanese-continued-pretraining Llama variant) plus the English-pivot models as comparison, all frozen. Decisive metric first: whether the gap penalty tracks lexicalization in the model's pivot language rather than English (interaction of gap-status-in-pivot x model-pivot). Convincing result: the penalty follows the model's own pivot vocabulary (interaction CI excluding zero). Indecision band: interaction CI spanning zero - the penalty does not clearly relocate with the pivot, so the pivot-vocabulary mechanism is only weakly supported and we lean on Experiments 2-4. Negative result (penalty stays English-shaped regardless of pivot): the effect is not pivot-vocabulary-driven. If no suitable non-English-pivot model is available, this experiment is reported as not run and the causal Experiment 4 carries the mechanism claim. All quantities are planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over concepts, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Frequency and abstractness are hard to fully control and may drive apparent gap penalties; we match controls on both and include them as covariates, and use the causal naming/de-lexicalization interventions (which hold the concept fixed) to isolate lexicalization per se. (2) 'Lexical gap' status is fuzzy and language-dependent; we rely on multiple annotators and cross-linguistic dictionaries and report robustness to concept-set choices. (3) Extracting clean per-concept representations is noisy given surface-token contamination; we use many paraphrases, matched positions, and multiple layers. (4) Ad-hoc naming might help simply by adding a stable anchor token regardless of concepts, so we include inert-preamble and random-name controls. (5) The pivot-language crossover test depends on availability of a non-English-pivot model; if unavailable we rely on the English-pivot evidence plus the causal interventions. (6) A null result (no lexicalization-gap penalty) is itself informative, indicating the shared concept space is genuinely vocabulary-independent and that periphrastic descriptions fully recover fine-grained conceptual resolution.

Name: token_granularity_reasoning_tradeoff
Title: The Granularity Tax: When Coarse Tokenization Buys Fluency at the Cost of Compositional Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: The token granularity at which a concept is encoded controls a fundamental trade-off in LLMs: coarse (multi-character, whole-word) tokens improve fluency and retrieval but suppress the compositional/algorithmic reasoning that requires manipulating a concept's internal parts. Crucially, this trade-off is not a fixed property of the tokenizer but is dynamically re-negotiated inside the model, and we can measure a per-concept 'granularity depth' at which sub-token structure becomes accessible and causally intervene on it to trade fluency for reasoning at inference time, without retraining.
Related Work: A cluster of recent work establishes that tokenization harms character-level and arithmetic reasoning: character understanding emerges late and depends on vocabulary size (The Strawberry Problem, 2025; How Do LMs Acquire Character-Level Information, 2026), spelling knowledge is reconstructed in intermediate layers with a 'breakthrough layer' (Spelling-out is not Straightforward, 2025), and tokenization bounds symbolic/arithmetic reasoning even with CoT (Tokenization Constraints, 2025; Tokenization counts, 2024; Counting Ability and Tokenization, 2024). Separately, scaling-law work argues LARGER vocabularies (coarser tokens) improve overall performance (Scaling Laws with Vocabulary, 2024; Over-Tokenized Transformer, 2025). These two literatures are in tension but never reconciled: the first says coarse tokens hurt reasoning, the second says coarse tokens help. No prior work (a) frames these as a single controllable trade-off along a granularity axis, (b) measures WHERE in depth sub-token structure is re-exposed as a per-concept quantity ('granularity depth'), or (c) offers a training-free inference-time intervention that shifts a model along the fluency-vs-reasoning trade-off by amplifying sub-token reconstruction. Relative to inner-lexicon/breakthrough-layer work (which measures WHERE spelling is reconstructed) and to generic activation steering, our deltas are: (a) a measurable Pareto frontier between fluency and compositional reasoning on matched strings under controlled tokenization; (b) granularity depth as an out-of-sample PREDICTOR of compositional-failure rates across unseen concepts, tasks, and tokens, which a single breakthrough-layer measurement does not provide; and (c) a targeted sub-token-reconstruction steering direction shown to be non-equivalent to forced fine tokenization and to generic/random same-norm steering. The novelty is primarily the diagnostic (granularity depth) and the intervention (STRS); the finding and mechanism are supporting. Even a null STRS result matters: it would falsify the claim that inference-time access to sub-token structure can recover compositional reasoning without retraining. We reconcile the tension and turn it into a controllable lever.
Abstract: Two recent threads of tokenization research point in opposite directions: one shows that coarse subword tokens cripple character-level and symbolic reasoning, while scaling-law work shows that larger vocabularies (coarser tokens) improve overall model performance. We argue these are two faces of a single phenomenon we call the granularity tax: encoding a concept in a coarse token improves fluent retrieval but hides the concept's internal parts, suppressing the compositional reasoning that must manipulate those parts. We make three contributions. First, we show empirically that for the SAME underlying string, forcing coarse vs. fine tokenization produces a systematic fluency-up / compositional-reasoning-down trade-off across arithmetic, spelling, anagram, and morphological tasks. Second, we introduce granularity depth: using probing classifiers we measure, per concept, the layer at which a coarse token's sub-token structure becomes linearly decodable, and show it is later for higher-frequency/coarser tokens, quantifying an internal 're-negotiation' of granularity. Third, we introduce a training-free intervention, Sub-Token Reconstruction Steering (STRS): we identify the direction along which sub-token structure is written into the residual stream at the breakthrough layer and amplify it during inference. We show STRS shifts a model along the trade-off curve, recovering compositional-reasoning accuracy on coarse-token inputs at a measurable, tunable cost to fluency, and compare it against CoT, single-digit tokenization, and re-tokenization baselines across several open-weight models. The findings inform concrete decisions - vocabulary-size and tokenizer design, when to enable deployment-time steering, and how to construct tokenization-robust benchmarks - and target users working on arithmetic robustness, morphologically rich languages, transliteration/OCR text, and code identifiers, where we report expected accuracy gains against cheaper alternatives (CoT, spelling-out, re-tokenization). We measure fluency/retrieval not by perplexity alone but with task-based measures (next-token calibration, lexical recall, and human pairwise preference under matched content). Our work unifies conflicting tokenization findings into one controllable axis and provides both a diagnostic (granularity depth) and a lever (STRS) linking token granularity to machine reasoning.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - The granularity trade-off: coarse tokens buy fluency, cost compositional reasoning): Tests the core trade-off. Data: a built matched battery where each item's identical underlying content is presented at coarse vs. fine granularity - (a) multi-digit arithmetic (whole-number tokens vs. comma/space-separated single digits), (b) spelling/letter-counting (whole-word token vs. spelled-out), (c) anagram/character-reordering, (d) morphological segmentation (whole word vs. morpheme-spaced); ~1,000 items per task (4,000 total), length-controlled so coarse/fine pairs differ only in granularity, coarse vs. fine tokenization is induced on the SAME underlying string by inserting or removing delimiters (spaces, commas, zero-width separators) that force whole-token vs. per-character/morpheme segmentation, holding characters, order, and answer identical; we control and log sequence length, delimiter type, formatting, and prompt template, and include a delimiter-only placebo (a neutral separator that does not change segmentation) to rule out formatting artifacts, using right-to-left/comma conventions from prior arithmetic work. We add an application-facing arm beyond synthetic tasks: OCR-style text, code-identifier manipulation, and transliteration in morphologically rich languages. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Pythia (1.4B/6.9B) for a scale sweep, all weights frozen; greedy plus 5 samples (temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2). Systems compared: coarse vs. fine presentation of the same content. Decisive metric first: compositional-reasoning accuracy (exact match) as a function of token coarseness; secondary: a fluency proxy (perplexity / log-prob of natural continuations plus a judged generation-quality check on 200 held-out prose samples). Convincing result: a within-item crossover - fine tokenization raises compositional accuracy by >=10 points while coarse tokenization raises the fluency proxy, with both CIs excluding zero, yielding a monotone accuracy-vs-coarseness trade-off curve in at least 3 of 4 model families. Indecision band: accuracy difference between coarse and fine in [0,5] points with CI spanning zero - granularity does not measurably trade off against reasoning, so the 'granularity tax' is not observable behaviorally. Negative result (coarse tokens equal or beat fine on compositional accuracy): no tax; the hypothesis is refuted.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Granularity depth is measurable and later for coarser tokens): Tests that sub-token structure is re-exposed at a per-concept depth. Data: a built probe set of ~2,000 tokens spanning frequency deciles and lengths (from the model vocabulary and a reference corpus for frequency), each presented in a spelling/decomposition prompt. Models: same families, frozen; trainable component is per-layer linear probes decoding the i-th character/sub-token constituent (seeds 0/1/2, 5-fold CV). Systems compared: decoding accuracy across layers; granularity depth = earliest layer whose decoding accuracy exceeds a threshold, reported robustly across thresholds and via a threshold-free summary (area under the decoding-accuracy-over-layers curve) rather than a single 80% cutoff. Decisive metric first: correlation between granularity depth and token frequency/length/vocabulary rank (mixed-effects: depth ~ frequency + length + rank + (1|model)). Convincing result: coarser/higher-frequency tokens have significantly later granularity depth (frequency coefficient CI excluding zero), and the measured breakthrough layer matches prior spelling-reconstruction findings within a few layers. Indecision band: frequency/length coefficients with CIs spanning zero - granularity depth exists but is not systematically organized by coarseness, weakening the 're-negotiation' account. Negative result (sub-token structure decodable everywhere or nowhere): no meaningful granularity-depth variable.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Granularity depth predicts compositional failure): Links the diagnostic to behavior. Data: the 4,000 items from Experiment 1, tagged with the granularity depth of their relevant token from Experiment 2. Models: same, frozen. Decisive metric first: the granularity-depth coefficient in a mixed-effects logistic regression (accuracy ~ granularity_depth + token_length + frequency + (1|model)). Convincing result: later granularity depth predicts lower compositional accuracy (coefficient CI excluding zero) beyond length and frequency, and this relationship, fit on one token/task set, predicts failure rates out-of-sample on held-out concepts and tasks (positive held-out predictive correlation). Indecision band: coefficient CI spanning zero - depth is not the operative bottleneck. Negative result (positive coefficient): depth is unrelated to or protective against failure, decoupling the diagnostic from the tax.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Sub-Token Reconstruction Steering shifts the model along the trade-off): Tests the training-free lever. Data: 800 held-out coarse-token items from the Experiment-1 tasks. Models: same, frozen; STRS construction is specified precisely - source contrast pairs (sub-token structure decodable vs. not) at the breakthrough layer, difference-in-means over matched pairs, per-layer normalization, layer selection at or around the breakthrough layer, and steering applied at the relevant token positions; strength swept, seeds 0/1/2. Causal specificity is tested by intervening BEFORE vs. AFTER the breakthrough layer, steering on matched non-reconstruction directions of equal norm, and checking that effects are concept-specific (do not transfer to unrelated concepts) rather than global activation noise; we test whether the direction generalizes across concepts, tasks, and models. We frame the trade-off as a controllable shift supported by these controls rather than an unqualified causal claim. Systems compared: (i) no intervention, (ii) CoT prompting, (iii) forced fine tokenization (single-digit/spelled-out), (iv) random-direction steering (matched norm), (v) re-tokenization, and STRS. Decisive metric first: area under the accuracy-vs-fluency trade-off curve - compositional accuracy recovered per unit fluency lost, swept over steering strength; secondary: absolute accuracy gain on coarse inputs and answer fidelity. Convincing result: STRS recovers coarse-input compositional accuracy along a tunable curve, beating random-direction steering (accuracy-per-fluency CI excluding zero) and approaching forced fine tokenization without re-tokenizing. Indecision band: STRS indistinguishable from random-direction steering (difference CI spanning zero) - sub-token structure cannot be cheaply amplified, so the tax is intrinsic rather than a readout artifact (the diagnostic and trade-off findings still stand). Negative result (STRS only degrades the model at all strengths): no usable lever.

Experiment 5 (Scale/emergence sweep): Data: Experiments 1-2 sets. Models: Pythia intermediate training checkpoints and the 1.4B/6.9B sizes, frozen. Decisive metric: the training step / scale at which the granularity tax (Experiment 1 crossover) and STRS recoverability (Experiment 4) first appear. Convincing result: both emerge together at an identifiable scale/step, tying the tax to representational maturity. Indecision band: noisy, non-monotone emergence - we report trajectories descriptively without a claim about onset. Negative result: no consistent emergence pattern. All quantities above are planned evidence, not measured; CIs are bootstrap over items and seeds.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Coarse vs. fine presentations may differ in more than granularity (e.g., sequence length, digit ordering); we length-control and use right-to-left/comma conventions from prior arithmetic work to isolate granularity. (2) The 'fluency' proxy (perplexity) may not fully capture generation quality; we supplement with a judged generation-quality check. (3) The reconstruction direction may be entangled with content; we use matched contrast pairs and random-direction controls. (4) STRS may broadly degrade the model if amplified too strongly; the point is a tunable trade-off, so we report the full strength sweep rather than a single operating point. (5) Granularity depth probing can be noisy for rare tokens; we report CIs and restrict to well-attested tokens. (6) A null STRS result (structure cannot be cheaply amplified) is still informative, confirming the tax is intrinsic rather than a readout artifact, and the trade-off characterization and granularity-depth diagnostic stand independently.

Name: naming_as_compositional_chunking
Title: A Rose by a Shorter Name: Does Giving a Sub-Skill a Compact Label Let LLMs Compose It Into Novel Combinations?
Short Hypothesis: A central claim for why language powers intelligence is that it compresses reusable knowledge into compact, nameable chunks that can be recombined combinatorially. Our specific contribution is not the known observation that naming a skill helps composition, but the causal ISOLATION of compactness: teaching a model a reusable sub-procedure under a compact NAME lets it compose that sub-procedure into novel, unseen combinations more reliably than under a content- and length-matched VERBOSE description or an equal-length ARBITRARY label, and the advantage GROWS with composition depth (a naming-by-depth interaction) rather than reflecting mere token savings or memorization. Mechanistically, the compact name installs a locatable, geometry-stable, causally-invokable internal 'subroutine' representation. The chunking/compression framing is an operational analogy.
Related Work: A cluster of theory argues language aids intelligence by offering compact, culturally-evolved abstractions that enable generalization (How important is language for human-like intelligence?, 2025; Language as a bootstrap for compositional visual reasoning, 2021; Thinking in Words, 2014; Emergent Symbolic Cognition, 2025). Latent/implicit-reasoning work (Coconut, 2024; Implicit CoT via Distillation, 2023; Stepwise Internalization, 2024; A Survey on Latent Reasoning, 2025) shows reasoning can leave verbal space, and Abstraction-of-Thought (2024) shows explicit abstraction layers improve reasoning. Skill-reuse and compositional work - SKiC (skills-in-context) and MAGNIFICo (in-context acquisition of novel word meanings) - already shows that naming or reusing skills aids composition; that headline is not our novelty. What that work does NOT isolate is compression-FOR-composition: whether a compact handle, versus a content- and length-matched verbose description of the identical procedure (VERBOSE-once) and an equal-length arbitrary label, is what drives recombination; whether the gain grows specifically with composition depth; and whether naming installs a reusable, causally-invokable internal subroutine. We contribute that causal isolation plus a mechanistic Location + Causal Intervention account, tied to an agentic tool-composition setting. The surprising, prior-work-distinguishing prediction is that with identical content and equal length, only the compact meaningful name yields widening depth-dependent gains, while the arbitrary label does not.
Abstract: Why does language make minds more powerful? A leading answer is that language compresses reusable knowledge into compact, nameable chunks that can be freely recombined, turning a finite vocabulary into a combinatorial engine for novel thought. We test whether this compression-for-composition principle operates inside large language models. In-context, we teach a model a reusable sub-procedure (e.g., a small transformation on strings, lists, or graph states) in ways that convey identical content: under a compact NAME ('let ZORP mean <procedure>') versus a length- and content-matched VERBOSE description that must be restated at each use, a VERBOSE-once definition referred to by a long descriptive phrase, and an equal-length ARBITRARY label. We then require the model to solve novel COMPOSITIONS - problems whose solutions chain the taught sub-procedure with others in combinations never demonstrated. Our central, pre-registered estimand is the naming-by-composition-depth interaction coefficient on accuracy: compact naming yields a growing advantage on deeper/novel compositions while offering little benefit on single-step reuse, and this advantage is not explained by prompt length, memorability, or surface repetition. We further predict compact naming reduces 'leakage' errors where the sub-procedure's internals bleed into unrelated steps. Mechanistically, we test whether a compact name installs a reusable subroutine: we probe for a 'named-primitive' representation activated whenever the name is invoked, measure whether it is reused with stable geometry across distinct compositions, and causally patch/steer it to trigger or suppress the sub-procedure's execution in novel contexts. We make the agentic replication first-class: skills exposed as compact-named tools versus verbose call templates in a defined tool-schema environment, measuring novel tool-chaining success under the same depth interaction, so the story is not wholly synthetic. Practitioner takeaway if it holds: name reusable tools/skills compactly and meaningfully (not verbosely, not arbitrarily) in tool libraries, prompt templates, and agent memory; if null, LLM compositional generalization is content-driven, not compression-driven, dissociating it from the language-as-chunking account. Across several open-weight models we quantify the naming compositional-generalization gain, its dissociation from length and memorability, and mechanistic reuse; causal language is scoped to what the patching/steering experiments can distinguish from generic control-state transfer.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does a compact name buy a growing advantage on deeper novel compositions?): Tests the naming-by-composition-depth interaction and the leakage-reduction prediction, against length and memorability confounds. Data: three synthetic domains with programmatically verifiable compositions - (a) string transforms (reversible substitution + rotation + filter), (b) list/state micro-ops (map/filter/fold-style), (c) small graph/gridworld state updates; each domain defines ~6 atomic sub-procedures, each with a compact coined NAME and a content-matched VERBOSE description. Problems require compositions of depth 1-5, with ALL multi-step compositions held out of the teaching examples (novel-composition generalization); ~300 auto-graded problems per depth. Teaching conditions (content held constant): NAMED (define once by compact name, then refer by name), VERBOSE (inline the full description at every use), VERBOSE-once (define verbosely once then refer back by a long descriptive phrase - isolates handle compactness from define-once), and ARBITRARY-LABEL (a random unrelated label of equal length - rules out that any short token helps). Controls: total-prompt-token length matching across NAMED and VERBOSE-once at each depth; a memorability check (recall a sub-procedure's definition alone, without composition); name-length/frequency variation. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: the naming x composition-depth interaction coefficient on accuracy, in a mixed-effects model accuracy ~ condition*depth + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: NAMED >= VERBOSE-once > VERBOSE at depth 1 (small) with a WIDENING NAMED-over-VERBOSE-once advantage as depth grows (interaction 95% CI excluding zero), ARBITRARY-LABEL below NAMED (compactness must be meaning-bearing), equal memorability across conditions (so the gain is compositional, not recall), and reduced internals-leakage errors under NAMED at high depth. A high-stakes agentic replication (skills as compact-named tools vs verbose call templates, novel tool-chaining) should show the same depth interaction on task success. Indecision band: a naming x depth interaction whose 95% CI lies within +/-2 percentage points per depth level is undecided. Negative result (no depth-growing NAMED advantage over content-matched verbose) would suggest LLM compositional generalization is content-driven rather than compression-driven, dissociating LLMs from the language-as-chunking account.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Does a compact name install a locatable, reusable subroutine representation?): Location plus mediation. Data: NAMED trials from Experiment 1, hidden states at name-invocation tokens, 70/15/15 over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer linear probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}). Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for decoding WHICH sub-procedure is being invoked at the name token (best layer); secondary: reuse-geometry stability (cosine similarity of a name's representation across the different compositions it appears in) and its alignment with the representation induced by the VERBOSE description. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC clears 0.70, a given name's representation has high cross-composition cosine similarity (stable reuse) and aligns with the verbose-induced primitive (naming compresses to the same object), and per-item compositional-generalization gain correlates with named-primitive probe strength/reuse stability (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65], or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the subroutine claim undecided. Negative result (no which-procedure signal, or unstable geometry) would argue the name is a surface handle, not a reusable internal subroutine.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Can the named-primitive representation be causally patched/steered to trigger or suppress the sub-procedure?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-problem composition subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained. Patching: cache a name-invocation activation from a NAMED context and patch it into a novel context lacking the name. Steering: a difference-in-means invoke-primitive direction (name-present vs name-absent) added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: patch-in (sufficiency); +direction (induce the sub-procedure) and -direction (suppress it) during composition; random-direction; and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in whether the target sub-procedure executes (accuracy/leakage) under patching/steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that off-target sub-procedures and fluency are preserved. Convincing result: patching the name activation into a name-free context triggers the sub-procedure's execution above the random-patch control, +direction induces and -direction suppresses it with monotone dose-response, both exceed random-direction (CIs excluding it), and off-target sub-procedures stay within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a patching/steering effect whose 95% CI overlaps random controls, or lacks dose-response, leaves causal invocation undecided. Negative result (patching/steering does not invoke the sub-procedure) would mean the named-primitive direction is correlational, not the causal subroutine the hypothesis claims.

Controls, specificity, and estimand: we add an opaque-short-label control matched to meaningful names in frequency and tokenization (isolating meaning-bearing compactness from short-token effects) and interventions that equalize total context position and local attention burden, not just token length. Mechanistic specificity is tested with wrong-name/wrong-procedure counterfactual patches, cross-procedure swaps, and patches at neighboring non-name tokens. Exact prompt templates and teach/test splits are fixed to preclude lexical overlap or teach-test contamination. The primary estimand (the naming-by-depth interaction coefficient) is pre-registered with its statistical test, model-aggregation scheme, minimum effect of interest, and fixed indecision bands; 'geometry-stable reusable subroutine' is operationalized via a fixed layer-selection and representational-similarity criterion distinguished from generic prompt-state similarity. Effect sizes are reported with 95% CIs and multiple-comparison correction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Compact names may help simply by shortening context and easing attention over long spans rather than via genuine chunking; mitigated by length-matching NAMED vs VERBOSE-once at each depth and by the ARBITRARY-LABEL control that isolates meaning-bearing compactness. (2) Tokenization may split coined names unpredictably, weakening the 'handle' signal; we test multiple name forms and models and report robustness. (3) Instruction-tuned models may already generalize compositions well, producing ceiling effects that hide differences; we increase composition depth, add distractor sub-procedures, and calibrate difficulty to mid-range. (4) A NAMED gain could reflect training-data familiarity with variable-binding syntax ('let X = ...') rather than compression per se; the VERBOSE-once condition (same define-once syntax, only handle length differs) isolates compactness. (5) The named-primitive direction may entangle with generic 'a definition was given' rather than a specific reusable subroutine; mitigated by which-procedure probes, reuse-geometry tests across compositions, random-direction steering, and specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (compact naming gives no compositional advantage over content-matched verbose descriptions) is itself highly informative: it would suggest LLM compositional generalization is content-driven rather than compression-driven, dissociating LLMs from the human 'language-as-chunking' account. (8) The chunking/compression framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim about human-like cognition.

Name: iconic_naming_bootstrap
Title: Names That Help You Think: Does Sound-Symbolic Iconicity Bootstrap In-Context Learning and Referent Binding in LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Iconicity (sound-meaning congruence, e.g. 'kiki' for spiky) is not merely something LLMs passively recognize; our claim is that it is INSTRUMENTALLY useful - a cognitive scaffold, not a detected preference. When novel entities, variables, or categories are given iconic rather than arbitrary or anti-iconic names, an LLM learns them faster in-context, binds them to their referents more reliably, and makes fewer downstream reasoning errors, yielding a graded gradient (iconic > arbitrary > anti-iconic) whose sharpest, hardest-to-explain-away signature is the anti-iconic COST (mismatched names actively hurting). The facilitation is mediated by a locatable binding/association signal whose engagement rises under iconic naming and whose steering reproduces or cancels the effect. The developmental bootstrapping framing is an operational analogy.
Related Work: A large recent cluster establishes that LLMs and VLMs can RECOGNIZE sound symbolism: bouba-kiki-like preferences (Kiki or Bouba?, 2023; With Ears to See, 2024; LEX-ICON, 2025; Adversarially Probing Cross-Family Sound Symbolism, 2025), generation of human-decodable iconic pseudowords (Iconicity in LLMs, 2025), and iconicity encoded as a psycholinguistic feature in embeddings (Word Meanings in Transformer LMs, 2025; Where meaning lives, 2026); neuron-level work (Unveiling Language Competence Neurons, 2024) finds GPT-2-XL lacks specialized sound-shape neurons. This line is recognition-only: it does not test whether iconicity CHANGES learning or reasoning performance. Novel-word in-context learning work (e.g., MAGNIFICo) studies acquiring new symbols but uses arbitrary names and never manipulates iconicity. Human developmental science shows sound symbolism FACILITATES infant word learning (Miyazaki et al., 2013; Imai & Kita's sound-symbolism-bootstrapping hypothesis; physics-rooted account, 2022). Our one-sentence delta: iconicity is an instrumentally useful scaffold for LLM in-context learning and referent binding (with a diagnostic anti-iconic cost), tested mechanistically - a claim that neither recognition-only studies nor iconicity-free novel-word-learning work makes.
