Novelty lives in both the behavioral finding (the graded gradient and anti-iconic cost) and the mechanistic mediation/steering test.
Abstract: Human infants learn words tagged with iconic sounds (round meanings for round-sounding words) faster than arbitrary ones, a phenomenon known as the sound-symbolism bootstrapping hypothesis. Large language models are known to RECOGNIZE iconicity, but no work asks whether iconicity is functionally useful to them: does giving an LLM a sound-symbolically congruent name for a new entity help it actually learn and reason about that entity? We test whether iconic naming acts as a cognitive scaffold. We construct in-context learning and reasoning tasks in which novel entities, categories, or variables (defined only by their properties in context) are assigned names drawn from three regimes: iconic (name's phonology matches the entity's property, e.g. a spiky object named 'kikith'), arbitrary (phonologically neutral names), and anti-iconic (name mismatches the property, e.g. a spiky object named 'boumo'). Holding all content identical, we measure whether name regime changes (1) in-context learning speed (accuracy vs. number of examples), (2) referent-binding reliability, and (3) downstream reasoning accuracy about the entities. We predict an iconicity gradient: iconic > arbitrary > anti-iconic, with anti-iconic names causing systematic binding errors; the anti-iconic cost (dropping below arbitrary) is the key falsifier that phonology is used rather than ignored. We pre-register a meaningful-effect threshold (a >=3 percentage-point gradient step surviving the memorability and scrambled-iconic controls). Mechanistically, we locate a binding/association signal (decoding which entity a name is currently bound to) and test whether iconic naming increases its strength and whether steering it reproduces or cancels the naming benefit; the causal criterion is that steering a difference-in-means binding-strength direction selectively moves binding accuracy, not generic reasoning, against a random-direction control. If confirmed, naming schemes become a cheap lever for prompt/variable design, synthetic-data labeling, and agentic tool/entity naming; if null, LLMs recognize iconicity but cannot exploit it, cleanly dissociating them from the human bootstrapping account. We expect first uptake from in-context-learning, computational-psycholinguistics, and interpretability communities. Across several open-weight models we quantify the iconicity-facilitation effect, its dissociation from mere name memorability/length, and its mechanistic mediation.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does iconic naming speed learning, tighten binding, and cut reasoning errors in a graded way?): Tests the predicted iconicity gradient (iconic > arbitrary > anti-iconic), including a systematic anti-iconic cost. Data: iconicity-graded pseudoword name banks built from validated cross-linguistic phoneme-to-meaning mappings (Bouba-Kiki shape/spectral cues; LEX-ICON size/speed/brightness dimensions) across four semantic dimensions (shape, size, speed, brightness); for each dimension we build iconic, arbitrary (phonologically neutral, length- and frequency-matched), and anti-iconic name sets, with iconicity validated by an independent classifier and human ratings on a sample. Three tasks, ~250 items per dimension each (content held identical across name regimes): (a) in-context category learning with learning curves over k labeled examples, (b) referent binding over N novel named entities with intervening distractor context, (c) downstream multi-step reasoning (comparison, sorting, relational inference) where the property matters. Controls: length/frequency matching, a scrambled-iconic control (same phonemes, wrong dimension), an orthographic-only vs IPA-provided variant, and a name-recall-alone memorability check. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: name-regime effect on referent-binding accuracy (primary), plus in-context learning-curve AUC and reasoning accuracy, in a mixed-effects model outcome ~ name_regime + dimension + task + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: a monotone gradient with iconic > arbitrary (95% CI excluding zero) AND anti-iconic < arbitrary (the sharpest signature that phonology is used, not ignored), surviving the scrambled-iconic and memorability controls and present under the IPA variant. Indecision band: if BOTH the iconic-minus-arbitrary and arbitrary-minus-anti-iconic differences have 95% CIs within +/-3 percentage points, the gradient is undecided. Negative result (no gradient, or gains explained by memorability/length) would show LLMs recognize iconicity but cannot exploit it as a learning scaffold, dissociating them from the human bootstrapping account.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Is there a locatable binding component whose engagement rises under iconic naming?): Location plus mediation. Data: binding trials from Experiment 1, 70/15/15 train/validation/test over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer logistic-regression linear probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}); name-token to entity-token attention is read out without training. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for decoding which entity a name is currently bound to (best layer); secondary: name-to-referent binding attention magnitude. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC clears 0.70, iconic naming yields higher probe-decodable binding and stronger binding attention than arbitrary while anti-iconic degrades both (CIs excluding zero), and per-item behavioral facilitation correlates with per-item binding-signal increase (Spearman rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65], or a mediation rho whose 95% CI is within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the mechanism undecided. Negative result (no binding signal, or it does not track naming) would sever any behavioral iconicity benefit from a binding mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Does steering a binding-strength direction reproduce or cancel the iconicity benefit?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item binding/reasoning subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; a difference-in-means binding-strength direction (correctly-bound vs mis-bound trials) is added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: +direction under arbitrary/anti-iconic naming (to recover the iconic-level benefit), -direction under iconic naming (to cancel it), random-direction, and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in binding accuracy (and mis-binding rate) under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that off-target reasoning is preserved. Convincing result: +direction under arbitrary/anti-iconic recovers a substantial share of the iconic advantage with a monotone dose-response, -direction under iconic cancels it, both exceed random-direction (CIs excluding it), and off-target reasoning stays within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a steering effect whose 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or shows no dose-response, leaves causal mediation undecided. Negative result (steering does not move binding) would mean the binding direction is correlational, not the causal scaffold the hypothesis requires.

Baseline, thresholds, and robustness: we add an iconicity-free novel-word-learning baseline (MAGNIFICo-style arbitrary names) as the reference point, pre-register the >=3 pp per-step gradient as the minimum effect of interest with explicit decision rules, and state the null/alternative hypotheses that must be excluded (memorability, phonotactic familiarity, tokenization artifacts). We control for semantic leakage from pseudoword construction and for length/frequency beyond simple matching, and report an orthographic-vs-IPA-vs-multi-tokenizer ablation; if these variants do not converge we interpret the failure mode (tokenization masking phonology) up front. The 'binding signal' is operationalized as decoding which entity a name is currently bound to, with the causal criterion that steering the binding-strength direction selectively moves binding accuracy against a random-direction control; effect sizes are reported with 95% CIs and multiple-comparison correction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Iconicity effects may be washed out by tokenization (pseudowords split unpredictably), muting phonological signal; mitigated by testing IPA-provided variants, spelled-out phoneme forms, and multiple tokenizers/models, and by reporting whether any facilitation survives. (2) The effect could be pure memorability rather than binding facilitation; the name-recall-alone control and the anti-iconic *cost* prediction isolate genuine dimension-congruence effects. (3) Arbitrary/anti-iconic classification of pseudowords is imperfect; we use validated cross-linguistic mappings, an independent iconicity classifier, and human-rated samples, plus the scrambled-iconic control. (4) Instruction-tuned models may be robust binders, yielding ceiling effects that hide differences; we increase entity count, add distractors, and lengthen context to avoid ceiling. (5) The binding direction may entangle with generic difficulty; random-direction and specificity controls address this. (6) Effects may be small or model/dimension-specific; we test multiple models and dimensions and report effect sizes. (7) A null result (iconic naming gives no learning/reasoning advantage) is itself highly informative: it would show LLMs recognize iconicity but cannot *exploit* it as a learning scaffold, cleanly dissociating them from the human bootstrapping account. (8) The developmental bootstrapping framing is an operationalized analogy, not a claim of human-like acquisition; findings are framed behaviorally and mechanistically.

Name: self_invented_shorthand
Title: Shorthand for Thought: Does an LLM's Self-Invented Compressed Notation Help Reasoning Up to a Compression Cliff?
Short Hypothesis: When a frozen LLM is induced to invent and reuse its own compressed private notation (a self-shorthand) for intermediate results during multi-step reasoning, task accuracy follows an inverted-U over compression pressure: light shorthand improves reasoning (working-memory offloading) while aggressive shorthand collapses it at a 'compression cliff' where the model can no longer decode its own symbols; the ability to decode self-invented symbols is a locatable, steerable internal signal whose strength predicts and causally gates where the cliff falls. We pre-register 'self-invented shorthand' operationally as a compact private notation the model itself coins for its own intermediate results and then reuses by referring back to its own symbols -- distinct from provided abbreviation legends/external codebooks, from generic scratchpads, and from mere brevity. Primary claim: the behavioral inverted-U/compression cliff; secondary: self-decodability as a controllable latent variable that gates the cliff; steering is a tertiary, not co-central, test.
Related Work: Emergent-communication work shows noise catalyzes compositional codes (Catalytic Role of Noise, 2021), discrete emergent language is more robust and generalizable than continuous features (Emergence of Machine Language, 2022), and compositionality aids transmissibility but not raw generalization (Compositionality and Generalization, 2020). Inter-LLM activation-communication work (Communicating Activations Between LM Agents, 2025; OPTi-MACS, 2023) shows non-natural-language message representations can outperform natural language between DISTINCT agents with TRAINED or fixed protocols. Latent/implicit-reasoning work (Coconut, 2024) removes verbalization entirely. Notation-effect work notes format changes reasoning, and my prior proposals covered tokenization granularity, naming-as-chunking, and information-density pacing. NONE test whether a SINGLE frozen model, in-context and without training, benefits from inventing and reusing its OWN compressed notation for its own downstream use, whether this benefit is non-monotonic with a self-decodability cliff, or whether self-symbol decodability is a locatable/steerable internal quantity that gates the cliff. We uniquely turn 'compressed private language' from a multi-agent trained protocol into a single-model, training-free, mechanistically-characterized reasoning resource with a predicted compression cliff. Delta in one sentence, versus the closest families: unlike Coconut/TokenSkip and other CoT-compression work (which remove or shorten verbalization) and unlike emergent-communication protocols (trained, shared between DISTINCT agents), we study a SINGLE frozen model that in-context invents and REUSES its own notation for its own downstream use. The novelty is located primarily in the phenomenon (a self-decodability compression cliff) and secondarily in the mechanism (self-decoding as a controllable latent variable), not in the task or dataset.
Abstract: Human experts invent shorthand — abbreviations, private notations, compressed diagrams — that let them offload working memory and reason faster, but only as long as they can still decode what they wrote. We ask whether large language models exhibit the same double-edged relationship between compressed language and intelligence. In a single frozen model, we induce the model to invent and reuse its own compressed private notation for intermediate results across a multi-step reasoning task, and vary the compression pressure from verbose natural language to aggressive symbol-dense shorthand. Our central prediction is a compression cliff: accuracy follows an inverted-U over compression — light shorthand improves reasoning by offloading working memory over long contexts, while aggressive shorthand collapses performance once the model can no longer reliably decode its own symbols. We further predict the cliff is not fixed by the notation's raw density but by the model's self-decodability — its ability to recover the meaning of symbols it just coined. Mechanistically, we test whether self-decodability is a locatable internal signal: a probe reading whether a coined symbol is still bound to its referent should predict impending decoding failure and the cliff location, and steering this decoding signal should move the cliff, letting the model tolerate more compression before collapse. Across several open-weight models and reasoning domains (math, multi-hop QA, state-tracking), plus a high-stakes clinical hand-off instance where compressed notation causes silent errors, we quantify the inverted-U, the self-decodability-to-cliff link, and steering controllability, reframing self-invented compressed language as a controllable lever on — and a hidden failure mode of — machine reasoning. We separate one primary hypothesis (the behavioral inverted-U with a self-decodability cliff) from one secondary mechanistic hypothesis (self-decodability is a readable, steerable latent that gates the cliff), and treat steering as subordinate rather than equally central. Beyond synthetic state-tracking we tie the phenomenon to realistic workflows where self-shorthand already appears -- agent scratch memory, tool-use traces, and long-context summarization -- and state the actionable takeaway: the cliff tells practitioners WHEN to prefer compressed/latent reasoning versus explicit chains of thought, and flags a concrete efficiency/safety hazard (aggressive compression that silently drops a decision-relevant detail while looking fluent).
Experiments:
Shared setup (applies to every experiment below): all runs use five frozen open-weight models -- Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B -- with no weight updates; the only trainable parameters anywhere are linear-probe weights (logistic or ridge regression on frozen hidden states). Decoding is greedy for the primary condition and temperature 0.7 for any sampled/spot-check condition, each such run repeated over seeds 0, 1, 2. All effect sizes carry 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) over 1000 item-level resamples, and behavioral tests use mixed-effects regression with crossed random intercepts for model and item, written (1|model)+(1|item). "Self-shorthand" means a compact private notation the model is instructed to invent for its own intermediate results and then reuse by referring back to its own symbols.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- Self-shorthand produces an inverted-U over compression pressure with a compression cliff): Tests whether task accuracy rises then falls as compression pressure increases. Data: three multi-step tasks -- 300 multi-step arithmetic items sampled from the GSM8K test split (1,319 available), 300 multi-hop QA items over 3-6 facts sampled from the 2WikiMultiHopQA dev set (12,576 available), and 300 synthetic state-tracking items we construct (entity-attribute updates over long contexts, answers auto-checkable) -- 900 base items, each run at four compression levels for 3,600 conditions; 300/task/level is the smallest sample giving stable per-model cliff estimates within a single-GPU-week budget. Compression levels: L0 verbose natural language (baseline), L1 short abbreviations, L2 coined single-token symbols, L3 aggressive symbol-dense shorthand (maximal abbreviation, dropped connectives); format is enforced and symbol reuse verified so only compliant trials count. Decisive metric first: final-answer accuracy as a function of compression level, tested for an inverted-U via mixed-effects logistic regression accuracy ~ compression_level (as ordered factor) * context_length + (1|model)+(1|item), with the per-model/per-task cliff located as the level of first significant drop; secondary: the compression_level x context_length interaction (offloading benefit should be largest on long-context items). Convincing result: mean accuracy rises from L0 to L1 or L2 by >= 3 points (CI excludes 0), then falls at L3 by >= 5 points from its peak (CI excludes 0), with the benefit significantly larger on the top context-length tercile. Indecision band: any level-to-level change within +/-2 points (CI overlapping 0) is treated as flat; if both the rise and the fall land in this band the inverted-U is unsupported. Negative result: monotonic decline with no L1/L2 benefit still supports a compression cliff (partial support), while flat accuracy across all levels refutes H1 entirely; a monotonic-decline outcome is reported as such rather than reframed.

Experiment 2 (H1 confounds -- Isolating self-authored reused compression from token count and abbreviation per se): Tests that the benefit comes from reusing self-invented compressed memory, not fewer tokens or the act of abbreviating. Data: the same 900 base items. Systems: L0 baseline; a length-matched control that equalizes total token budget across levels; a fixed-external-code control that supplies a provided abbreviation legend instead of self-invented symbols; and a no-reuse control that writes shorthand but never refers back. Decisive metric first: accuracy difference between self-invented-reused shorthand and each control at the L1/L2 peak; secondary: accuracy under length-matching to rule out "fewer tokens to attend to". Convincing result: self-invented-reused shorthand exceeds the no-reuse and fixed-external-code controls by >= 3 points at the peak (CIs exclude 0) and the benefit survives length-matching. Indecision band: differences within +/-2 points mean self-authorship and reuse are not separable from generic abbreviation at our power. Negative result: if the fixed-external-code or no-reuse control matches self-shorthand, the effect is not about self-invented reusable compression, weakening H1's mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Self-decodability is a locatable signal that tracks the cliff better than raw density): Tests whether the model's ability to decode its own symbols predicts the cliff. Data: the reference points in the L0-L3 traces from Experiment 1, split 70/30 by item. Two measures at each symbol reference: an interleaved behavioral spot-check ("what does <symbol> stand for?") on a held-out subset, and a linear probe (only probe trainable) on hidden states at the reference token decoding the bound referent, per-layer held-out AUROC. Decisive metric first: per-layer held-out decoding AUROC and its drop across compression levels; secondary: model comparison of two predictors of per-item accuracy -- a density-only baseline versus a self-decodability-based predictor (nested-model likelihood-ratio / delta-AUROC). Convincing result: decodability drops sharply at the located cliff level (>= 0.10 AUROC decrease from L1/L2 to L3, CI excludes 0), per-item decodability predicts per-item error at Spearman rho >= 0.2, and the decodability predictor beats the density-only predictor of accuracy (delta-AUROC >= 0.05, CI excludes 0). Indecision band: a decodability-versus-density predictor gap within +/-0.03 AUROC means the cliff cannot be attributed to decodability over density. Negative result: if raw density predicts the cliff as well as decodability, or decodability does not fall at the cliff, H2's decodability-gates-the-cliff claim fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 -- Steering the decoding signal moves the cliff): Tests whether the decoding signal is causal and steerable. Data: the same reference points. We derive a difference-in-means "symbol-binding/decoding" direction from decodable-minus-failed-decode reference contrasts at the best probe layer; systems are plus-direction steering, minus-direction steering, random-direction steering of matched norm, and no-steer. Decisive metric first: shift in the located cliff level under plus-direction steering versus random-direction and no-steer (does the model tolerate a denser level before collapse?); secondary: minus-direction induced early collapse at mild compression, plus specificity (L0 accuracy within 1 point, fluency by perplexity). Convincing result: plus-direction steering pushes the cliff to a higher compression level (or raises L3 accuracy by >= 3 points over random-direction, CI excludes 0) while minus-direction lowers accuracy at L1/L2, both with preserved L0 accuracy and a monotonic dose-response. Indecision band: cliff-shift effects within +/-2 accuracy points of random-direction steering leave the direction unproven. Negative result: no cliff movement beyond random steering means self-decodability, even if readable, is not a usable causal gate, and the behavioral inverted-U (Experiment 1) stands alone.

Experiment 5 (H1 and H2 -- High-stakes clinical hand-off instance): Tests whether aggressive self-shorthand silently drops a decision-relevant detail and whether decoding-direction steering mitigates it. Data: 300 clinical hand-off / note-summarization vignettes adapted from MedQA (USMLE, 12,723 questions) and constructed hand-off cases, where the model compresses a patient case into shorthand and then answers a fine-grained downstream question; 300 supports paired contrasts under expert spot-checking. Systems: L0 verbose, L3 aggressive shorthand, and L3 with plus-direction decoding steering. Decisive metric first: confident-error rate on the downstream question (wrong answer with high stated confidence) at L3 versus L0; secondary: recovery under steering. Convincing result: L3 raises confident downstream error over L0 and plus-direction steering reduces it by >= 5 points (CIs exclude 0). Indecision band: an L3-versus-L0 gap within +/-2 points is inconclusive for high-stakes transfer. Negative result: no L3 degradation means aggressive self-shorthand is safe here, bounding the failure-mode claim to benign tasks.

Experiment 6 (Probe construct validation and compliance accounting): To ensure the self-decodability probe reflects SYMBOL BINDING rather than generic latent state, we validate it against a gold standard: the probe must (a) agree with the interleaved behavioral 'what does <symbol> stand for?' spot-check, and (b) fail (drop to chance) on shuffled symbol-referent pairings and on matched non-symbol tokens. We define 'reuse verified' precisely -- a coined symbol counts as reused only if it reappears in a later step in a referring position -- and report the fraction of trials excluded for non-compliance (no coinage, no reuse, or covert verbose reasoning) plus a sensitivity analysis re-including them. Throughout, controls hold task difficulty, output length, and model uncertainty fixed (length-matched budgets, difficulty-stratified items, entropy-matched contrasts) so the cliff cannot be attributed to fewer tokens or harder items, and the fixed-external-code, random-symbol, and forced-verbosity arms isolate self-authored reusable compression from mere brevity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Instruction-tuned models may refuse or inconsistently follow the self-shorthand instruction, or covertly keep verbose reasoning; we enforce and verify symbol reuse, analyze only compliant trials, and include base-model variants. (2) The offloading benefit may be absent if models already handle long contexts well, flattening the inverted-U to a monotonic decline; a monotonic result (no benefit, only a cliff) is itself informative and the cliff/self-decodability mechanism still holds. (3) Compression confounds with token count and content; mitigated by length-matched budgets, fixed-external-code and no-reuse controls, and the decodability-vs-density predictor comparison. (4) Self-decodability spot-checks may perturb the reasoning trace; we use a held-out subset and the non-invasive hidden-state probe as the primary measure. (5) The decoding direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by matched decodable/failed contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and L0 specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) The 'shorthand for thought' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like working memory. (8) The clinical hand-off experiment is scoped as a bounded, high-stakes DOWNSTREAM demonstration (expert-spot-checked vignettes), not a clinical-grade evaluation; a null there simply bounds the failure-mode claim to benign tasks. (9) Negative-result value: if no cliff or no self-decodability gating emerges, the field learns that self-invented compression is either uniformly safe or uniformly harmful, redirecting effort away from decodability-based compression control.

Name: metaphor_scaffold_reasoning
Title: Thinking Through the Concrete: Do LLMs Recruit Source-Domain Structure as a Scaffold for Abstract Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: When reasoning about an abstract target domain, an LLM recruits an internal representation of a concrete source domain (per Conceptual Metaphor Theory) and imports that source's relational/geometric structure into its inference. Concretely: reasoning accuracy is a graded function of source-target structural isomorphism, so a metaphor whose source structure is ISOMORPHIC to the target's true structure causally improves abstract reasoning, while a structurally MISMATCHED source causally corrupts it BELOW a literal, metaphor-free baseline and concentrates errors on a predicted mismatch-lure. The below-literal mismatch corruption (and its orientation-flip steering on literal prompts) is the sharpest, least pre-empted signature. This scaffold is a locatable, steerable internal signal dissociable from surface metaphor phrasing, not mere phrasing.
Related Work: Prior work shows metaphor knowledge is encoded in PLM middle layers (Metaphors in PLMs, 2022), that CMT-style prompting improves reasoning behaviorally (CMT as a Prompting Paradigm, 2025), and that training-data metaphors can causally drive cross-domain misalignment via latent features (Metaphors are a Source of Cross-Domain Misalignment, 2026); grounding-theory work (Meaning without Reference, 2022; The Vector Grounding Problem, 2023; Mechanistic Emergence of Symbol Grounding, 2025) and abstract-concept work (BACH-V, 2026; How Deep is Love, 2025) study whether abstractions connect to concrete representations, and BACH-V shows abstract value probes transfer to concrete events. These ingredients - CMT prompting, latent metaphor features, metaphor-based steering, abstract grounding - are individually pre-empted. What none of them provides is the integrated, falsifiable law we test: (1) reasoning accuracy graded by source-target structural alignment, (2) below-literal corruption under structurally mismatched sources with predicted mismatch-lure concentration, (3) a source-domain quantity decodable on abstract trials from a probe trained ONLY on concrete source stimuli (with an orientation flip under mismatch), and (4) orientation-specific steering that rescues or induces those errors, including on literal prompts. We contribute this as a controlled metaphor-structure evaluation suite with validated graded alignments, positioning it as a synthesis with new predictions rather than a wholly new paradigm.
Abstract: Conceptual Metaphor Theory holds that humans reason about abstract domains (time, quantity, social status, causation) by mapping them onto concrete source domains (space, physical size, verticality, force). We ask whether large language models do the same computationally: when an LLM reasons about an abstract target, does it recruit an internal representation of a concrete source domain and import that source's relational structure into its inference? We make three claims. First, a structure-alignment law: for abstract reasoning problems whose correct answers depend on a specific relational structure, framing the problem with a metaphor whose source domain is structurally isomorphic to the target improves accuracy, whereas a structurally mismatched source (identical surface metaphor style, but wrong mapping) degrades it below a literal, metaphor-free baseline. We define structural alignment formally (the source relation preserves the target's ordering/orientation and transitivity) and predict a dose-response between graded source-target alignment and accuracy, plus a diagnostic failure mode where a mismatched metaphor induces systematic, predictable mismatch-lure errors. Second, representational recruitment: on abstract-reasoning trials, a probe trained only on concrete source-domain stimuli can decode the source-domain quantity from the model's hidden states, and this decodable source signal is stronger when the metaphor is aligned and mis-oriented under mismatch. Third, a causal scaffold: the source-domain representation is a locatable direction that, when steered, changes abstract-reasoning behavior in the predicted direction and can rescue mismatched-metaphor errors or induce them under literal framing. We pre-register the falsification criteria distinguishing the alignment law from generic framing effects. Concrete stakes: a mismatched spatial metaphor for time in scheduling, a mis-oriented force metaphor for causation in medical/policy 'which factor drove the outcome' vignettes, and a verticality metaphor for social status in ranking could each silently flip a decision; we release the graded-alignment corruption suite as a diagnostic for interpretability and safety teams. If the law holds, prompt-auditing should screen for mismatched metaphors; if null (metaphor is decorative), that constrains strong CMT-style mechanistic claims. Across several open-weight models we quantify the alignment law, the recruited-source-signal-to-behavior link, and steering controllability, reframing metaphor from decorative phrasing into a causal computational scaffold for machine abstraction.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does a structurally aligned metaphor help and a mismatched one corrupt abstract reasoning?): Tests the structure-alignment law: aligned metaphor improves accuracy, structurally mismatched metaphor degrades it below a literal baseline, with a dose-response and a diagnostic mismatch-lure error mode. Data: four CMT domain pairs - TIME<-SPACE, QUANTITY<-VERTICALITY/SIZE, SOCIAL-STATUS<-VERTICALITY, CAUSATION<-FORCE - with ~250 relational-reasoning items each (comparison, ordering, transitive-inference, dominance), ~1000 total, whose correct answer depends only on the underlying relational structure. Each item carries a labeled correct answer AND a labeled mismatch-lure (the answer following a wrongly-oriented mapping). Framings (within-item, content-, register- and length-matched, format-enforced): LITERAL (plain relational statement), ALIGNED (canonical source, correct-orientation mapping), MISMATCHED (same metaphor register, structurally wrong mapping), and NEUTRAL-metaphor (irrelevant source) to separate figurative phrasing from structure. Alignment/mismatch labels are validated by independent annotators; a graded-alignment variant with partially-consistent mappings supports a dose-response test. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: accuracy by framing in a mixed-effects model accuracy ~ framing*target_domain + (1|model) + (1|item), with the predicted ordering ALIGNED > LITERAL > NEUTRAL ~ MISMATCHED; secondary: mismatch-lure error rate and the continuous structural-alignment dose-response slope. Convincing result: ALIGNED > LITERAL and MISMATCHED < LITERAL (both 95% CIs excluding zero), mismatch errors concentrate on the labeled mismatch-lure (evidence the wrong source structure was applied), and the alignment dose-response slope CI excludes zero. A high-stakes CAUSATION<-FORCE replication on medical/policy 'which factor drove the outcome' vignettes should show the mismatch corruption transferring to consequential causal attribution. Indecision band: if BOTH the aligned-minus-literal and mismatched-minus-literal differences have 95% CIs within +/-2 percentage points, the alignment law is undecided. Negative result (metaphor framing does not move accuracy, or mismatch does not corrupt) would show metaphor is decorative phrasing, not a computational scaffold.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Is a concrete source-domain quantity recruited and readable during abstract reasoning?): Location plus mediation. Data: abstract-reasoning trials from Experiment 1, plus a separate set of literal concrete source-domain stimuli (spatial/size/force comparisons) used ONLY to train the probe; 70/15/15 over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer linear probes/regressors are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}). Decisive metric: held-out AUROC/regression accuracy for decoding the source-domain quantity on abstract trials, from a probe trained solely on concrete source stimuli, against a literal-only-probe baseline (best layer). Convincing result: source-quantity is decodable on abstract trials above the literal-only baseline, decodability is higher under aligned than literal framing and MISORIENTED under mismatched framing (the probe reads the wrong value in a way that predicts the behavioral lure), and per-item recruited-signal strength/orientation correlates with per-item accuracy and lure errors (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: abstract-trial decoding AUROC in [0.55, 0.65] over the literal baseline, or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves recruitment undecided. Negative result (no source signal beyond generic magnitude, or no orientation flip under mismatch) would argue against genuine source recruitment.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Does steering the source-domain direction rescue mismatch errors and induce them under literal framing?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; a difference-in-means source-domain direction (high vs low source-quantity concrete stimuli) is added at chosen orientations over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: +correct-orientation during MISMATCHED or LITERAL framing (to rescue/boost accuracy), wrong-orientation during LITERAL framing (to induce mismatch-lure errors without any metaphor in the prompt), random-direction, and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in accuracy and mismatch-lure error rate under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that off-target reasoning and fluency are preserved. Convincing result: correct-orientation steering rescues mismatched/literal accuracy and wrong-orientation steering induces the mismatch-lure errors, both with monotone dose-response and exceeding random-direction (CIs excluding it), off-target accuracy within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a steering effect whose 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or lacks dose-response, leaves the causal-scaffold claim undecided. Negative result (steering the source direction does not move abstract reasoning) would mean the recruited source signal is correlational, not the causal scaffold claimed.

Controls, specificity, and power: we add stronger controls for plausibility, familiarity, sentiment, lexical overlap, and answer prior - including non-metaphoric paraphrases and source-swapped variants - and, in Experiment 2, cross-source probes, source-identity decoding, layerwise localization, and literal-matched descriptions without metaphor to rule out generic magnitude decoding. Experiment 3 adds multiple steering methods, layer/site sensitivity, bidirectionality, and off-target checks. We specify prompts-per-condition and how inference aggregates across the five models with item/model/domain-level power, replace absolute related-work language with defensible positioning against the closest cited families, report effect sizes with 95% CIs and multiple-comparison correction, and present probe results as evidence of recruitment only where the intervention tightly links the decoded signal to behavior. The strongest, least pre-empted target is below-literal mismatch corruption with predicted mismatch-lure concentration and orientation-flip steering on literal prompts.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Aligned vs mismatched framings may differ in fluency/plausibility rather than pure structure; mitigated by length/register matching, the neutral-metaphor control, annotator-validated alignment labels, and the content-matched steering that isolates the source representation from surface phrasing. (2) Instruction-tuned models may reason robustly from the literal content and ignore the metaphor, muting effects; a small/null alignment effect on aligned items would still be informative, and the MISMATCH-corruption prediction (metaphor actively hurting) is the sharpest, most novel test even if aligned metaphors merely match the literal baseline. (3) A probe trained on concrete stimuli decoding on abstract trials could reflect generic magnitude features shared by both rather than genuine source recruitment; mitigated by domain-specific probes, the orientation prediction under mismatch (probe reads the WRONG value in a way that predicts behavior), and random-direction steering controls. (4) The steering direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by orientation-specific (not just magnitude) predictions, specificity checks, and dose-response. (5) Some abstract domains may lack a single canonical source, making mismatch design ambiguous; we restrict to well-established CMT mappings and report robustness across the four pairs. (6) Effects may be model- or domain-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) The CMT framing is operationalized behaviorally/mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like embodied cognition.

Name: categorical_warping_llm
Title: Categorical Warping: Can an Ad-Hoc Label Scheme Causally Reshape What an LLM Can Discriminate?
Short Hypothesis: A core Whorfian claim is that the categories a language provides warp perception of within-category vs. across-category differences (compression within, expansion across a boundary). We hypothesize that this warping is a dynamic, controllable property of a trained LLM: introducing a novel, ad-hoc labeling scheme in-context causally compresses the model's internal representation of items sharing a new label and expands the gap across new label boundaries, and that this induced geometric warp measurably changes the model's fine-grained discrimination and relational reasoning on the very same items — even when the labels are meaningless nonce words with no pretraining semantics.
Related Work: Cognitive science establishes categorical perception and label-feedback effects, framing them as inference under uncertainty (Cibelli/Regier, 2016/2017; Lupyan, 2012). A deep-learning account (2021) shows fine- vs coarse-grained labels distort semantic geometry, but by *training* a network on those labels. In LLMs, BICAUSE (2025) shows language internalizes causal-order biases and Sapir-Whorf-reproduction studies (2025) probe behavioral alignment; 'When Less Language is More' (2025) ablates language components to help reasoning; number-geometry work (2025/2026) characterizes fixed relational structure. All existing LLM work is observational on *pretrained* vocabularies (color, number, causal order) or removes language rather than adding new categories. No prior work asks whether an *arbitrary, in-context ad-hoc labeling scheme* can causally rewarp an already-trained model's discrimination geometry within a single forward pass, dissociates this from pretrained label semantics using nonce labels, or links the induced geometric warp to changes in downstream relational reasoning. The closest prior negative result is the digit-count structural-boundary finding (categorical boundaries form only along pre-existing structural axes); we formulate the proposal as a direct ADJUDICATION test with a falsifiable contrast - structural-only boundaries vs. arbitrary in-context boundaries - and predict arbitrary labels can warp geometry because in-context labels supply a task-relevant partition the model must track for the prompt, unlike the semantically inert non-structural boundaries prior work tested. The strongest true delta we claim is arbitrary NONCE-label repartitioning with partition-specific sign reversal and steering, not generic 'categorical warping.' We turn linguistic relativity into a controllable, mechanistic intervention.
Abstract: Linguistic relativity predicts that the category boundaries a language supplies warp cognition: items sharing a label are perceived as more similar (within-category compression) and items across a boundary as more different (across-category expansion). Prior LLM studies test this observationally on pretrained vocabularies (color, causal order). We ask a sharper, causal question: can an arbitrary labeling scheme, introduced only in-context, dynamically rewarp what an already-trained LLM can discriminate and reason about? We construct continuous, controllable stimulus spaces (e.g., numeric magnitudes, HSL colors described in text, feature-vector 'creatures') and impose novel partitions via labels, including nonce labels with no pretraining meaning. Measuring representational distances in hidden states, we test whether presenting a labeling scheme compresses same-label pairs and expands different-label pairs relative to a no-label baseline, and whether the boundary location tracks the arbitrary partition we chose rather than any pretrained structure. We then test behavioral consequences: does the induced warp make the model worse at fine within-category discrimination and better/worse at across-boundary comparisons on identical items? Finally, we test the mechanism causally: we isolate a 'label-warp direction' and steer along it to reproduce or cancel the geometric warp and its behavioral signature, and compare it to an inference-time analog of coarse vs. fine labeling pressure. Across several open-weight models we quantify the compression/expansion index, boundary-placement fidelity to arbitrary partitions, the label-warp-to-behavior correlation, and steering controllability. Success is defined beyond known in-context compression/expansion: partition-specific SIGN REVERSAL on identical item sets (the same pair compresses under one arbitrary scheme and expands under another) plus transfer to behavior, effects that must survive nonce labels and label-removal-at-test. We are explicit that the novelty spans a finding (arbitrary labels warp), a mechanism (a steerable label-warp direction), and a controllability tool, and we pre-register what practitioners should conclude in both positive and null regimes. The significance is prompt-time causal reconfiguration of what a model discriminates - relevant to controllable abstraction, task framing, interpretability, and safe prompt-time steering, for benchmark designers and prompt/alignment engineers - not merely a Whorfian analogy; we avoid any broad Whorfian conclusion unless the effect survives nonce labels, repartition reversal, and behavior-without-label-at-test. This reframes linguistic relativity in LLMs from a fixed bias into a controllable, mechanistically-grounded lever on machine discrimination.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Continuous stimulus spaces and label schemes): Prerequisite. Data: three built spaces with ground-truth metric structure - (a) integer magnitudes 1-100, (b) colors specified as HSL text (hue 0-360), (c) synthetic 'creatures' defined by 4 continuous features; for each we prepare no-label, real-word-label, and nonce-word-label (e.g., 'blicket','dax') conditions plus multiple arbitrary boundary placements so a given item pair is same-label under one scheme and different-label under another, and a scrambled-label control (labels assigned randomly to items). ~600 item pairs per space, length/format-matched across conditions. Decisive metric first: verification that schemes are format-matched and that swapped partitions truly cross-classify the same pairs. Convincing result: every target pair appears as both same-label and different-label across schemes; else pairs are regenerated. Indecision/negative bands are design checks, not hypotheses.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Ad-hoc labels causally rewarp discrimination geometry, boundary follows the imposed partition, even for nonce labels): The central Whorfian-warp test. Data: the pairs above, used as is. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and a larger model (Qwen2.5-14B) for scale, all weights frozen. We prompt with the labeling scheme in-context, present item pairs, and extract each item's hidden state with a pre-specified protocol: layer selection (swept, reported per layer), token positions (the item mention at matched positions), pooling (mean over item-span tokens), distance metric (cosine and Euclidean), and surface-form invariance checks. Controls to separate categorical warp from lexical priming and generic ICL state change include paraphrased prompts, position swaps, label-token substitution, non-word/symbol labels, and delayed label-removal tests. Systems compared: no-label baseline, real-word labels, nonce labels, swapped arbitrary partitions, coarse vs. fine schemes, and scrambled-label control. Decisive metric first: the same_label coefficient in a regression of representational distance on true metric gap and a same-label indicator (distance ~ metric_gap + same_label + (1|layer) + (1|model)) - the Compression-Expansion Index. Convincing result: a significant negative same_label coefficient (within-label compression) with boundary-aligned across-label expansion, present even for nonce labels, that REVERSES when the same items are re-partitioned by a different arbitrary scheme (sign flip CI excluding zero), while the scrambled-label control shows no warp; coarse schemes converge items and fine schemes differentiate them, matching the labeling-geometry prediction. Indecision band: same_label coefficient CI spanning zero, or a warp that does not follow the swapped partition - in-context labels do not reliably rewarp geometry, so category structure looks rigidly pretrained rather than dynamically Whorfian. Negative result (positive same_label coefficient, or nonce labels show no effect while only real words do): no genuine categorical warp beyond lexical priming, refuting the causal claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 - The warp changes behavior and behavior tracks geometry): Tests downstream consequences. Data: the same items rendered as (i) fine within-category discrimination (which of two same-label items is larger/redder?), (ii) across-boundary comparison, (iii) odd-one-out and analogy tasks; item spacing calibrated to mid-range difficulty to avoid ceiling/floor. Models: same four, frozen; 5 samples/item, temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: imposed scheme vs. no-label baseline, including a condition where labels are ABSENT at test time (scheme shown during exposure, removed at query) so behavior change cannot be explained only by explicit rule-following; effects are analyzed with model-by-model and domain-by-domain interaction terms (not pooled random effects only), since the warp may be heterogeneous. Decisive metric first: change in within-category discrimination accuracy under an imposed scheme; secondary: the mixed-effects correlation between per-pair behavioral change and per-pair measured geometric warp. Convincing result: within-category discrimination degrades and across-boundary judgments shift under an imposed scheme (accuracy-change CI excluding zero), and per-pair behavioral change correlates with geometric warp (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: behavioral-change CI spanning zero while geometry warps - the geometric warp has no behavioral teeth, so the phenomenon is representational-only. Negative result (no behavioral change or negative geometry-behavior correlation): warp does not shape discrimination.

Experiment 4 (H3 - A label-warp direction steers the warp and its behavior on and off): Tests causal controllability. Data: contrast pairs (same items, labeled vs. unlabeled) to compute a mid-layer difference-in-means 'label-warp direction'; 400 held-out pairs per space for evaluation. Models: same four, frozen; steering strength tuned on a dev split, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: +direction steering (induce warp without presenting labels), -direction steering (cancel a presented scheme's warp), and multiple baselines - random-direction (matched norm), a generic-instruction direction, a label-token direction, and a task-state direction - plus no-steer; we test cross-partition and cross-domain transfer of the direction. Minimal success is a pre-registered fraction of the warp reproduced or cancelled beyond every baseline with a meaningful effect size. Decisive metric first: fraction of the Compression-Expansion Index reproduced (by +steering) or cancelled (by -steering) relative to the label-presentation effect; secondary: matched fraction of the behavioral discrimination change. Convincing result: +steering reproduces and -steering cancels a substantial share of both the geometric and behavioral warp, significantly beyond random-direction steering (difference CI excluding zero). Indecision band: recovered/cancelled fraction under 20% and within the random-direction control's CI - the warp is not captured by a single steerable direction. Negative result (steering has no effect or destroys general output): no isolable causal mechanism. All quantities are planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over pairs, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) In-context labels may bias representations trivially via lexical priming rather than genuine categorical warping; mitigated by nonce labels, swapped arbitrary partitions of identical items, and scrambled-label controls that isolate the categorical (boundary-structured) component. (2) Hidden-state distances may reflect the prompt's surface tokens rather than the concept; we extract item representations at matched positions and control for true metric gap. (3) Warp effects may be small or layer-specific; we report multiple layers, models, and effect sizes with bootstrap CIs. (4) Behavioral discrimination tasks could be at ceiling/floor for some spaces; we calibrate item spacing to mid-range difficulty. (5) The label-warp direction may entangle with generic content shifts; random-direction and cancellation controls address this. (6) A null result (arbitrary in-context labels do not warp geometry) is itself informative, indicating LLM category structure is rigidly pretrained rather than dynamically Whorfian.

Name: exact_number_word_gating
Title: One, Two, Many: Does the Availability of an Exact Number Word Gate Whether an LLM Holds an Exact vs. Approximate Quantity?
Short Hypothesis: A tempered form of the anumeric-language finding may transfer into LLMs at inference time: an LLM's ability to store and operate on an EXACT quantity shows a regime-dependent reliance on whether a compact exact number WORD is available in the representation it is using. When the exact word is unavailable - our strongest, cleanest manipulations being within-language approximate-quantifier framing and ablation of a located number-word feature (with a low-numeracy pivot language as a secondary, competence-confounded variant) - the model falls back toward an approximate, magnitude-based (log/Weber-law) representation, producing the ratio-dependent error signature of anumeric speakers rather than random noise. 'Availability of a number word' means the compact lexical/numeral form is usable in the working representation, distinct from mere tokenizer presence. We claim regime-dependent reliance on approximate representations, not a full transfer of strong-Whorfian cognition.
Related Work: Human cross-cultural work shows exact number cognition depends on number WORDS: anumeric Amazonian speakers fail exact-matching beyond ~3 while their approximate number sense stays intact (Frank/Everett/Gibson 2008; da Silva Sinha et al. 2026), and verbal interference selectively suppresses EXACT (not approximate) numerical representation in numerate adults (Frank, Fedorenko, Lai, Saxe, Gibson 2011); number-word procedures, not perception, are argued to originate exact integers (Schneider/Barner 2017; Everett 2012). In LLMs, a rich interpretability literature characterizes number REPRESENTATIONS (sublinear/log mental-number-line, Number Representations 2025; sinusoidal precise encoding, Pre-trained LMs Learn Accurate Number Representations 2025; stable relational geometry, The Representational Geometry of Number 2026) and COUNTING mechanisms (internal-counter heads, CountScope 2025; System-2 counting 2026; Sequential Enumeration 2025). The Weber-law approximate substrate is thus already established and is NOT our novelty. What this work adds is the causal GATING claim: that removing exact-number-word availability (via within-language approximate-quantifier framing or feature ablation) forces a regime switch from exact symbolic handling to approximate magnitude computation, with exact-vs-approximate SELECTIVITY (a double dissociation) and steering-based rescue. This existing LLM work studies how numbers are encoded/counted assuming the number word exists; it does not test that switch.
Abstract: One of the strongest claims about language and thought is that exact number cognition depends on possessing exact number words: speakers of 'anumeric' languages, and numerate adults under verbal interference, can approximate quantities but cannot reliably represent exact ones beyond three, while their approximate number sense stays intact. We ask whether the same dependence governs large language models, in a tempered form: an LLM's capacity to store and manipulate an EXACT quantity shows a regime-dependent reliance on whether a compact exact number word is available in the representation it is currently using; when that word is unavailable, the model reverts toward an approximate, magnitude-based representation and produces the ratio-dependent (Weber-law) error signature characteristic of anumeric humans rather than random errors. We lead with the two cleanest manipulations - within-language approximate-quantifier framing that forbids exact numerals, and ablation of a located number-word feature - and treat a low-numeracy pivot language and a verbal-interference control as secondary, competence-confounded checks. Across exact matching, exact subtraction, and set-equality tasks we test whether the anumeric regimes selectively degrade EXACT performance while sparing APPROXIMATE (larger-vs-smaller) judgments, and whether the residual errors follow a distance/ratio-dependent curve. Mechanistically, we locate an exact-number-word representation, show it is decodable on success and degraded under anumeric regimes, and causally steer it to induce or rescue the exact-to-approximate fallback. Beyond a high-stakes medical-dosing instance we add a realistic downstream setting where exact number words are naturally removed - multilingual/quantity extraction and summarization under paraphrase - to argue prevalence. If gating holds, numeracy stress tests under paraphrase/pivot-language framing and safeguards that preserve exact lexical representations are warranted; if null, it narrows theories of numerical competence in LLMs and redirects interpretability away from lexical causation. We claim regime-dependent reliance on approximate representations, not full strong-Whorfian transfer. Across several open-weight models we quantify the gating effect, its exact-vs-approximate selectivity, the anumeric error signature, and mechanistic mediation.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Do anumeric regimes selectively degrade EXACT quantity cognition while sparing APPROXIMATE?): Tests the gating claim: removing a compact exact number word selectively harms exact tasks but not magnitude comparison. Data: a quantity battery of ~900 items, ~300 per task - (a) exact matching (produce/verify a set of exactly N, N up to ~20), (b) exact subtraction/addition on set sizes, (c) set-equality (are these two sets exactly equal?); each item is paired with a matched APPROXIMATE control over the identical stimulus (which set is larger? roughly how many?) that needs only magnitude. Items span a range of target values and, for comparison/equality, a range of between-set ratios (to support the Weber-law fit in Experiment 2). Ground truth is auto-checkable. Regimes (content held constant): NUMERATE baseline (exact numerals allowed); APPROXIMATE-QUANTIFIER framing (forbids exact numerals, forces vague quantifiers for intermediate representations while still requiring an exact final answer); LOW-NUMERACY PIVOT LANGUAGE (reasoning required in a language with a restricted/unusual numeral system relative to the model's strong languages, back-translation checked); and a VERBAL-INTERFERENCE control (interleaved demanding verbal task) adapting the human paradigm. Compliance verified. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: the regime x task_type interaction on accuracy, in a mixed-effects model accuracy ~ regime*task_type + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: anumeric regimes lower EXACT-task accuracy (matching, exact subtraction, equality) while sparing APPROXIMATE comparison (interaction 95% CI excluding zero) - the signature that the number WORD, not the magnitude, is lost. Indecision band: a regime x task_type interaction whose 95% CI lies within +/-2 percentage points is undecided (generic difficulty could then explain any drop). Negative result (anumeric regimes harm exact and approximate equally, or neither) would indicate LLM exact-number ability does not depend on an available number word.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Under anumeric regimes, do exact errors follow the ratio-dependent Weber-law signature, with a small-number floor?): Tests whether the residual errors are magnitude-based rather than random. Data: the degraded exact trials from Experiment 1, using the ratio-varied and value-varied items; plus a high-stakes clinical instance (dosing/count vignettes under approximate-quantifier framing). Models, seeds and decoding as Experiment 1. Decisive metric: the fitted Weber fraction per regime and the slope of error probability against between-quantity ratio (error rises as ratio approaches 1) and against target value. Convincing result: on degraded exact trials errors are ratio/distance-dependent (a monotone ratio-error curve, Weber fraction reliably larger than the numerate baseline, 95% CI excluding it) rather than uniform, exact performance survives for very small N (~1-3) as a subitizing-like plateau, and the clinical approximate-quantifier framing produces ratio-dependent dosing errors. Indecision band: if the anumeric-minus-numerate Weber fraction difference has a 95% CI within a pre-registered small margin (e.g., +/-10% relative), or the ratio-error slope CI overlaps zero, the magnitude-fallback signature is undecided. Negative result (errors stay uniform/random, no ratio dependence) would show the degradation is generic noise, not a fallback to an approximate magnitude representation.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Is there a locatable exact-number-word representation, degraded under anumeric regimes?): Location plus mediation. Data: hidden states on exact-success vs exact-failure trials and numerate vs anumeric framings, 70/15/15 over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer linear probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}). Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for whether an exact-number-word is active, and probe accuracy for decoding the exact value (best layer), compared across regimes. Convincing result: exact-value decodability and the word-active signal are lower under anumeric regimes than numerate (CI excluding zero), and the per-item drop in exact-word/exact-value decodability predicts the per-item exact-accuracy drop (Spearman rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: an anumeric-minus-numerate AUROC drop whose 95% CI is within +/-0.05, or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the representational account undecided. Negative result (no exact-word signal, or it does not track the regime/behavior) would detach the behavioral gating from any number-word representation.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Does steering the exact-number-word direction rescue or induce the exact-to-approximate fallback?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item exact subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; a difference-in-means exact-number-word direction (numerate vs approximate-quantifier framing of identical items) added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: +direction under anumeric regimes (rescue), -direction under the numerate baseline (induce fallback without any framing change), random-direction, and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in exact-task accuracy AND the shape of the error distribution (ratio-dependent vs random) under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that approximate-comparison accuracy and fluency are preserved. Convincing result: +direction under anumeric regimes rescues exact accuracy and restores random (non-ratio-dependent) errors, -direction under numerate induces the exact-to-approximate fallback and the Weber-law error signature, both with monotone dose-response and exceeding random-direction (CIs excluding it), approximate accuracy within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a steering effect whose 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or lacks dose-response, leaves causal gating undecided. Negative result (steering the exact-word direction does not move exact behavior or error shape) would mean the direction is correlational, not the causal gate the hypothesis claims.

Difficulty controls, localization, and pre-registration: we add hard controls for generic difficulty - a paraphrase-only control that preserves exact numerals, length-matched prompts, and a non-numeric lexical ablation of equal magnitude, plus a dedicated experiment ruling out working-memory/difficulty (rather than number-word gating) as the cause. Pivot-language runs are restricted to models/languages with demonstrated high numeric competence and include within-language baselines to separate numeracy from translation/resource effects; the verbal-interference regime is demoted to a secondary check given its weaker LLM grounding. The exact-number feature/direction is validated with held-out localization robustness across seeds, prompts, and models, and causal steering adds random-direction, neighboring-semantic-direction, and matched-norm controls plus a check that non-numeric tasks are unaffected. In Experiment 2 the Weber-law fit is compared against uniform/noise models. Operational definitions of number-word availability, exact vs approximate task, and the fallback signature, plus the mixed-effects regime x task_type analysis with multiple-comparison handling and pre-registered pass/fail thresholds, are fixed in advance; effect sizes are reported with 95% CIs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Instruction-tuned models may covertly re-introduce exact numerals despite approximate-quantifier framing (they still have the tokens in context), muting the effect; we enforce and verify that intermediate representations avoid exact numerals, and rely on the pivot-language and steering (feature-ablation) regimes which do not depend on prompt compliance. (2) The low-numeracy-pivot-language regime confounds number-word availability with general language-resource competence; the within-language approximate-quantifier manipulation and the content-matched steering are the primary clean tests, and cross-lingual analyses are accuracy-stratified. (3) Approximate framings may just add difficulty/noise rather than a magnitude fallback; the ratio-dependent Weber-law error signature and the exact-vs-approximate SELECTIVITY (not raw drops) distinguish a genuine fallback from generic degradation. (4) The exact-number-word direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; mitigated by numerate-vs-approximate matched contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and approximate-task specificity checks. (5) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (6) A null result (anumeric regimes do not selectively harm exact number cognition, or errors stay random) is itself highly informative: it would dissociate LLMs from the human anumeric finding, indicating LLM exact-number ability rests on magnitude representations rather than number words. (7) The anumeric/Whorfian framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like cognition.

Name: verbal_interference_llm
Title: Verbal Interference in LLMs: Using a Concurrent Linguistic Load to Reveal Which Reasoning Depends on Language
Short Hypothesis: Just as concurrent verbal load selectively impairs language-dependent (but not language-independent) reasoning in humans, forcing an LLM to simultaneously generate fluent surface language while it reasons will selectively degrade tasks that recruit shared language-production machinery, and testing for this SELECTIVE competition signature (beyond non-specific impairment) yields a measurable, task-graded probe of how far an LLM's reasoning shares language-production resources - framed as a competition assay, not a claim of clean dissociation.
Related Work: Two literatures bear on this. (1) LLM latent/implicit reasoning: Coconut (Reasoning Beyond Words, 2024), implicit CoT distillation (2023/2024), latent-CoT mechanistic studies (2025/2026), and SAE-based latent reasoning features (2026) all study REMOVING or REPLACING verbalization to see if reasoning survives in continuous space. (2) Cognitive neuroscience: verbal-interference/dual-task paradigms (Verbal interference paradigms, 2022) show that occupying the language system with a concurrent verbal task selectively impairs cognition that recruits language, and fMRI dissociation studies (The boundaries of language and thought, 2009; Intuitive physical reasoning, 2024; A human brain network for abstract formal reasoning, 2025) show formal/physical reasoning dissociates from the language network. No prior LLM work imports the LOADING logic of verbal interference: instead of ablating language components, we occupy the language-production pathway with a concurrent fluent-generation demand and measure which reasoning tasks are selectively taxed. Our methodological delta is competition-under-load versus lesion-based necessity: ablation/localization work on LLM language networks REMOVES units to test necessity, whereas CLL leaves the network intact and OCCUPIES the language-production pathway, exposing resource-sharing that lesions cannot distinguish from redundancy. We pre-define 'language dependence' operationally from independent task features and human annotations (not post hoc labels), and we reposition the contribution as a controlled behavioral assay for linguistic resource competition, in which null and non-selective outcomes are central tests: failure to find selective interference despite strong controls would itself challenge the human analogy and refine language-vs-thought claims in LLMs. This distinguishes CLL from ablation-based and latent-reasoning studies which manipulate the substrate rather than compete for it.
Abstract: In humans, a classic way to test whether a cognitive task depends on language is verbal interference: participants perform a task while a concurrent verbal load occupies the language system, and tasks that recruit language are selectively impaired. Neuroscience shows that formal, logical, and physical reasoning dissociate from the language network, while other cognition (e.g., verbal memory, categorization) does not. We import this loading paradigm into large language models to ask which forms of machine reasoning depend on the language-production pathway. We introduce Concurrent Linguistic Load (CLL): the model is required to interleave, token-by-token or step-by-step, its reasoning with the generation of fluent, semantically demanding but task-irrelevant surface text (e.g., continuing a florid narrative), imposing sustained demand on language production. We measure how much CLL degrades accuracy across a battery of reasoning tasks spanning a hypothesized language-dependence gradient: verbal/word-problem reasoning, arithmetic, symbolic logic, spatial/relational reasoning, and pattern-matrix tasks. Our central prediction is a task-by-load interaction: language-heavy tasks are selectively impaired by CLL relative to control loads (a non-linguistic counting load, or a length-matched inert load), whereas abstract symbolic/spatial tasks are relatively spared. We then localize the shared bottleneck by measuring, under CLL, competition in language-production components (attention heads and MLP neurons identified via next-token fluency contributions) and test whether the size of a task's CLL cost predicts its overlap with language-production circuitry. Across several open-weight models we quantify the interference gradient, control-load specificity, and circuit-overlap correlation. We are explicit about what is novel at each level: the paradigm (CLL, competition-under-load), the finding (task-by-load interaction), the mechanism (a shared language-production bottleneck), and the setting (multiple frozen open-weight LLMs). We compare CLL against the closest baselines - direct ablation/localization of language units on at least one model, hidden-state reasoning suppression, length/overhead controls, and generic dual-output prompting - so load-based and lesion-based conclusions can be contrasted. Downstream, the result informs benchmark design, the interpretation of chain-of-thought, claims about latent/hidden reasoning, and safety auditing of assistants under concurrent generation demands; either outcome is valuable, since selective impairment supports resource-sharing structure while null or non-specific impairment falsifies a popular human analogy and redirects methodology. We frame the result as a competition assay rather than a clean dissociation. This reframes 'does an LLM think in language?' as an empirically testable, task-graded competition probe.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Task battery with a language-dependence gradient): Prerequisite. Data: ~200 items each for (a) verbal GSM-style word problems (adapted from GSM8K's 1,319-item test set), (b) numeric-only arithmetic (built), (c) propositional/symbolic logic (built), (d) spatial/relational reasoning (adapted from BIG-Bench spatial and relational-ordering tasks), (e) abstract pattern/matrix tasks (adapted from ARC-style and symbolic sequence-completion sets); 1,000 items total, calibrated to mid-range baseline accuracy so interference has room to show. Decisive metric first: per-task no-load baseline accuracy in the 40-85% window. Convincing result: all five tasks fall in that window on the target models, enabling sensitive interaction tests. Indecision band: a task at 85-95% baseline - near ceiling, reducing power; we add harder items. Negative result (a task at ceiling/floor): it is rebalanced or dropped.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Concurrent Linguistic Load selectively degrades language-dependent reasoning): The central dissociation test. Data: the 1,000 items above, used across four load conditions: (i) no-load baseline; (ii) Concurrent Linguistic Load (CLL) - the model interleaves each reasoning step with a fixed quota of fluent, task-irrelevant narrative continuation; (iii) non-linguistic control load - interleave a numeric counting/tally task matched for token quota; (iv) inert control load - interleave copying a fixed filler string (matched length). Loads are imposed by structured prompting that alternates reasoning and load spans with strict format/quota enforcement; the linguistic and control loads are matched separately on token count, syntactic complexity, semantic coherence, and output-alternation structure so any CLL-specific effect isolates linguistic competition from autoregressive overhead. We record and report compliance-failure, truncation, latency, and answer-position effects, and re-run the interaction conditioning on these nuisances. A direct language-unit ablation/localization baseline from prior work is included on at least one model to contrast load-based with lesion-based conclusions. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B (scale), all weights frozen; 5 samples/item, temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2. Exact prompt templates, interleaving schedules, and the task-battery composition are fixed in advance, and a pre-registered power analysis (mixed-effects: accuracy ~ task_type * load_condition + (1|model) + (1|item)) sets the minimum items per cell for the target interaction effect size. Systems compared: the four load conditions across the five task types. Decisive metric first: the task_type x load_condition interaction coefficient from a mixed-effects logistic regression (accuracy ~ task_type * load_condition + (1|model) + (1|item)). Convincing result: CLL's accuracy drop is significantly larger for verbal/word-problem and verbal-logic tasks than for numeric arithmetic and abstract spatial/matrix tasks, and larger than the drop under the non-linguistic and inert control loads (95% CI on the relevant interaction contrasts excluding zero) in at least 3 of 4 models; a compliance check confirms the load task was actually performed (load-span fluency/accuracy above a floor) so drops are not task abandonment. Indecision band: the CLL-specific interaction contrast CI spanning zero (CLL degrades all tasks about equally, like the inert load) - interference is non-specific, so no language-vs-thought dissociation is revealed. Negative result (abstract tasks degrade more than verbal tasks under CLL): the predicted gradient is reversed, refuting the shared-language-bottleneck account.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Interference scales with genuine linguistic demand): Rules out mere token overhead. Data: the verbal and word-problem items under graded CLL - short vs. long, and coherent narrative vs. word-salad - matched for token count; ~400 items x 4 CLL variants. We also add within-task, item-level manipulations of linguistic surface form to test whether CLL cost tracks language demand INSIDE a task family, not just across coarse task categories. Models: same, frozen. Decisive metric first: slope of CLL cost vs. genuine language-production demand (coherent-narrative load minus matched word-salad/overhead load). Convincing result: interference grows with coherent linguistic demand beyond token-count-matched non-linguistic overhead (slope CI excluding zero). Indecision band: slope CI spanning zero - cost tracks token overhead, not linguistic demand, so 'linguistic' interference is not established. Negative result: word-salad interferes as much as coherent narrative, indicating a generic-capacity, not language-specific, bottleneck.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Behavioral CLL cost tracks language-production circuit overlap): Tests the mechanistic prediction. Data: the 1,000 items; language-production components S_lang per model identified by a precise protocol - contribution to next-token fluency on held-out fluent-continuation spans (attribution/logit-lens) - and VALIDATED on independent fluency tasks before use; each reasoning task's causally-important components localized by activation patching on no-load correct-vs-incorrect contrasts (400 items/task). Overlap analyses are adjusted for baseline task difficulty and length. Models: same, frozen; seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: per-task behavioral CLL cost vs. per-task Jaccard overlap with S_lang. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation across tasks between CLL cost and S_lang overlap; secondary: measured competition in S_lang (change in activation norm/attention allocation during reasoning spans under CLL vs. no-load). Convincing result: positive CLL-cost-to-overlap correlation (95% CI excluding zero) and measurable S_lang competition under CLL, so the tasks hurt most are those reusing language-production circuitry. Indecision band: correlation CI spanning zero with |rho|<0.3 - behavioral interference is not explained by circuit overlap, leaving the mechanism unlocated even if the behavioral dissociation holds. Negative result (negative correlation): the tasks that share language circuitry are the least hurt, contradicting the loading account. All effect sizes carry bootstrap CIs over items, seeds, and models; every number is planned, not measured.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) CLL may degrade all tasks non-specifically via added context length/format burden; mitigated by length-matched non-linguistic and inert control loads and by testing the task x load INTERACTION rather than raw drops. (2) The model may abandon the load to protect the reasoning task (or vice versa), confounding interpretation; we monitor load-task compliance and analyze only compliant trials. (3) Even 'non-linguistic' loads pass through the same tokenizer/decoder, so control loads are not perfectly language-free; we use the graded load-quality manipulation to isolate the effect of genuine linguistic demand. (4) Task-type language-dependence labels are hypotheses; a flat interference gradient would itself be an informative result (reasoning shares one bottleneck regardless of surface form).
