(5) Language-production component identification is noisy; we report multiple models and use overlap correlations rather than single-component claims. (6) Prompt-based interleaving is imperfect control over 'concurrency' compared to true dual-tasking; we treat CLL as an operationalization and note this framing limitation explicitly.

Name: answer_deferral_typology
Title: Think Verb-Last: Does Answer-Deferring Word Order Delay an LLM's Commitment and Reduce Premature-Answer Errors?
Short Hypothesis: Human psycholinguistics shows head-final (verb-late, SOV) languages defer the pivotal predicate, forcing the parser to keep multiple hypotheses open, whereas head-initial (SVO) languages front the verb and encourage early prediction. Our specific, testable claim is a causal chain about reasoning STRUCTURE, not about the commitment probe itself: when an LLM is scaffolded into an answer-deferring, verb-final reasoning structure (a within-item, content- and length-matched manipulation), it commits to a final answer later in its chain-of-thought and keeps competing candidate answers alive longer, which selectively reduces premature-commitment errors on problems that require revising an initially tempting wrong answer. The internal 'answer-commitment' direction is a measurement/steering tool used to test that chain (structure -> delayed commitment -> fewer revision errors), not the novelty. The head-initial/head-final framing is an operational analogy, not a claim of human-like parsing.
Related Work: Human work shows head-initial SVO languages afford more prediction while head-final SOV languages rely on rich pre-verbal structure building, holding hypotheses open until the verb (Prediction in SVO and SOV, 2023; Hyper-active gap filling, 2015; Hindi verbal-prediction limits, 2021; Word order affects formulation time course, Tzeltal 2015). In LLMs, word-order studies focus on training-time inductive biases via synthetic/artificial languages (Ravfogel 2019; White & Cotterell 2021), on representation of grammatical role (BERT word order, 2022), and on incremental garden-path processing (2024); BICAUSE (2025) shows LLMs internalize language-specific causal-order attention biases. Recent commitment-boundary work shows that a model's eventual answer is often decodable or steerable partway through its trace. Our contribution is orthogonal to that decodability result: we do not merely read commitment, we intervene on reasoning STRUCTURE and test whether that intervention shifts WHEN commitment happens and, through it, revision-error rate - a causal claim (structure -> delayed commitment -> lower revision errors) that decodability work does not make. The cross-lingual SVO/SOV variant is a secondary robustness test of whether native verb-final grammar reproduces the within-language effect, not the core manipulation, and is always stratified on per-language competence. The novelty is thus the structural intervention and its revision-specific behavioral law, not the probing/steering mechanism.
Abstract: Languages differ in where they place the verb: head-initial languages (English, SVO) front the predicate and let listeners predict early, while head-final languages (Japanese, Hindi, SOV) defer the verb, forcing the comprehender to keep multiple interpretations open until it arrives. We ask whether this typological trade-off shapes how large language models reason: does an answer-deferring, verb-final reasoning structure make a model commit to its answer later and hold competing candidate answers alive longer, thereby avoiding premature-commitment errors on problems that require overriding a tempting-but-wrong first guess? We construct reasoning items with a strong intuitive lure and manipulate, within-item and content-matched, whether the reasoning trace is structured answer-early (conclusion stated up front, then justified) versus answer-late (all evidence marshalled first, conclusion deferred to the end), plus a native cross-lingual variant across SVO and SOV languages as a secondary robustness check. We pre-register first-answer-commitment position (as a fraction of the trace) as the primary metric and candidate-answer persistence as the backup, targeting at least a 0.10-of-trace shift, and we measure lure-error rate on revision-requiring vs. non-revision problems. We predict answer-late structure defers commitment, sustains multiple candidates longer, and selectively reduces lure errors where revision matters, while offering no benefit (or a cost) where the first guess is correct. Beyond toy lure batteries we anchor the effect on a subset of a widely used reasoning benchmark (GSM8K/GSM-IC). Mechanistically, we locate an 'answer-commitment' direction from hidden states contrasting pre- vs post-commitment steps, test whether answer-late structure lowers its early engagement, and steer it to delay or force commitment, causally reproducing or cancelling the behavioral effect. If confirmed, answer-deferring structure is a cheap prompt-format knob (and a CoT diagnostic) for reducing premature-answer errors in revision-heavy tasks; if null, LLM reasoning commitment is independent of surface reasoning-order structure, telling prompt engineers that answer placement is not a usable lever. Across several open-weight models we quantify the commitment-timing effect, its revision-specificity, and steering controllability.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does answer-deferring, verb-final structure delay commitment and keep candidates alive longer?): Tests whether an answer-late reasoning structure defers first answer-commitment and sustains competing candidates longer than an answer-early structure. Data: a lure battery of ~1000 items, 250 per family - (a) misleading-premise math adapted from GSM-IC (Shi et al. 2023, ~58k released problems), (b) Cognitive-Reflection-Test-style traps (templated, since only ~7 canonical CRT items exist), (c) multi-hop logic where an early sub-conclusion is superseded by later evidence (constructed), (d) belief-bias syllogisms (constructed from standard belief-bias templates). Each item carries a labeled correct answer AND a labeled lure answer and is tagged revision-requiring (intuitive first guess wrong) vs non-revision (first guess correct). We use 250 per family to keep 5 models x 3 structures x 4 decoding passes affordable. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Mistral-7B-Instruct; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus one greedy pass. Structures (within-item, content- and length-matched, format-enforced): answer-early (state the tentative conclusion first, then justify), answer-late (marshal all evidence, defer the conclusion to the final tokens), and a free baseline. We verify structure compliance and analyze only compliant traces. Measurement: at each reasoning step read the implicit answer via next-token probabilities on constrained answer slots for the correct vs lure candidate; define first-commitment position = earliest step (as a fraction of trace length) where the eventual answer's probability crosses a dominance threshold of 0.5 and stays, and candidate persistence = number of steps both correct and lure remain above a 0.2 liveness threshold. Decisive metric: first-commitment position (fraction of trace) in a mixed-effects model controlling trace length; secondary: candidate persistence. Convincing result: answer-late yields a later first-commitment position than answer-early (difference 95% CI excluding zero and exceeding 0.10 of the trace) and longer candidate persistence. Indecision band: if the first-commitment-position difference has a 95% CI within +/-0.05 of the trace fraction, or trace-length matching is imperfect enough that the effect is confounded, the timing claim is undecided. Negative result (no shift in commitment timing) would indicate LLM reasoning commitment is independent of surface reasoning-order structure.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Does deferred commitment selectively reduce lure errors where revision is needed?): Tests the revision-specific behavioral benefit, plus a native cross-lingual variant. Data: the same battery from Experiment 1, using the revision-requiring vs non-revision tags. Cross-lingual variant: translate the items into SVO languages (English, Spanish) and SOV languages (Japanese, Hindi, Turkish), back-translation checked, to test whether native verb-final grammar reproduces the answer-late effect; all cross-lingual analyses are stratified on per-language task accuracy to separate structure from language-resource competence. Models, seeds and decoding as Experiment 1. Decisive metric: the structure x revision-status interaction on lure-error rate. Convincing result: answer-late reduces lure-error rate on revision-requiring items significantly more than on non-revision items (interaction 95% CI excluding zero), may slightly raise errors on non-revision items (a deferral cost), and native SOV framing shows the same direction after competence stratification. Indecision band: if the structure x revision interaction has a 95% CI within +/-2 percentage points, the selective-benefit claim is undecided. Negative result (answer-late does not selectively cut revision errors) would show deferral buys no genuine revision benefit, weakening the functional analogy to head-final comprehension.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Is there a locatable answer-commitment direction whose early engagement answer-late structure lowers?): Location plus mediation. Data: hidden states cached on the traces of Experiment 1, contrasting pre-commitment vs post-commitment steps (defined by the first-commitment crossing), 70/15/15 train/validation/test over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer logistic-regression linear probes are trainable, 5-fold CV over seeds {0,1,2}. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for pre- vs post-commitment steps (best layer). Then: whether answer-late structure lowers early-trace projection onto this answer-commitment direction versus answer-early, and the Spearman correlation between per-item projection timing and per-item first-commitment position. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC clears 0.70 and generalizes, answer-late lowers early projection (CI excluding zero), and projection timing tracks first-commitment position (rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65], or a projection-timing rho whose 95% CI is within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the mechanism undecided. Negative result (no decodable commitment direction, or its timing does not track structure) would sever the behavioral timing effect from any internal commitment signal.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Does steering the commitment direction delay or force commitment and reproduce or cancel the behavioral effect?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item revision-requiring subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; the difference-in-means commitment direction from Experiment 3 is added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: -commitment-direction during answer-early reasoning (to delay commitment), +commitment-direction during answer-late reasoning (to force early commitment), random-direction, and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in lure-error rate on revision items under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that non-revision accuracy is preserved. Convincing result: -direction under answer-early reduces revision lure errors (reproducing the answer-late benefit) with a monotone dose-response, +direction under answer-late cancels the benefit, both exceed random-direction (CIs excluding it), and non-revision accuracy stays within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: if the steering effect's 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or shows no dose-response, the causal claim is undecided. Negative result (steering does not move commitment timing or lure errors) would mean the commitment direction is correlational, not the causal lever the hypothesis claims.

Baselines, ablations, and pre-registration: as additional baselines we include free-form CoT, answer-early, answer-late, a shuffled-order paraphrase control (same sentences, scrambled order), and a deliberation-length-matched control that adds equivalent non-deferring reasoning tokens, so the effect is separated from extra compute, verbosity, and format compliance. Revision-requiring items are labeled by whether the intuitive first guess is wrong (verified against the labeled lure), and we ablate on compliance, trace length, and answer correctness to show the effect is not verbosity. The claim hierarchy (H1 timing, H2 revision-specific behavior, H3 mechanism) is pre-registered with the acceptance and indecision criteria above; effect sizes are reported with 95% CIs and Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Answer-late structure may simply give the model more evidence before answering (a 'more deliberation' effect) rather than a genuine deferral/open-hypothesis effect; mitigated by strict length/content matching, by testing the revision-specific interaction rather than raw accuracy, and by the native cross-lingual variant. (2) Instruction-tuned models may resist the imposed structure or emit the answer regardless of placement; we enforce format, verify structure compliance, and analyze only compliant trials. (3) Reading implicit commitment via answer-slot probabilities is approximate for free-form traces; we use constrained answer slots and multiple liveness thresholds, reporting robustness. (4) Cross-lingual SVO/SOV differences confound grammar with training-data resource level; the within-language answer-early/answer-late manipulation is the primary clean test and all cross-lingual analyses are accuracy-stratified. (5) The commitment direction may entangle with generic confidence/difficulty rather than answer commitment per se; mitigated by matched pre/post-commitment contrasts, held-out validation, random-direction steering, and non-revision specificity checks. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (word-order structure does not shift commitment timing or revision errors) is itself informative, indicating LLM reasoning commitment is independent of surface reasoning-order typology. (8) The head-initial/head-final framing is an operationalized analogy to human prediction-vs-deferral, not a claim of human-like parsing; findings are framed behaviorally and mechanistically.

Name: counterfactual_marker_reasoning
Title: Mood Matters: Does a Grammatical Counterfactual Marker Unlock an LLM's Counterfactual Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: Bloom's contested claim - that languages lacking a dedicated counterfactual/irrealis marker impair counterfactual reasoning - can be tested cleanly inside LLMs. Narrowing the claim to its sharpest, most novel form: framing an identical problem with an explicit counterfactual mood marker (subjunctive/irrealis) versus an unmarked indicative selectively REDUCES 'actual-world intrusion' errors (importing real-world facts the hypothetical overrides), by more strongly engaging an internal 'irrealis mode' that keeps the actual and hypothetical worlds distinct; steering that irrealis direction reproduces or cancels the marker's benefit. The manipulation isolates grammatical MOOD from lexical counterfactual cues, and the headline contribution is a confound-reduced mechanistic adjudication of Bloom's marker->reasoning claim.
Related Work: Bloom (1981) argued Chinese speakers reason counterfactually less because Chinese lacks a distinct subjunctive marker; this is contested (Exploring counterfactuals in English and Chinese, 2023, shows Chinese uses lexical/contextual cues). Recent LLM linguistic-relativity work is largely observational: BICAUSE (Under the Shadow of Babel, 2025) shows LLMs internalize language-specific causal-order attention biases; the Sapir-Whorf reproduction study (2025) probes behavioral alignment; grammatical-concept work (LLMs Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts, 2025; Naturalistic Causal Probing for Morpho-Syntax, 2022; A Geometric Notion of Causal Probing, 2023) shows number/gender/tense are shared, linearly-encoded, causally manipulable directions. Crucially, that number/gender/tense steering concerns feature IDENTITY, not a reasoning CAPABILITY: showing a tense direction is steerable does not imply that a mood MARKER changes counterfactual-reasoning accuracy or intrusion errors. Our delta is exactly that link - grammatical mood marking -> counterfactual reasoning behavior - via a within-item, mood-vs-lexical-cue-controlled manipulation, plus a located 'irrealis mode' that separates actual from hypothetical worlds and is steered to reproduce/cancel the effect, and a released multilingual counterfactual minimal-pair benchmark. The cross-lingual strong/weak-marker comparison is a secondary, competence-stratified robustness test, not the core claim; the headline contribution is the mechanistic adjudication of Bloom, with the located irrealis representation and the causal behavior change as the supporting evidence.
Abstract: A landmark and still-contested claim in the language-and-thought literature (Bloom, 1981) holds that speakers of languages lacking a dedicated counterfactual/irrealis marker reason counterfactually less readily than speakers of languages with an explicit subjunctive. Human tests are confounded by culture and education; large language models offer a clean testbed where content can be held fixed and only grammatical mood varied. We ask whether the presence of a counterfactual mood marker causally changes how well an LLM reasons about hypothetical, contrary-to-fact worlds. We construct counterfactual-reasoning items (contrary-to-fact conditionals requiring the model to compute what would follow in a hypothetical world without contaminating it with actual-world facts) and manipulate, within-item and content-matched, whether the antecedent is grammatically marked as counterfactual (subjunctive/irrealis) versus stated in unmarked indicative form, plus a native cross-lingual variant across strong-marker (English, Spanish) and weak-marker (Chinese, Indonesian) languages as a secondary check. We define actual-world intrusion formally as choosing the labeled answer that follows from reverting to real-world facts the hypothetical overrides, with rule-based labeling validated by inter-annotator agreement on a sample, and we predict the counterfactual marker raises accuracy and reduces intrusion errors, selectively on genuinely contrary-to-fact items. Mechanistically, we locate an 'irrealis mode' direction from hidden states contrasting counterfactual versus factual framings, test whether the marker increases its engagement and whether items with stronger engagement suffer fewer intrusions, and causally steer it: adding the direction under unmarked framing should recover the benefit, subtracting it under marked framing should cancel it. We release the content-matched marked/unmarked (and multilingual) minimal-pair items as a reusable benchmark, and pre-register a claim hierarchy (behavioral effect first, representation association second, causal steering third), not claiming that probe/steer alone proves mechanism. If the marker helps, prompt templates and multilingual benchmarks may systematically bias measured reasoning, and hypothetical/planning/instruction-following tasks are exposed to intrusion errors; if null (a live possibility), this is the cleanest evidence to date against Bloom's mechanistic reading, since cultural confounds are absent. Across several open-weight models we quantify the marker effect, its dissociation from language resource level, and steering controllability, delivering a mechanistic adjudication of Bloom's hypothesis.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Does a counterfactual mood marker causally improve counterfactual reasoning and cut actual-world intrusions?): Tests whether an explicit counterfactual/irrealis marker raises counterfactual accuracy and lowers actual-world intrusion errors, selectively on genuinely contrary-to-fact items. Data: ~400 counterfactual-reasoning items, each a contrary-to-fact scenario with a question requiring reasoning in the hypothetical world; each is paired with a matched FACTUAL (indicative, real-world) control and includes an 'already-true' subset where the hypothetical coincides with reality (selectivity control). Each item carries a labeled correct counterfactual answer AND a labeled actual-world-intrusion lure (the answer following from reverting to real-world facts). We use 400 items to fit the marker x item-type interaction with adequate power while keeping five-model coverage affordable. Marked and unmarked forms are content-, entity-, and length-matched; marker strength is validated by independent grammaticality ratings. Manipulation (within-item): MARKED form with an explicit subjunctive/irrealis marker (If A had been Q...; were A to be Q...) vs UNMARKED indicative conveying the same hypothetical content lexically (Assume A is Q now; then...). Cross-lingual variant (secondary): translate items into strong-marker (English, Spanish) and weak-marker (Chinese, Indonesian) languages, back-translation checked, accuracy-stratified. A length-matched non-mood reflection preamble is added as a control against generic extra structure. Models: five frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models - Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B; inference only; temperature 0.7 with seeds {0,1,2} plus greedy. Decisive metric: actual-world intrusion rate (primary) and counterfactual accuracy, in a mixed-effects model outcome ~ mood_marker*item_type + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: MARKED framing lowers intrusion and raises accuracy selectively on contrary-to-fact items (marker x item_type interaction 95% CI excluding zero) with little effect on factual/already-true controls, the non-mood reflection control does not reproduce it, and native strong-marker languages track the effect after competence stratification. Indecision band: a marker x item_type interaction whose 95% CI lies within +/-2 percentage points is undecided. Negative result (no marker benefit, intrusions unchanged) would be the cleanest evidence to date AGAINST Bloom's mechanistic reading, since cultural confounds are absent.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Is there a locatable irrealis-mode direction the marker more strongly engages?): Location plus mediation. Data: hidden states on matched marked-vs-unmarked and counterfactual-vs-factual contrasts, 70/15/15 over items. Model: the same five frozen models; only per-layer logistic-regression probes are trainable (5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}); a difference-in-means irrealis direction is derived without training. Decisive metric: held-out probe AUROC for hypothetical/irrealis vs factual mode (best layer); then whether the marker increases projection onto the irrealis direction and whether per-item irrealis engagement correlates with fewer intrusion errors (Spearman). Convincing result: best-layer AUROC clears 0.70, MARKED framing raises projection onto the irrealis direction (CI excluding zero), and engagement predicts fewer intrusions (rho CI excluding zero). Indecision band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65], or a mediation rho within +/-0.1 of zero, leaves the mechanism undecided. Negative result (no irrealis direction, or it does not track the marker) would detach any behavioral marker benefit from an internal actual-vs-hypothetical separation.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Does steering the irrealis direction reproduce or cancel the marker's benefit?): Causal test. Data: a held-out 200-item counterfactual subset disjoint from probe training. Model: the same five frozen models; no weights trained; the irrealis direction is added or subtracted at the located layer over a dose sweep, seeds {0,1,2}. Systems compared: +irrealis-direction during UNMARKED reasoning (to recover accuracy / cut intrusions), -irrealis-direction during MARKED reasoning (to cancel the benefit), random-direction, and no-steer. Decisive metric: change in actual-world intrusion rate (and accuracy) under steering versus no-steer, with a specificity check that factual-item accuracy and fluency are preserved. Convincing result: +direction under UNMARKED reproduces a substantial fraction of the marker benefit with a monotone dose-response, -direction under MARKED cancels it, both exceed random-direction (CIs excluding it), and factual-item accuracy stays within +/-2 pp of no-steer. Indecision band: a steering effect whose 95% CI overlaps random-direction, or shows no dose-response, leaves causal mediation undecided. Negative result (steering does not move counterfactual behavior) would mean the irrealis direction is correlational, not causal, weakening the mechanistic adjudication of Bloom's hypothesis.

Controls, examples, and power: we add controls against alternative explanations - an uncertainty/hedging-prompt control, a complexity-matched non-mood paraphrase, and a lexical-counterfactual-cue ablation - and provide concrete example items showing marked vs unmarked forms differing only in grammatical mood, not lexical counterfactuality, emphasis, or discourse naturalness. We report model-selection rationale and a minimum-detectable-effect estimate across the five models with explicit handling of ceiling effects. The irrealis probe must clear AUROC 0.70 AND generalize to held-out items AND show factual-item non-effects; the causal test uses layer/site specificity, a dose-response, and a transfer check that the direction does not merely induce generic hypothetical language. Effect sizes are reported with 95% CIs and multiple-comparison correction, and the multilingual minimal-pair set is released as a benchmark artifact.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Unmarked indicative framings may still convey counterfactuality lexically well enough that the model reasons correctly, muting the marker effect; a null result is itself informative (it would provide the cleanest evidence to date AGAINST Bloom's mechanistic reading, since cultural confounds are absent) and we sharpen sensitivity with intrusion-error metrics and difficulty-calibrated items. (2) Cross-lingual differences confound grammar with training-data resource level; the within-language marked/unmarked manipulation is the primary clean test and cross-lingual analyses are accuracy-stratified. (3) Marked vs unmarked forms may differ in length/emphasis rather than mood per se; we length-match, use independent marker-strength ratings, add a non-mood reflection control, and rely on content-matched steering to isolate mood. (4) The irrealis direction may entangle with generic difficulty or hedging rather than a genuine actual-vs-hypothetical world separation; mitigated by matched contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and factual-item specificity checks. (5) Instruction-tuned models may reason counterfactually robustly regardless of marking, yielding ceiling effects; we calibrate item difficulty, include harder multi-step hypotheticals, and test multiple models. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we report effect sizes with CIs across models. (7) Bloom's hypothesis framing is operationalized behaviorally/mechanistically, not as a claim about human-like cognition.

Name: private_speech_zpd
Title: Chain-of-Thought as Private Speech: Testing the Vygotskian Zone of Proximal Development in LLM Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's chain-of-thought behaves like children's private (self-directed) speech: its amount follows an inverted-U over task difficulty (peaking at moderate difficulty), it shifts from overt to abbreviated/covert form as competence rises, and — the key falsifiable claim — it is beneficial only inside a 'zone of proximal development' (moderate difficulty), while being wasteful overhead on easy items and actively interfering on already-mastered ones, so reasoning should be self-regulated by difficulty rather than applied uniformly.
Related Work: Developmental psychology (Vygotsky; Fernyhough) establishes that private speech follows a developmental trajectory: it appears most at intermediate task difficulty, peaks and then internalizes/abbreviates as skill grows, forming a zone of proximal development. Recent cross-domain work shows GPT-4o produces child-like private speech (Private speech: similarities between an LLM and children, 2026) and reviews inner speech as a cognitive tool (Alderson-Day & Fernyhough, 2023). In ML, 'Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning' (2025) reports reasoning-token length rises then falls over fine-tuning (an inverted-U over TRAINING), latent-reasoning work (Coconut, 2024) internalizes CoT, and 'Why think step by step?' (2023) explains WHEN reasoning helps via data locality. However, no prior work (a) tests the inverted-U of reasoning emission as a function of per-item DIFFICULTY (a within-model, inference-time developmental law, not a training-time one), (b) tests the Vygotskian ZPD prediction that forced reasoning hurts at difficulty extremes, or (c) links overt-to-covert abbreviation of CoT to per-item competence. Our PRIMARY novel contribution is the ZPD-benefit law (H2): CoT benefit peaks at intermediate per-item difficulty and turns non-positive at both extremes - a per-item, inference-time law distinct from generic accuracy-vs-length 'overthinking' and from training-time inverted-U reports. The exact new empirical claim is per-item difficulty-conditioned emission and benefit, not aggregate overthinking. Relative to (i) difficulty-adaptive/uncertainty-gated controllers, our delta is the predicted INTERIOR peak and harm-at-extremes plus its developmental abbreviation signature; (ii) overthinking papers, our delta is per-item difficulty conditioning rather than length-accuracy averages; (iii) developmental-analogy papers, our delta is a falsifiable quantitative law rather than a qualitative resemblance. 'Covert/abbreviated' is defined operationally (shorter length, fewer explicit steps, higher operator-to-filler token ratio) and 'mastered'/'approaching mastery' by per-item direct-answer accuracy bands with robustness to alternative calibration. We separate the behavioral analogy from any mechanistic claim: the probe and controller are an efficiency result, not evidence of human-like inner speech. We turn the developmental theory of private speech into concrete, falsifiable predictions about self-regulated inference-time reasoning.
Abstract: Children talk to themselves while solving hard problems, and developmental psychology gives a precise account of this 'private speech': its quantity follows an inverted-U over task difficulty, it is concentrated in a learner's zone of proximal development (ZPD), and it becomes abbreviated and covert as competence grows. We propose that an LLM's chain-of-thought (CoT) is a computational analog of private speech and obeys the same developmental laws — at inference time and per item, not merely over training. We make three falsifiable predictions. (1) Emission: when allowed to reason freely, a model's spontaneous CoT length forms an inverted-U over graded difficulty, peaking at intermediate difficulty rather than rising monotonically. (2) ZPD benefit: the accuracy gain from CoT over direct answering is largest at intermediate difficulty and small or negative at the extremes — forced reasoning is wasteful overhead on trivial items and can interfere on already-mastered items. (3) Abbreviation: as items move from moderate toward mastered, spontaneous CoT compresses (shorter, more elliptical), mirroring overt-to-covert internalization. We test these across difficulty-graded arithmetic, logic, and word-problem suites on several open-weight models with controlled per-item difficulty calibration. We then add a lightweight mechanistic component: a probe that reads a model's own competence/difficulty estimate from early hidden states, used to build a self-regulated 'ZPD-gated' reasoning controller that spends CoT only where it helps, and compare it to always-CoT and never-CoT baselines on accuracy and token cost. The downstream payoff is concrete: a ZPD-gated controller that spends CoT only in the beneficial difficulty band should cut tokens at matched accuracy (or raise accuracy at matched budget) relative to always-CoT and to entropy-, margin-, and uncertainty-gated controllers, which we quantify on an application-relevant domain (e.g., multilingual customer-support or clinical-triage QA) as well as benchmark suites. If the ZPD law holds, adaptive-effort systems should gate on predicted difficulty with harm-avoidance at the easy extreme; if it fails (benefit rises monotonically), the simpler 'CoT helps more when harder' view stands and difficulty-gating offers no interior advantage. Confirming these predictions reframes CoT as difficulty-self-regulated private speech and yields a principled, training-free efficiency lever.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Difficulty-graded task suites with calibrated per-item difficulty): Prerequisite. Data: built suites of ~300 items each - multi-digit arithmetic (operand size/carry count as the surface difficulty axis), propositional/multi-hop logic (number of inference steps), and GSM-style word problems (number of reasoning steps); 900 items. Per-item empirical difficulty = direct-answer error rate estimated from 20 samples/item per model, giving a continuous difficulty score independent of the surface axis. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, all weights frozen, seeds 0/1/2. Decisive metric first: spread and reliability (split-half) of the calibrated difficulty score. Convincing result: difficulty spans a wide range with split-half reliability >=0.7, and is not confounded with item length (|correlation| < 0.3). Indecision band: reliability 0.5-0.7 - we increase samples/item. Negative result (difficulty not separable from length): the calibration is unusable and we redesign items.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Spontaneous reasoning emission forms an inverted-U over difficulty): Tests the emission law. Data: the 900 items, elicited under a permissive prompt that neither forbids nor mandates chain-of-thought. Models: same four, frozen. Systems compared: a quadratic vs. a monotonic model of CoT length over difficulty. Pre-registered primary endpoint: an interior-maximum (two-lines / Lind-Mehlum U) test confirming the turning point lies strictly inside the observed difficulty range, together with the sign and significance of the quadratic coefficient in length ~ difficulty + difficulty^2 + (1|model) + (1|item) and AIC/BIC preference of the quadratic over the monotonic model. Length is analyzed controlling for token-budget cap, prompt length, and answer format to rule out ceiling artifacts. Convincing result: a significant negative quadratic term (95% CI excluding zero) with an interior peak at intermediate difficulty, and AIC/BIC favoring the quadratic, in at least 3 of 4 models. Indecision band: quadratic-term CI spanning zero but AIC/BIC roughly tied - emission is not clearly inverted-U (could be monotone or flat), so the private-speech emission law is unsupported at this resolution. Negative result (positive quadratic or strictly monotone increasing length): reasoning emission does not follow the developmental inverted-U.

Experiment 3 (H2 - CoT benefit is a zone-of-proximal-development function of difficulty): Tests the ZPD-benefit claim. Data: the 900 items, each evaluated under forced-direct (no CoT), forced-CoT, and free conditions; 10 samples/condition/item. Models: same four, frozen. Decisive metric first: the per-item CoT benefit = accuracy(CoT) - accuracy(direct), fitted as benefit ~ difficulty + difficulty^2. Convincing result: benefit peaks at intermediate difficulty, is within +/-2 points of zero on easy items, and is significantly negative (interference) on a subset of already-mastered-but-nontrivial items (negative-benefit CI excluding zero), with qualitative confirmation that forced CoT introduces errors the direct answer avoided. Indecision band: benefit rises monotonically with difficulty with no interior peak and no negative region (quadratic CI spanning zero) - CoT is simply more useful on harder items, the ordinary view, and the distinctive ZPD prediction (harm at extremes) fails. Negative result (benefit flat or U-shaped): no ZPD structure.

Experiment 4 (H3 - CoT abbreviates as items approach mastery): Tests the internalization prediction. Data: within a fixed surface-difficulty band, items split into 'newly-in-ZPD' vs. 'approaching-mastery' by per-item direct accuracy; ~300 items/band. Models: same four, frozen. Decisive metric first: spontaneous CoT length; secondary: number of explicit steps and an ellipsis/compression score (operator-to-filler token ratio). Convincing result: CoT shortens and becomes more elliptical as items approach mastery (length and compression CIs excluding zero) within the matched surface band. Indecision band: length difference CI spanning zero with |effect| below one step - no measurable abbreviation. Negative result (CoT lengthens toward mastery): contradicts overt-to-covert internalization.

Experiment 5 (H4 - A self-difficulty probe supports a ZPD-gated controller that beats uniform reasoning): Tests the self-regulation payoff. Data: question-only early-layer hidden states (before any reasoning) for the 900 items, 70/30 item-disjoint split; controller evaluated on 300 held-out items. Models: same four, frozen; trainable component is a lightweight linear probe predicting calibrated difficulty (seeds 0/1/2). Systems compared: always-CoT, never-CoT, random-gated (matched CoT budget), matched-hardness difficulty/uncertainty-gated baselines (entropy-, margin-, and confidence-gated at matched budget), and ZPD-gated (emit CoT only when predicted difficulty is in the middle band); the probe and controller are tested for cross-model and cross-domain generalization (trained on one family/domain, evaluated on held-out ones). Decisive metric first: accuracy at matched token budget (and, jointly, the accuracy-vs-average-tokens frontier); secondary: probe AUROC/correlation for predicting difficulty. Convincing result: ZPD-gating matches or exceeds always-CoT accuracy (its 95% CI lower bound at or above always-CoT) at a fraction of the tokens, and beats random-gating at equal budget (difference CI excluding zero), with probe AUROC >=0.65. Indecision band: ZPD-gating within 1 accuracy point of random-gating at equal budget - the model's internal difficulty estimate adds no usable signal, so the controller is not justified even if the probe is weakly above chance. Negative result (ZPD-gating below never-CoT or below random-gating): self-regulated private speech is not a useful lever. All numbers are planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over items, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Instruction-tuned models may be strongly primed to always emit CoT, flattening the spontaneous inverted-U; we mitigate with permissive prompts, base/less-aligned models, and by measuring emission via willingness-to-abbreviate rather than raw presence. (2) 'Difficulty' calibrated from direct-answer error may conflate item difficulty with model-specific gaps; we calibrate per-model and also report the surface difficulty axis. (3) The inverted-U could be an artifact of length ceilings (max tokens) or format; we cap generously and length-control. (4) Interference (negative CoT benefit on mastered items) may be small or model-dependent; a monotonic (non-ZPD) result is itself informative, distinguishing LLM reasoning from human private speech. (5) The competence probe may capture surface features rather than genuine self-difficulty estimation; we test generalization across task families and use question-only (pre-reasoning) activations. (6) The developmental/private-speech framing is an analogy operationalized behaviorally, not a claim of human-like inner experience; we frame all findings behaviorally and mechanistically.

Name: future_tense_present_bias
Title: Does Grammar Make an LLM Impatient? Testing the Linguistic Savings Hypothesis Inside Language Models
Short Hypothesis: The famous Linguistic Savings Hypothesis (grammatically obligatory future-time reference makes speakers more present-biased) can be tested causally inside LLMs: framing the same intertemporal choice with strong future-tense grammar (a) increases the model's present-bias (steeper discounting) and (b) increases the internal represented psychological distance between 'now' and the future outcome, and steering along a latent future-distance direction reproduces or cancels this present-bias — providing the first mechanistic, causally-controlled test of whether grammatical future marking shapes machine intertemporal choice.
Related Work: Chen's Linguistic Savings Hypothesis (2013, 712 cites) correlated weak grammatical future-time reference (FTR) with higher savings; follow-up lab studies (2017, 2019) and a psycholinguistic framework (2023) find inconclusive/contested effects, limited by imperfect control over framing and confounds in human populations. Separately, interpretability work shows LLMs encode time as linear/curvilinear representations (Language Models Represent Space and Time, 2023; Time Travel Engine, 2026), exhibit human-like log-compressed temporal distance around a subjective 'now' (The Other Mind, 2025), and encode grammatical tense/aspect as steerable orthogonal directions (Steering Tense and Aspect, 2025). No prior work connects the FTR grammar hypothesis to LLM intertemporal CHOICE behavior, nor tests whether grammatical future framing causally alters the internal represented distance-to-future that drives discounting, nor uses latent-direction steering to isolate grammar's effect from content. Recent causal human studies fail to reproduce or reverse Chen's direction; we foreground these and frame the study as an empirical test of COMPETING SIGN predictions (present-bias increase vs. decrease vs. null), not a confirmation of Chen. The exact novel unit of analysis is a within-item, grammar-only manipulation of FTR on LLM intertemporal choice. The mechanistic novelty is distinguishing a specific future-DISTANCE representation (distance-to-outcome that scales discounting) from generic temporal/tense encoding: existing tense/aspect steering work moves grammatical tense directions but does not show they alter the represented distance that drives intertemporal CHOICE, which we test directly. We are the first to (1) operationalize FTR-strength as a within-item, content-matched framing manipulation, (2) link behavioral present-bias to internal temporal-distance geometry, (3) causally steer a future-distance direction to reproduce/cancel the effect, and (4) release a grammar-controlled intertemporal-choice benchmark, converting a contested socioeconomic correlation into a controlled mechanistic experiment and a reusable benchmark for causal language-to-decision effects.
Abstract: One of the most striking claims about language and thought is Chen's Linguistic Savings Hypothesis: languages that grammatically force speakers to mark the future as distinct from the present (strong future-time reference, FTR) foster more present-biased, impatient behavior. Human studies of this claim are contested because grammar cannot be cleanly separated from culture and economics. Large language models offer a controlled testbed: we can hold content constant and vary only grammatical future framing. We test whether the way an LLM is asked to talk about the future causally changes how impatiently it chooses. We construct matched intertemporal-choice items (sooner-smaller vs. later-larger rewards over money, health, and effort) and render each in weak-FTR framing (present-tense/futureless phrasing) versus strong-FTR framing (obligatory, explicit future marking), plus a native cross-lingual variant across languages spanning the FTR spectrum (Chinese/German=weak, English/Spanish=strong). Behaviorally, we estimate each model's discount rate and present-bias per framing and test whether strong-FTR framing steepens discounting. Mechanistically, using probes on temporal representations we measure the internal 'psychological distance' the model assigns to the future outcome and test whether strong-FTR framing inflates it, correlating this distance with behavioral impatience. Finally, we isolate a latent future-distance direction and steer along it to causally induce or cancel present-bias, comparing against random-direction and content-matched controls. We state one PRIMARY hypothesis (H1: within-item strong-FTR framing changes present-bias on identical content) and treat the cross-lingual, representational, and steering analyses as secondary/exploratory, pre-registering the estimand for each (choice-logit shift, discount-rate shift, or mediation via the distance probe). Beyond adjudicating Chen, the work matters for prompt sensitivity and controllable temporal bias - e.g., deliberately shifting a model toward patience for long-horizon agentic planning prompts - and speaks to distinct audiences: linguistics, interpretability, agentic planning, and model-based cognitive science. A positive result yields a controllable lever on temporal preference; a null or sign-reversed result is the cleanest evidence to date against a mechanistic reading of the Linguistic Savings Hypothesis. Across several open-weight models we quantify the FTR present-bias effect, its dissociation from mere accuracy, the distance-to-behavior link, and steering controllability, delivering the first mechanistic adjudication of a famous linguistic-relativity claim and a benchmark for causal language-to-decision effects.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup - Intertemporal-choice battery): Prerequisite. Data: a built battery of ~400 base items, each a binary choice between a sooner-smaller and a later-larger reward, spanning three domains (money, health, effort) and a grid of delays (1 week to 5 years) and reward ratios, enabling per-model discount-rate estimation via hyperbolic/exponential fits. Decisive metric first: coverage of the delay x ratio grid sufficient to fit a stable discount curve (bootstrap SE on the discount rate). Convincing result: the grid yields discount-rate fits with tight SEs and choices spanning both options (no ceiling/floor). Indecision band: many items at ceiling/floor (one option always chosen) - we widen the ratio/delay grid. Negative result: choices are option-invariant, and the battery is redesigned to avoid saturation.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Strong future-time-reference framing steepens discounting): The central behavioral test, holding content constant. Data: each of the 400 items rendered in (a) weak-FTR framing (present-tense/futureless phrasing, e.g., 'you receive X in a year') and (b) strong-FTR framing (obligatory explicit future marking, e.g., 'you WILL receive X, one year from now, in the future'), verified by an independent FTR-strength rating; content, numbers, and delays held identical and framings matched on sentence length, lexical frequency, semantic valence, and prompt format (verified by independent ratings) so that only grammatical future marking varies. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Aya-23-8B, all weights frozen; choices and a separately-elicited indifference point collected, 5 samples/item, temperature 0.7, seeds 0/1/2. Systems compared: strong- vs. weak-FTR framing within item. A pre-registered power analysis sets items and samples for the target FTR effect size, with a documented failure-mode plan for null or sign-reversed outcomes. Decisive metric first: the FTR-strength coefficient on discounting/present-bias in a mixed-effects model (choice/discount ~ FTR_strength + delay + ratio + domain + (1|model) + (1|item)), stratified by decision consistency. Convincing result: strong-FTR framing yields significantly steeper discounting / more sooner-smaller choices (FTR coefficient 95% CI excluding zero) in at least 3 of 5 models, not explained by decision-consistency differences. Indecision band: FTR coefficient CI spanning zero with a standardized effect below 0.1 - grammatical future framing does not measurably move impatience, the cleanest evidence to date against a mechanistic reading of the Linguistic Savings Hypothesis in this controlled setting. Negative result (strong-FTR framing makes the model more patient): the hypothesized direction is reversed.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Native cross-lingual FTR variant): Tests that native grammatical FTR reproduces the within-item framing effect. Data: the items translated (back-translation checked) into languages spanning the FTR spectrum (Chinese, German = weak-FTR; English, Spanish = strong-FTR). Models: same five, frozen; all cross-lingual analyses accuracy/consistency-stratified. Decisive metric first: the FTR-strength coefficient across native languages, controlling for a resource-level covariate. Convincing result: native strong-FTR languages show steeper discounting than weak-FTR languages after stratification (coefficient CI excluding zero), converging with Experiment 2. Indecision band: coefficient CI spanning zero once resource level is controlled - cross-lingual differences are competence-driven, so the within-item framing test (Experiment 2) remains the primary evidence. Negative result (reversed cross-lingual ordering): the native-grammar prediction fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 - Strong-FTR framing inflates internal represented future-distance, which tracks impatience): Mechanistic representational test. Data: hidden states on the future-outcome mention across framings. Models: same five, frozen; trainable component is a temporal-distance probe (following prior space-and-time representation work) validated on held-out delays and against alternative probe families (linear vs. nonlinear, and a control probe predicting surface delay tokens), so the probe tracks represented psychological distance rather than surface tokens (seeds 0/1/2), matched positions, multiple layers. Decisive metric first: represented distance-from-now for the delayed outcome, tested for inflation under strong-FTR framing; secondary: per-item Spearman correlation between represented distance and behavioral impatience. Convincing result: strong-FTR framing significantly inflates represented future-distance (CI excluding zero) and per-item distance correlates with impatience (Spearman CI excluding zero). Indecision band: distance-inflation CI spanning zero - framing does not move the internal distance representation, so any behavioral effect is not mediated by represented distance. Negative result (strong-FTR compresses represented distance): contradicts the mediation account.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Steering a future-distance direction induces or cancels present-bias): Causal test. Data: 300 held-out items (disjoint from probe validation). Models: same five, frozen; a 'future-distance' direction discovered via difference-in-means between near- and far-future outcome representations (and between weak- vs. strong-FTR framings of identical items), with the discovery protocol and layer selection fixed in advance; strength tuned on a dev split, seeds 0/1/2. Ablations steer against random, reward-magnitude, and nonspecific latent directions of matched norm. Systems compared: +direction steering (increase represented distance), -direction steering (decrease it), no-steer, random-direction steering (matched norm), and a content-matched reward-magnitude-direction control. Decisive metric first: induced change in present-bias (beta) parameter; secondary: fraction of the FTR framing effect reproduced (+) or cancelled (-). Convincing result: +steering increases present-bias and -steering cancels the strong-FTR framing effect, significantly beyond random-direction and reward-magnitude controls (difference CI excluding zero). Indecision band: steering effect within the control directions' CIs - present-bias is not controllable via this direction, so the mechanistic link is unproven even if Experiments 2 and 4 hold. Negative result (steering has no effect or destroys coherent choice behavior): no causal handle on grammar-induced impatience. All quantities are planned evidence with bootstrap CIs over items, seeds, and models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Instruction-tuned models may answer intertemporal choices in a rigid, framing-insensitive way, yielding null behavioral effects; we mitigate with graded reward ratios/delays to avoid ceiling/floor, multiple models including base variants, and per-item indifference elicitation. (2) Strong- vs weak-FTR framings may differ in length/emphasis rather than grammar per se; we length-match, use independent FTR-strength ratings, and rely on the native cross-lingual variant plus content-matched steering to isolate grammar. (3) Cross-lingual differences confound grammar with training-data resource level; all cross-lingual analyses are accuracy/consistency-stratified and the English within-item framing manipulation (same language, only grammar varies) is the primary test. (4) Temporal-distance probes may capture surface delay tokens rather than psychological distance; we use held-out probe validation, matched positions, and multiple layers. (5) The future-distance steering direction may entangle with reward magnitude or generic content; random-direction and reward-magnitude-direction controls address this. (6) A null result (grammatical framing does not shift LLM present-bias) is itself informative — it would provide the cleanest evidence to date against a mechanistic reading of the Linguistic Savings Hypothesis, since human confounds are absent here.
